prompt: Write a novel about a teenage heroine who grows up and ends up changing the world

outline.name: The City Above
outline.description: Seventeen-year-old Mara Venn is introduced in Lumen, a glittering floating city above the drowned London basin. As an apprentice cartographer, she maps transit routes, maintenance corridors, citizenship tiers, and restricted districts. Her fascination with the hidden connections beneath official maps contrasts with the Council’s insistence that the mainland is dead. Mara’s family life is established: her mother Sela repairs filtration membranes, her father died years earlier in an alleged accident, and her younger brother Eli suffers from a chronic respiratory condition. Mara believes Lumen’s harsh social order is necessary for humanity’s survival, though small inconsistencies in the city’s maps begin to trouble her.

outline.name: The Treatment
outline.description: Eli’s breathing worsens, and Mara accompanies Sela to a clinic seeking a newly developed treatment. The administrator explains that the medicine is restricted to citizens with higher status or greater occupational value. Mara sees doses being stored behind the clinic counter while Eli is denied care. She argues with the administrator and learns that medical access, housing, and even family size are controlled by citizenship tier. Sela warns Mara not to challenge the system, fearing that their family could lose its remaining privileges. Eli tries to reassure Mara, but his worsening cough makes the injustice impossible for her to ignore.

outline.name: Lines on a Map
outline.description: Mara returns to the Office of Cartography and struggles to concentrate while mapping new restrictions around the lower residential rings. Master Orin Vale praises her technical talent but cautions her against questioning the political meaning of official boundaries. Mara notices that supply routes serving elite districts are absent from public maps and that old maps contain erased coastal markings. She begins considering the abandoned archives beneath the office as a possible source of medical records. At home, Sela considers selling citizenship credits to pay for Eli’s treatment, a decision that would endanger their housing and legal protections.

outline.name: The Sealed Archive
outline.description: Mara uses her maintenance access to enter the forbidden archive levels after hours. She searches obsolete medical files for a treatment comparable to Eli’s, navigating damaged storage rooms and automated security systems. Instead of medical records, she finds pre-Continuance environmental surveys and maps that contradict Lumen’s official history. Satellite images show lights and cultivated land on the supposedly lifeless continents. The discovery unsettles her, but she convinces herself the files may be outdated or falsified. She copies several records before a second person enters the archive.

outline.name: The Boy from Broadcast
outline.description: The intruder is Tomas Rusk, a junior communications aide and son of Council Minister Rusk. He recognizes the archive files as classified and initially threatens to report Mara. Their argument reveals their opposing assumptions: Mara believes maps should show reality, while Tomas believes dangerous truths must be managed by authorities. He quietly admits that his mother died from a treatable illness despite their family’s elite status, creating a crack in his loyalty. When security begins searching the archive, Tomas helps Mara hide and escape. Their reluctant alliance begins when he agrees to investigate the medical records in exchange for seeing what she found.

outline.name: The World Below
outline.description: Mara and Tomas decode the copied files and discover that the oceans around the former British coast are receding. Reports from survey drones describe coastal settlements, farms, and functioning communities across the mainland. Further documents reveal that Lumen’s atmospheric stabilizers release concentrated greenhouse gases and toxic particulates toward the surface. A concealed Council memorandum calls the resulting suffering an acceptable containment cost. The final files describe the Crown Seal, a planned system that would permanently enclose Lumen and accelerate global ecological collapse. Mara’s faith in Lumen’s leaders breaks, but she still wants to use the evidence to obtain Eli’s medicine rather than expose the entire city.

outline.name: A Bargain with the Clinic
outline.description: Mara and Tomas attempt to pressure the clinic by threatening to reveal proof of withheld medicine and falsified public health reports. The administrator alerts the Council instead. Eli is removed from the family’s care and transferred to a restricted ward, while Sela is arrested for attempting to obtain unauthorized treatment. Mara returns home to find their apartment sealed and their citizenship credits frozen. Tomas realizes that his family’s influence cannot protect him from the consequences of the archive breach. He creates a false maintenance order that grants Mara temporary access to the restricted hospital levels, and together they plan to free Sela and escape.

outline.name: The Descent Capsule
outline.description: Mara and Tomas release Sela from a transport holding area but cannot reach Eli, who is moved before they arrive. Sela insists that Mara leave with the evidence rather than surrender. Using Tomas’s codes, they reach an external service deck and enter a cargo descent capsule meant for repair crews. Lumen’s security forces detect the theft, and the capsule launches under fire. Mara experiences terror as the floating city recedes above the clouds, while Tomas watches the propaganda screens continue describing the mainland as uninhabitable. The capsule loses control during descent and crashes near the ruins of Tilbury.

outline.name: The Living Shore
outline.description: Mara and Tomas are rescued from the wreck by a coastal settlement built among the elevated remains of Tilbury’s transport hub. They meet Imani Okafor, a former Lumen atmospheric engineer who now directs the settlement’s water and power cooperative, and Nia Vale, a teenage boat mechanic. The settlement’s working gardens, fog nets, reed-bed purifiers, and communal workshops immediately challenge Mara’s belief that the mainland is dead. Imani distrusts both fugitives, especially Tomas, whose family helped spread propaganda against surface communities. She agrees to shelter them temporarily but demands that they contribute labor while their motives are investigated.

outline.name: What Ignorance Costs
outline.description: Mara works in the settlement’s mapping room and discovers that Lumen’s climate network has damaged the region’s water and soil. She meets children suffering from illnesses associated with atmospheric toxins, forcing her to confront the human consequences of the system that supported her life. Nia challenges Mara’s assumptions about education, intelligence, and civilization, while Tomas is publicly confronted by families who recognize his father’s broadcasts. Imani explains that she fled Lumen after uncovering falsified emissions data and being blamed for a deadly array malfunction. Mara admits that her ignorance benefited her, even though she never chose the policy that caused the harm.

outline.name: The Cooperative
outline.description: Mara learns how the Tilbury community makes decisions through rotating councils and shared labor rather than permanent authority. A dispute over stored water shows that cooperation is difficult and requires accountability, not simple goodwill. Mara helps map a leaking distribution network, earning practical trust from residents. Tomas struggles with the absence of fixed hierarchy and repeatedly suggests centralized solutions. Imani tells them that the mainland is not an idealized alternative: communities have fought, hoarded resources, and been manipulated by Lumen. Still, its people have survived by sharing knowledge. A coded radio message summons Imani to a wider network meeting.

outline.name: The Network of Shorelines
outline.description: Imani takes Mara, Tomas, and Nia through a network of settlements linked by tidal routes, old rail lines, and encrypted radio. Mara sees flooded cities repurposed as schools, hospitals, and archives, as well as desert settlements harvesting underground ice and island federations operating converted cargo ships. Each community has adapted differently, but all exchange data and supplies. Mara begins producing maps collaboratively with residents rather than imposing Lumen’s classifications. At a former university, scientists reveal that climate recovery remains possible if the Crown Seal is stopped. The group learns that the Council plans to activate it within months.

outline.name: The Relay Station
outline.description: Imani leads the group to an abandoned mainland relay station where she once worked on Lumen’s atmospheric network. They recover fragments of the original control architecture and discover that the Crown Seal’s activation has already begun. The system is designed to make Lumen dependent on the very enclosure that will poison the planet. Archived maintenance logs reveal that sections of the city are being quietly evacuated, with lower-tier families sent to dangerous mainland work colonies. One transfer list includes Eli, who has been moved to a research hospital as a test subject. Mara’s personal crisis becomes inseparable from the larger struggle.

outline.name: The Argument
outline.description: The group debates whether to attack Lumen’s climate network immediately. Imani argues that dismantling the system may be the only way to stop the Crown Seal, even if thousands inside the city lose air, water, or buoyancy support. Mara insists that Lumen’s ordinary citizens cannot be treated as part of the regime and that they must be given a chance to act. Tomas supports her but is shaken when a mainland faction proposes assassinating Council leaders and calls civilian casualties unavoidable. The debate exposes their different understandings of sacrifice, justice, and responsibility. They agree to infiltrate Lumen, broadcast the truth, rescue Eli, and attempt a controlled conversion.

outline.name: The Route Beneath the Thames
outline.description: Mara uses old cartographic records to identify a maintenance tunnel beneath the drowned Thames that connects to Lumen’s lower infrastructure. The group prepares for the return journey, gathering technical equipment and establishing relay contacts across the mainland. Nia insists on joining despite Imani’s concern about her age, arguing that the outer platforms require mechanics who know improvised systems. Mara records a public statement but cannot find words that do not sound like propaganda. Before departure, she receives confirmation that Eli is alive but undergoing dangerous atmospheric experiments. The team enters the submerged tunnel as Council patrols begin searching the coast.

outline.name: Return to Lumen
outline.description: The group reaches Lumen through abandoned infrastructure and disguises themselves as maintenance workers. Mara is struck by the city’s familiarity: transit music, crowded markets, school groups, and gardens still glowing beneath artificial sunlight. Her sympathy grows as she realizes that most citizens are frightened and dependent, not malicious. Former colleagues in the Broadcast Ministry secretly assist Tomas, while others report suspicious activity out of fear. Sela’s location is unknown, and Eli’s hospital transfer is imminent. Mara begins marking safe routes and resource stores on an illegal map intended for public use.

outline.name: The Lower Rings
outline.description: Mara and Nia move through the lower residential rings, where workers suffer failing air filters and ration cuts while the upper districts prepare for the Crown Seal celebration. Sela has been released but is forced into unpaid filtration labor under threat of losing housing. She reunites with Mara and learns that Eli has been moved to the central research hospital. Sela refuses to blame her daughter for leaving, but warns that exposing the truth could make Lumen’s descent chaotic and deadly. Mara sees people organizing quietly around shared shortages, suggesting that resistance already exists beneath the Council’s control.

outline.name: The Father’s Secret
outline.description: Tomas confronts Minister Rusk in the Broadcast Ministry, hoping to use family access to obtain Eli’s location and emergency channel codes. His father claims that secrecy protected humanity from panic and insists that the mainland communities would destroy Lumen if admitted into the city. He reveals that Mara’s father did not die in an accident: he was killed after attempting to sabotage an early climate array and expose its emissions. The Council concealed the murder and used the tragedy to recruit Tomas’s father into its inner circle. Mara struggles with anger, grief, and pride when Tomas tells her what he learned.

outline.name: The Hospital of Useful Lives
outline.description: Mara, Imani, and Nia infiltrate the research hospital while Tomas remains in the Ministry. They find Eli among patients being used to test atmospheric adaptation treatments, including medicines that Lumen has withheld from lower-tier families. Imani identifies a mainland-developed treatment that can stabilize him, but the hospital lacks the correct equipment and time. Mara discovers records showing that the Council has classified certain citizens as expendable test populations. The group rescues Eli and several other patients, but security detects the breach. They retreat toward the central tower with the medicine, the patients, and evidence of the experiments.

outline.name: A Truth Too Large
outline.description: The resistance cell prepares the broadcast from the Ministry’s emergency studio. Mara wants to release every document immediately, but Imani warns that raw evidence without a credible alternative could trigger panic, violence, and the destruction of critical infrastructure. They assemble testimony from mainland communities, medical records, climate data, and technical plans for converting the network. Sela organizes medical workers to prepare emergency clinics, while Lumen technicians begin quietly disabling Crown Seal stations. Tomas must decide whether to expose his father publicly and risk losing access to the channels they need.

outline.name: The First Broadcast
outline.description: Mara begins the broadcast and shows Lumen citizens images of living mainland communities, rising forests, functioning clinics, and children who have been harmed by the city’s emissions. Council systems interrupt the transmission, and Minister Rusk declares Mara a terrorist attempting to destroy Lumen. Tomas seizes emergency channels and counters the interruption with the founders’ signed records, hidden evacuation lists, and proof of medical withholding. For the first time, Lumen sees the mainland as inhabited by real people rather than monsters from official lessons. The transmission spreads across illicit networks before security forces can shut it down.

outline.name: The City Divides
outline.description: The broadcast ignites protests throughout Lumen. Lower-tier workers occupy transit hubs and clinics, while some elite citizens demand that the Council seal the city and proceed with activation. Schools close, food distribution falters, and security forces clash with protesters. Across the mainland, communities mobilize to protect refugees and block Council supply routes, but some factions call for immediate retaliation. Mara is horrified that truth has not produced unity. She uses the map network to publish safe routes, food stores, and open medical centers, turning information into a practical tool for survival.

outline.name: The Crown Seal Begins
outline.description: The Council initiates the Crown Seal ahead of schedule, claiming that unrest proves the need for permanent isolation. Atmospheric pressure changes ripple through Lumen, causing structural failures and violent weather across the North Atlantic. Imani reaches the central control chamber and discovers that simply shutting down the system will make the city lose altitude. The Council has deliberately designed the network so that Lumen cannot safely disconnect. Mara studies the architecture and identifies a possible third option: redirecting the buoyancy and climate load through abandoned mainland relay stations, converting the enclosure into an open regulator.

outline.name: No Single Hero
outline.description: Mara presents the conversion plan to engineers in Lumen and across the mainland. It requires simultaneous cooperation from dozens of relay stations, manual repairs on outer platforms, medical preparation, and volunteers willing to guide citizens through a dangerous descent. Imani warns that someone must coordinate the central system continuously. Mara initially volunteers to remain behind, and Tomas argues that he should take the risk instead. Their conflict reveals their shared tendency to turn responsibility into heroic sacrifice. They create a distributed command structure so that no one person controls the outcome or becomes the movement’s indispensable symbol.

outline.name: The Emergency Channels
outline.description: Tomas confronts his father in the Broadcast Ministry and demands access to the emergency channels. Minister Rusk refuses, still insisting that order requires obedience. Security forces loyal to the Council begin firing on protesters, including elite families who have attempted to leave restricted districts. Seeing that the regime will sacrifice anyone necessary, Rusk finally releases the authorization codes. He broadcasts the mainland relay coordinates and admits that the city’s official history was manufactured. Security officers shoot him, and Tomas must continue the operation while hearing his father die over the open channel.

outline.name: The Outer Platforms
outline.description: Nia leads a team of young mechanics across Lumen’s exposed outer platforms to repair relay cables and redirect damaged buoyancy engines. They face failing walkways, toxic condensate, and automated defenses still following Council commands. Nia’s practical knowledge and willingness to trust volunteers allow workers from rival citizenship tiers to cooperate. On the mainland, engineers begin activating corresponding relays while communities evacuate low-lying settlements. Mara guides the teams through service routes using maps she once produced for bureaucratic control. The city begins to descend, and every delay threatens a catastrophic fall.

outline.name: Open Doors
outline.description: As the descent begins, Sela organizes medical workers to treat injured protesters, Council officers, and frightened elite citizens without checking status. Mara broadcasts instructions to open sealed gardens, share oxygen reserves, unlock emergency shelters, and ignore citizenship restrictions. Some citizens respond with generosity; others hoard food and attack mainland refugees. The resistance must prevent both security forces and desperate crowds from destroying essential infrastructure. Eli, stabilized by the mainland treatment, helps identify hospital resources and communicates with other patients. The city’s old social order starts collapsing faster than any replacement can form.

outline.name: The Storm Wall
outline.description: The Crown Seal partially activates, creating a vast atmospheric disturbance over the North Atlantic. Weather systems twist toward Lumen and the coastal settlements, threatening to destroy both. The mainland relay teams lose contact with several stations, and the central control system begins making contradictory adjustments. Imani discovers that the final manual array must be aligned from an exposed platform. Mara tries to keep the distributed teams coordinated while Tomas handles a flood of conflicting reports. The storm’s approach forces them to choose between a risky conversion attempt and abandoning the city’s outer systems.

outline.name: The Broken Bridge
outline.description: Imani reaches the final control array but is trapped when an access bridge collapses. Mara has a clear route to the central chamber and could complete the conversion without her, but doing so would leave the final alignment uncertain. She turns back despite Imani’s order to continue. Together they cross damaged platforms while the city tilts beneath them. Tomas coordinates volunteers to lower equipment through the broadcast network, and Nia redirects a failing engine. Mara and Imani reach the array just as the storm wall begins to form over the exposed mainland.

outline.name: The Descent
outline.description: Mara and Imani manually align the final relays while mainland communities activate the converted network. Lumen shudders as the Crown Seal changes from enclosure to atmospheric dispersion. Toxic condensate floods the lower rings, and Mara uses her maps to guide citizens toward safe zones. Tomas broadcasts instructions and connects isolated communities despite repeated signal failures. The floating city descends toward the drowned foundations of old London. At the last moment, the buoyancy load disperses through the mainland relays, stabilizing Lumen above the exposed ruins rather than allowing it to crash into the sea. The storm weakens before reaching the coast.

outline.name: After the Fall
outline.description: The immediate crisis ends, but thousands are dead, injured, displaced, or missing. Lumen’s structures are damaged, its food systems disrupted, and its former Council dissolved or in hiding. Mainland communities arrive to provide aid, yet many residents distrust them and blame Mara for the destruction. Former elite families attempt to preserve their privileges under new administrative names, while surface factions demand punishment and reparations. Mara refuses to declare victory. She helps establish emergency councils and insists that survival decisions include both Lumen citizens and mainland representatives.

outline.name: The Open Archive
outline.description: Mara becomes a public symbol, celebrated by some as the Cartographer of Truth and condemned by others as a terrorist. She rejects offers of permanent authority and instead creates an open archive containing Council orders, climate data, maps, medical research, and testimony from survivors. Master Orin Vale joins her after admitting that he helped conceal politically inconvenient routes. The archive becomes contested territory: some want to restrict records to prevent renewed conflict, while Mara argues that hidden knowledge enabled the old regime. Eli survives but remains weak, reminding everyone that political liberation cannot undo individual damage.

outline.name: The Tribunals
outline.description: Public tribunals begin for Council officials, security commanders, and administrators who enforced the citizenship tiers. Tomas testifies against his father’s allies and exposes the Broadcast Ministry’s methods. The process divides the new alliance between those seeking revenge and those demanding strict legal standards. Mara struggles when witnesses reveal that people she trusted benefited from the system. Imani argues that accountability must include repair, not only punishment. Sela helps survivors obtain medical care and legal representation. The tribunals establish a fragile principle: no future government may control justice through secret classifications or inaccessible records.

outline.name: The First Fracture
outline.description: The alliance breaks over control of Lumen’s remaining energy systems and the distribution of stored supplies. A mainland federation attempts to seize the central generators, claiming that Lumen owes the world everything it possesses. Lumen workers resist, fearing another outside authority. Mara mediates poorly, pushing a rapid redistribution plan that ignores local concerns and deepens the conflict. Sabotage damages a power station, causing deaths and forcing her to acknowledge that good intentions can reproduce coercion when imposed from above. She begins developing a decision process based on shared data, rotating authority, and negotiated timelines rather than emergency command.

outline.name: The Prison Map
outline.description: A Lumen faction opposed to mainland integration imprisons Mara and accuses her of betraying the city by revealing its technology. In confinement, she meets citizens who supported the Council because they feared mainland retaliation and others who resent Mara’s public influence. Instead of trying to persuade them with speeches, she teaches them to read the city’s infrastructure maps and trace how scarcity was manufactured. A guard secretly provides evidence of remaining sabotage cells. Mara realizes that changing the world means building institutions that can survive disagreement, including the disagreement of people who distrust her.

outline.name: The Engineering Cooperative
outline.description: After her release, Mara helps Imani establish a planetary engineering cooperative. Its purpose is to dismantle the harmful climate arrays, restore wetlands and forests, and keep all environmental data publicly accessible. Imani recruits former Lumen technicians alongside mainland engineers, forcing both groups to confront old resentments. Tomas rebuilds the communications network and creates channels that cannot be controlled by a single ministry. Nia launches an apprenticeship program connecting young people from the floating city and coastal settlements. Eli begins medical training, determined to make treatment available according to need rather than rank.

outline.name: The Drought Year
outline.description: Several years later, a severe drought in North Africa threatens to revive the old politics of hoarding and exclusion. Communities argue over water, migration, and the use of restored atmospheric technology. Some leaders propose closing borders and reserving supplies for citizens of their own federations. Mara travels between councils, presenting shared climate models and helping negotiate voluntary migration corridors. She makes another mistake by trusting a charismatic regional leader who secretly diverts water. The betrayal nearly destroys the alliance, but open records and independent local observers expose it before violence spreads. The crisis demonstrates that cooperation must be continually practiced, not merely declared.

outline.name: A Harbor, Not a Fortress
outline.description: Over the next decade, Lumen is physically and politically transformed. Its former elite towers become hospitals, schools, laboratories, and public workshops. Bridges, ferries, and restored rail lines connect the city to the mainland. Citizenship tiers disappear unevenly, resisted by families who benefited from them, while voluntary migration allows people to choose where they can contribute and belong. Mara’s living maps are created by communities rather than officials and include languages, ecological systems, care networks, and unresolved questions. She and Tomas debate whether the alliance is becoming too bureaucratic, while Imani reminds them that durable structures must outlast their founders.

outline.name: The First Generation
outline.description: Two decades after the descent, Mara is an adult whose life has been shaped by organizing, travel, failure, and compromise rather than a single triumphant revolution. Eli works as a physician at a clinic that treats patients without regard to status. Tomas teaches history and requires students to study his own role in propaganda. Imani, older and increasingly frail, continues advising the engineering cooperative. Nia becomes a respected leader in the apprenticeship network. At a restored school in the London basin, children born after Lumen’s transformation study the full history of the drowned city, the mainland, and the Crown Seal.

outline.name: What We Have Not Discovered
outline.description: At the school’s opening ceremony, Mara is asked to speak about the day she changed the world. She rejects the idea that one person transformed history and explains that change began when separated communities exchanged knowledge and chose one another’s survival. She describes safety purchased through another person’s suffering as only a more elaborate danger. At dawn, she stands on Lumen’s upper deck and sees forests returning along the retreating shoreline, ferries crossing between settlements, and the former fortress functioning as a connected harbor. Children unfold an incomplete map filled with blank spaces and questions. Mara kneels beside them and asks what they have not yet discovered. They begin drawing new routes across the page, linking places once kept apart.

chapters.name: The City Above
chapters.content:
At dawn, Lumen cast no shadow.

The city floated above the cloud deck on a lattice of buoyancy engines and pressure chambers, its underside hidden in silver vapor. From the upper observatory, Mara Venn could see only the bright curve of the world: cloud, light, and the faint blue line of the Atlantic beyond. The mainland was somewhere under the white, drowned and empty, according to every lesson she had ever been given.

She preferred the city’s lower levels, where things had edges.

At six seventeen, Mara stepped off the maintenance tram into the Office of Cartography and pressed her palm to the access plate. The door recognized her work band, unlocked, and admitted her into a corridor that smelled of hot wiring, dust, and the bitter tea Master Vale kept forgetting to drink.

“Late,” said Orin Vale.

Mara glanced at the wall clock. “I’m two minutes early.”

“You’re late according to the map.”

He stood beneath the morning projection, a translucent city suspended in the air between them. Lumen rotated slowly: concentric residential rings, silver transit lines, the green-lit gardens of the upper districts, and the dark infrastructure beneath. Official maps made the city look like a perfect wheel.

Mara knew it was not.

“The east service route changed overnight,” she said. “Transit Control closed Gate Twelve.”

“Gate Twelve is not part of today’s assignment.”

“It intersects the southern filter corridor.”

“Then the southern filter corridor is not part of today’s assignment either.”

Master Vale said this mildly, almost kindly. He was a narrow man with white hair clipped close to his skull and a habit of tapping his stylus against his thumb when someone said something inconvenient. “You are mapping public transit access, Apprentice Venn. Not investigating every door that fails to open.”

Mara looked back at the projection. “If the route is closed, the public map will be wrong.”

“The route is restricted.”

“That’s different from closed.”

Vale’s stylus stopped tapping.

For a moment the only sound was the hum of the projection engine. Beneath them, beyond the office floor, Lumen woke in layers. Pumps engaged. Kitchens vented steam. Trams slid from their docks with the soft electric whine of something too expensive to rattle.

Vale reached into the projection and pinched the east service route out of existence.

“Use the approved boundary,” he said.

Mara lowered her eyes. “Yes, Master Vale.”

The map brightened as he adjusted the view. A blue line appeared across the lower residential rings, clean and unbroken. It led from the workers’ dormitories to the central market, bypassed the filtration plant, and ended at a checkpoint marked with the white star of the Civic Guard.

Mara knew the route had three gates, not one. She knew the second gate had been closed for eleven days, because she passed it each morning on the tram. She knew water workers were being redirected through an unheated maintenance tunnel, because her mother had come home with frostbite on two fingers.

None of that belonged on the public map.

She sat at her station and pulled the city’s layers around her.

Transit. Utilities. Housing. Citizenship classification.

The last layer always made her uncomfortable, though she had never admitted it aloud. Lumen’s citizens were arranged by tier, each tier represented in a different shade of gold. Founders’ families occupied the upper rings, where the air was cleanest and the gardens grew beneath filtered sunlight. Technical citizens lived closer to the engines. Labor citizens filled the lower rings, where the walls sweated condensation and the filters were replaced only when the maintenance schedule allowed it.

Mara’s family was Tier Four: essential labor, limited mobility, provisional medical access.

She had once asked her mother why the word provisional appeared on their household card.

“Because everything can be taken away,” Sela had said.

She had been repairing a filtration membrane at the kitchen table. The membrane lay spread before her like a thin, translucent skin, its fibers shining blue beneath the work lamp. Mara had been twelve then, old enough to understand that their apartment, their food allocation, and Eli’s clinic appointments all depended on Sela’s work remaining essential.

Old enough to understand, but not old enough to argue.

Now Mara traced the gold boundaries on her screen. She connected each checkpoint to its nearest transit station, then added the service corridors hidden beneath the official grid. Her map bloomed with small lines that no citizen would ever see.

The city was full of secret routes.

Some were secret because they carried oxygen, water, waste, or power. Some were secret because Council officials preferred them that way. And some, Mara suspected, were secret because the city would look less orderly if anyone saw how much of it depended on people moving through places they were not supposed to enter.

She liked those routes best.

At eight, the office windows brightened. The artificial sun rose over Lumen’s central tower, spilling amber light across the desks. In the distance, the suspended gardens opened their petals, each flower a solar collector disguised as beauty. A flock of maintenance drones moved between the towers, their rotors flashing.

Beyond the glass, the clouds parted.

For less than a minute, Mara saw the world below.

Water spread across the basin in a broad gray sheet. Towers protruded from it like broken teeth. The old London district—if the ruins below were London—lay half submerged and softened by distance. Around it, the ocean reached inland through what had once been streets.

Then the clouds closed.

“Don’t stare,” said Tavi, the apprentice at the next station.

“I wasn’t.”

“You were.”

Mara returned to her screen. “Did you see anything?”

“Nothing worth seeing.”

Tavi’s family lived in the Third Ring. His father worked for the Broadcast Ministry, and his mother had once been a Council archivist. He wore his citizenship band openly, a polished strip of gold around his wrist. Mara’s band was gray, with a narrow blue mark indicating technical aptitude.

“Master Vale says the mainland is uninhabitable,” Tavi continued.

“He’s right.”

“He says there are no stable settlements below the cloud line.”

“That’s what I said.”

Tavi leaned closer. “My little sister’s class watched a survey recording yesterday. It showed trees.”

“Old footage.”

“It showed a river.”

“Old rivers still exist.”

“Doesn’t matter,” Tavi said. “If anything lived down there, the Council would know.”

Mara watched the blue line of the official route pulse on her screen.

Of course they would know. The Council monitored every atmospheric current, every salvage zone, every weather pattern across the North Atlantic. Lumen had survived because its leaders made decisions based on more information than ordinary citizens could bear.

That was what Mara believed.

The city could not afford panic. It could not afford people demanding access to places they did not understand, medicine that had not been allocated to them, or air that had not been measured. Every resource had a limit. Every map needed a border.

“Trees don’t prove habitation,” she said.

Tavi grinned. “You sound like a lesson.”

Mara saved her route and began the next layer.

By midday, her eyes ached from projection light. She took the tram down through six residential rings, then walked the remaining distance to the southern filter district.

Lumen’s lower levels were always warmer than the upper city and somehow colder. Heat from the engines collected in the corridors, while drafts slipped through seams in the walls. The air tasted metallic. Advertisements glowed above the walkways:

SERVICE IS SURVIVAL.

REPORT UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS.

A HEALTHY CITY IS A DISCIPLINED CITY.

Mara passed beneath the slogans carrying a packet of ration bread and a replacement coil for her mother. The coil was wrapped in paper stamped with the Office of Filtration’s seal. Sela had sent her a message during the morning shift.

Need coil before evening. Don’t let Eli climb the west stairs.

Mara had sent back: I won’t.

She found Sela in the membrane workshop, standing beneath a bank of ultraviolet lamps. Her mother wore a white repair apron streaked with chemical dye. Her dark hair had escaped its tie and clung to her forehead.

“You came,” Sela said.

“You asked me to.”

“I ask you not to come too.”

“That usually means you need something.”

Sela took the coil from her. “You’re learning sarcasm.”

“Eli is home?”

“He should be.”

The workshop doors opened onto a narrow residential passage. By the time Mara reached their apartment, she could hear Eli coughing.

He was sitting on the floor beside the heater, his back against the wall. He had a school tablet open in his lap, though its screen had gone dark. At twelve, he was all elbows and solemn eyes, with a respirator looped around his neck instead of over his mouth.

Mara dropped beside him. “How long?”

He tried to wave her away. “I’m fine.”

“How long?”

“Since lunch.”

Sela came in behind her and set the coil on the counter. “Eli, mask.”

“I can breathe.”

“You’re coughing.”

“That doesn’t mean I can’t breathe.”

“It means put on the mask.”

He obeyed, though he did it with exaggerated annoyance. Mara checked the seal around his mouth and nose, then activated the small monitor clipped to his collar. The display showed his oxygen saturation wavering just below the recommended line.

Sela saw it too.

“Clinic,” she said.

Eli groaned. “Again?”

“You need the inhalant.”

“They’ll say my allocation is used.”

“Then we’ll speak to them.”

Mara knew that tone. Sela only used it when she was frightened.

Their apartment occupied the far end of a Tier Four block, two rooms and a narrow kitchen tucked beneath a ventilation shaft. The ceiling trembled whenever the upper transit loop passed overhead. On the wall beside the heater hung the only photograph they owned: Mara at nine, Eli at four, and their father crouched between them with one hand on each of their shoulders.

Jon Venn had been dead for eight years.

The official record called it an industrial accident. A pressure failure at an atmospheric relay. His body had never been recovered. Sela had refused the memorial certificate and kept the photograph instead.

Mara remembered very little of him clearly. His hands, mostly. They had been broad and scarred, with a crescent-shaped burn across one thumb. He had taught her how to fold paper maps without creasing the streets.

“Every line means someone is trying to get somewhere,” he had told her.

She had been too young to understand why that mattered.

Now Eli coughed again, harder this time.

Sela reached for her coat. “We leave in five minutes.”

The clinic stood three rings above their block, inside a bright, polished building where the walls displayed health statistics in moving bands of green. Mara had been there so often that the reception clerk recognized them.

“Tier Four respiratory,” the clerk said without looking up.

“Eli Venn,” Sela replied. “His saturation is falling.”

“Have you used the prescribed inhalant?”

“His allocation ran out.”

“That allocation was issued nine days ago.”

“His condition has worsened.”

The clerk tapped at her console. “The next standard appointment is in six days.”

Sela leaned forward. “He needs treatment now.”

“I can request an emergency review.”

“How long?”

“Two to four hours.”

Eli bent double behind them, coughing into his sleeve.

Mara felt something sharp move through her chest. “You have the treatment here.”

The clerk’s expression did not change. Behind her, through a transparent partition, Mara could see a storage cabinet lit from within. Small silver inhalant cartridges rested in neat rows.

“Those are restricted doses,” the clerk said.

“Restricted to whom?”

“Approved patients.”

“Eli is an approved patient.”

“Not for that allocation.”

Mara turned toward the cabinet. “What makes someone approved?”

The clerk finally looked at her. “Please step away from the counter.”

“Is it citizenship tier?”

“Mara,” Sela warned.

“Occupational value?”

“Step away.”

“Age?”

The cabinet continued glowing behind the clerk, full of medicine.

A man in a blue medical coat approached from the treatment corridor. His badge identified him as Administrator Pell. Mara had seen him before, always immaculate, always moving quickly past patients who sat coughing in the waiting area.

“What is the problem?” he asked.

“My son requires respiratory treatment,” Sela said.

“Your son has a standing care plan.”

“His care plan isn’t working.”

Pell glanced at Eli’s monitor. “His numbers are within tolerable limits.”

“Tolerable?” Mara said.

Pell’s eyes shifted to her gray citizenship band. “You are not the patient’s guardian.”

“I’m his sister.”

“Then allow your mother to speak.”

“My mother is speaking.”

Sela caught Mara’s wrist. Her fingers were cold.

Pell lowered his voice. “The clinic cannot dispense restricted medicine without authorization. You know this.”

Mara looked at the cabinet again. “What if he stops breathing before the authorization arrives?”

“Then emergency services will determine the appropriate response.”

The sentence seemed to settle over them like dust.

Eli straightened slowly. His face had gone pale beneath the brown of his skin. “Mara,” he whispered. “Don’t.”

She wanted to break the cabinet glass. She wanted to seize one of the silver cartridges and press it into his hand. She wanted to ask why a city that could hold itself in the sky could not keep a child’s lungs open.

Instead, Sela pulled her back.

“We’ll wait for the review,” her mother said.

Pell had already turned away.

They sat for three hours beneath a wall screen showing smiling citizens in clean gardens. The screen announced that Lumen’s health system was the most advanced in human history. It displayed a map of disease reduction across the city, the lower rings rendered in reassuring green.

Mara stared at the map until the colors blurred.

When the review finally came, the answer was no.

Eli received a diluted inhalant and instructions to return if his condition became critical. Sela signed the form with a hand that shook only once.

On the way home, Eli slept against her shoulder on the tram. Sela sat opposite them, clutching the empty medicine packet.

“Don’t look at me like that,” she said.

Mara looked out at the passing city. “Like what?”

“Like I allowed it.”

“You didn’t.”

“I brought you there.”

“They refused him.”

“And what did you do?” Sela asked.

Mara turned.

Sela’s face was tired, not angry. That made it worse.

“You argued with a clerk,” she continued. “You nearly got us removed from the clinic. Do you think they would give him medicine because you shouted?”

“No.”

“Then don’t confuse anger with action.”

Mara glanced at Eli. His breath rasped softly through the mask.

“What am I supposed to do?”

Sela looked down at the packet in her hands. “Stay employed. Keep your access band clean. Don’t give them a reason to review our household.”

“Those are not the same as helping him.”

“They are, in Lumen.”

The tram curved around the central tower. Through the window, Mara saw the upper districts suspended above them, bright as another world. Gardens climbed the sides of the towers. Water spilled in controlled silver ribbons through open channels. The Founders’ Ring glittered beneath its protective dome.

Below, the lower residents queued for ration checks.

Lumen was safe because it was controlled. That was the truth repeated in schoolrooms, clinics, broadcasts, and every official map. The city had survived the flood because people accepted limits. There were only so many filters, only so much clean water, only so many medical doses. If everyone received whatever they wanted, the systems would fail and everyone would die.

Mara had believed this all her life.

She still believed it now.

But as the tram carried them home, she opened her work tablet beneath the edge of her coat and brought up the southern filter district.

The public route showed three access points.

Her private layer showed six.

She added a seventh.

It was not marked on any current map. The corridor ran behind the clinic, through an old maintenance spine, and ended at a sealed door beneath the central hospital. Mara had found it while checking utility overlaps two weeks earlier. The door had no active designation, no route number, no explanation.

She zoomed closer.

A line of obsolete text appeared beneath the seal, half erased by a system update.

ARCHIVE TRANSFER—AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY.

Mara stared at it until the tram lights flickered.

Then she copied the coordinates into a private file, gave the file no name, and closed the map before Sela could see.

Above them, Lumen shone without shadow.

Below, the clouds hid everything the city had decided was gone.

chapters.name: The Treatment
chapters.content:
By morning, Eli was breathing as if each breath had to climb a hill.

Mara woke to the sound: a thin rasp, a pause too long for sleep, then a cough that tore through him. She sat up beneath the thermal sheet. The filtration unit hummed above the door, pulling stale air through its membrane. Pipes clicked inside the walls. Somewhere below, a freight tram chimed as it crossed from the residential ring to the industrial decks.

Another cough.

“Eli?”

Her mother’s cot creaked. “I’m here.”

Mara crossed the room. Their apartment was one room divided by curtains, with sleeping cots on one side and a foldout table on the other. The wall display showed the hour and the city’s current pressure level.

**STABLE: 96.4%.**

The number had been falling for three days.

Eli lay curled beneath his blanket, his face too small against the pillow. He was twelve, though illness had kept him from growing as quickly as the children in the upper-ring broadcasts. The inhalant mask rested beside him.

Mara picked it up and shook it.

Empty.

“Where’s the cartridge?”

“Used the last of it,” Sela said.

“You said there was one left.”

“I thought there was.”

Eli opened his eyes. “It’s not so bad.”

His voice was barely audible.

Mara touched the monitor patch at his throat. Its indicator blinked yellow, then red. She pressed the sensor twice, hoping it had misread him.

“Your oxygen’s dropping.”

“It does that.”

“It isn’t supposed to.”

Eli tried to shrug and began coughing again. Mara held his shoulders while Sela fitted the empty mask over his mouth, as if its shape alone might help. His ribs moved sharply beneath his sleep shirt.

Sela stood in the doorway wearing gray repair coveralls, membrane sealant on one thumb. “Clinic,” Mara said.

“The queue will be full.”

“Then we go before it is.”

“Mara—”

“He needs treatment.”

They both knew what treatment meant. The clinic had a new inhalant, developed from stabilized atmospheric compounds and approved for chronic respiratory decline. Public announcements called it a triumph of Lumen medicine. It could open damaged airways and slow the scarring caused by recycled particulates.

It was also restricted.

Their family’s allocation had expired twelve days earlier. Sela’s work classification had been downgraded after two filtration membranes failed in her sector. Mara was too young to carry a full occupational designation. Eli was listed as dependent labor, nonproductive.

The clinic had supplied only diluted maintenance doses since then.

Sela wrapped Eli in his coat. “We know what he needs.”

“Then why are we still standing here?”

“Because wanting it doesn’t make us eligible.”

They left the apartment beneath the low ceiling of the residential ring. The corridor smelled of hot metal, disinfectant, and damp fabric. Condensation gathered around the ventilation grilles despite the city’s claim that its air was clean.

A notice glowed on the wall:

**CONSERVE AIR. REPORT UNAUTHORIZED VENTILATION. COMMUNITY STABILITY IS INDIVIDUAL RESPONSIBILITY.**

Someone had scratched beneath it:

**WHOSE COMMUNITY?**

The mark had been painted over, but not well.

“Keep moving,” Sela said.

Eli leaned against her. Mara took his other side. His weight was frighteningly slight.

At the security arch, their bands flashed: Sela’s gray labor band, Mara’s gray technical band, Eli’s thin white dependent band. The arch read each identity in turn. Mara’s displayed a mapmaker’s emblem and a warning about provisional mobility. Sela’s listed her work authorization and household status. Eli’s showed only his name, birth date, and a red medical flag.

The arch paused over him.

“Respiratory distress detected,” it announced.

“We’re going to the clinic,” Mara said.

“Medical transit authorization required.”

Sela produced a folded referral. “Emergency referral.”

“Referral expired.”

“It was issued yesterday.”

“Medical transit authorization required.”

“He can’t walk two rings without treatment,” Mara said.

“Please remain calm. Respiratory assistance will arrive according to priority.”

“What priority?”

The machine did not answer.

Eli bent forward, coughing into his sleeve. Mara turned toward the nearest terminal.

“Call medical response.”

“Do not,” Sela said.

“His oxygen is falling.”

“If you trigger a public emergency code, they’ll record it.”

“They’re already recording it.”

Sela gripped her wrist. “Mara.”

The arch chimed. “Household conduct advisory initiated.”

A woman carrying a crate of filter plates emerged from the lower passage. She saw Eli, set down the crate, and forced the pressure door open by hand. The door shrieked against its track.

“You’ll lose less time arguing with the machine,” she said.

Sela pulled Eli through. Mara followed.

At the first landing, Eli stopped. His body sagged against Mara.

“Sit.”

“I’m fine.”

“Sit down.”

“There isn’t time.”

Sela struck the emergency panel. “Open.”

“Please remain calm. Respiratory assistance will arrive according to priority.”

“Open the door!”

The panel displayed the pressure mechanism. Mara recognized the model from a maintenance survey. She slid a fingernail beneath the casing and pulled the manual latch.

The door unlocked with a dull clunk.

Sela stared at her. “You’ll damage it.”

“It was going to open.”

Eli managed a breathless laugh. “Mara wins.”

She almost smiled. Then he coughed again.

They carried him down. The stairs connected the rings through badly repaired landings and pressure doors. These routes were not shown on public maps. Official transit ended at Gate Twelve, where residents were directed through the bright central concourse. But Gate Twelve had been closed for months, and workers were sent through the maintenance spine instead.

Mara had added the spine to her private map.

At the third landing, an overhead light flickered. Below them, the city opened into a shaft full of pipes and moving platforms. Lumen’s inner structure descended farther than any public map admitted. Mara had always liked that fact. It made the city feel less like a sealed machine and more like a body with hidden organs.

Today the thought made her sick.

At the bottom, Sela caught her breath. “We have to get him to intake.”

A pair of orderlies pushed past with an empty stretcher.

“Please,” Sela said. “Our son is in distress.”

One orderly glanced at Eli’s band. “Clinic queue is through the main hall.”

“We came from the lower ring.”

“Then you know the queue.”

Mara stepped in front of them. “He needs immediate assessment.”

The orderly’s expression hardened. “Everyone here has a reason they think they’re first.”

“He’s turning blue.”

“Take a number.”

Sela pulled Mara away.

The clinic occupied a former recreation hall. Its entrance projected green leaves and the words:

**HEALTH IS THE FOUNDATION OF PRODUCTIVITY.**

Families crowded the benches. A child slept beneath an oxygen hood. Two filtration workers argued with a clerk over a revoked housing certificate. An old man held a paper bag against his chest while the woman beside him repeated that he had already paid the consultation fee.

The air smelled of antiseptic and overheated plastic.

Mara brought Eli to the counter. “Dependent respiratory patient. His oxygen is falling. He needs the new inhalant.”

The clerk scanned their cards. Her face was lit from below by the terminal.

“Allocation expired.”

“We know. That’s why we’re here.”

“Renewal request denied.”

“Why?”

“Household classification.”

“He needs the medicine, not a classification.”

“I can provide a diluted maintenance dose.”

“It isn’t working.”

“That is not a clinic determination.”

Mara saw the administrator through smoked glass. Behind him stood a transparent cabinet illuminated from within. Rows of inhalant cartridges gleamed on its shelves, each marked with a green authorization seal.

She crossed the room.

“Administrator Pell.”

The man looked up. His blue medical coat was spotless, and a silver authorization band circled his wrist.

“Who are you?”

“Mara Venn. My brother needs the restricted inhalant.”

Pell glanced toward Eli. “Your family has been informed of the allocation policy.”

“He can’t breathe.”

“His maintenance dose is approved.”

“It doesn’t work.”

“Then he may require an evaluation.”

“We’re asking for one.”

“An evaluation is not the same as treatment authorization.”

Mara pointed to the cabinet. “Those are the restricted doses.”

“Yes.”

“Then give him one.”

“Your brother does not qualify.”

“What qualifies someone?”

Pell folded his hands. “Occupational value. Citizenship tier. Prognosis. Household contribution.”

“He’s twelve.”

“Which is why his occupational value is projected, not current.”

“He’s a child.”

“A dependent citizen,” Pell said.

The phrase was so calm that it took a moment to become real. Behind him, dozens of doses waited in their cabinet.

A man on the nearest bench turned his head.

Mara lowered her voice. “You have medicine in stock.”

“For authorized patients.”

“And he isn’t authorized because?”

“Because the city must allocate treatment where it produces the greatest long-term benefit.”

“His life is not a production calculation.”

“Everything in Lumen is a calculation. Air, water, pressure, housing, medical supplies.”

“You decide who gets to live.”

Pell’s eyes sharpened. “We decide how many people can continue living.”

He tapped the terminal. Their household file appeared between them.

**VENN HOUSEHOLD: ESSENTIAL LABOR, LIMITED MOBILITY, PROVISIONAL MEDICAL ACCESS.**

Mara had seen the classification before. She had not understood that every word carried a separate threat.

Pell touched the line beneath it. “Your mother’s employment maintains a modest priority. Your apprenticeship contributes projected technical value. Your brother’s condition consumes resources without a corresponding occupational return. That is not cruelty. It is sustainability.”

“His lungs don’t know his tier.”

“No. But the city does.”

Eli coughed. He bent nearly double.

Sela hurried to him. “Eli, look at me.”

An attendant brought the diluted inhalant. Its container was cloudy and half-filled. His monitor flashed red.

Mara turned back to Pell. “How many doses are in that cabinet?”

“The inventory is restricted.”

“How many?”

“That information is not available to you.”

“Are you saving them for upper-ring patients?”

“This clinic serves the entire city.”

“Then why is the medicine locked away while my brother is suffocating?”

Pell stepped from behind the counter. “Medical distribution cannot be determined by emotional pressure.”

“He is a patient.”

“He is a dependent without current treatment authorization.”

“Because you decided he wasn’t worth the medicine.”

Pell lifted his wrist. “Security.”

Sela looked toward him. “Please. We’re not causing trouble.”

“Your son is in distress.”

“Then treat him.”

“Your household is in arrears on medical credits.”

“I can work extra shifts.”

“You already exceed safe exposure limits.”

“I can sell credits.”

“That would affect your housing stability.”

Sela’s face drained of color.

Mara understood then that this was not only about medicine. The same number governed Eli’s treatment, their apartment, their pressure level, their food, and whether Sela could keep her repair assignment.

“How many children are we allowed to have?” Mara asked.

Pell looked at her.

“Is that part of the calculation too?”

“Household expansion requires authorization.”

“You mean family size.”

“Population planning.”

“Who authorizes it?”

“Your citizenship tier determines your household allowance.”

“And if someone has another child?”

“Then housing and medical allocation are reassessed.”

The room seemed to contract. She imagined an official deciding whether a baby consumed too much air.

Eli collapsed onto a bench. The attendant hurried over with the diluted inhalant. His chest jerked beneath his coat.

“Give him the restricted dose,” Mara said.

The attendant looked toward Pell.

“Do not,” Pell ordered.

The attendant’s hands trembled. “If we don’t give him something—”

Pell turned to Mara. “If you continue inciting staff to violate procedure, your household may face a conduct review.”

“What does that mean?”

“Employment eligibility, housing assignment, dependent registration, citizenship credits.”

“You can take our home because I asked for medicine?”

“Not without review.”

“And Eli?”

“His dependent status may be reassessed if your household cannot demonstrate responsible care.”

Sela went still.

Mara stared at Pell. “You’ll blame us for not being able to buy what you refuse to sell us?”

“Access is based on eligibility.”

“Eligibility is based on access.”

“That is your interpretation.”

“Then tell me the difference.”

Pell’s mouth tightened. “Security.”

Two officers entered through the clinic doors. One scanned the room, noting faces and bands.

Eli inhaled the diluted medicine. He coughed, inhaled again, and coughed until tears ran from his eyes. The monitor stayed red.

Mara knelt beside him. “Stay with me.”

“I am.”

“Keep breathing.”

“Trying.”

“You’re doing it.”

He gripped her fingers. His nails were pale.

Pell pointed toward the restricted ward. “Transfer him for observation.”

Sela rose. “I’m going with him.”

“Family access is not authorized.”

“I’m his mother.”

“Observation staff will contact you.”

“You said his condition was his household’s responsibility.”

“Then you should have maintained his allocation.”

Eli was lifted onto a stretcher. Mara followed as the attendants rolled him toward a door marked **AUTHORIZED CARE ONLY**.

“Wait,” Sela said. “Eli, look at me.”

He turned his head.

“We’ll be here.”

“You promise?”

Sela’s face broke for only a second. “I promise.”

The scanner flashed red across her path.

“Family access denied,” said the door.

“He’s twelve,” Mara said.

“Dependent patient transfer.”

“Open it.”

“Your household authorization does not include restricted ward access.”

The door began to close. Eli twisted toward them.

“Mara.”

“I’m here.”

“Don’t let them—”

The seal cut off the rest.

Mara stood with her hand against the metal. On the other side, wheels rattled away.

Sela lowered Mara’s hand. “We go home.”

“No. We find someone who can authorize treatment. Master Vale. The Ministry. Anyone.”

“They’re not going to help.”

“They’re hiding medicine.”

“They’re rationing it.”

“They’ve decided Eli is expendable.”

“Quiet.”

“Why? Because the walls listen?”

“Because people do.”

Sela pulled her into the stairwell. Only there did she release her.

The stairwell was colder than the clinic. Through a small inspection window, Mara could see clouds slipping beneath Lumen, white and endless. Far below, something dark broke the cloud cover: perhaps the tip of a submerged tower, perhaps old machinery suspended in mist.

She blinked, and it vanished.

“You will say nothing about the cabinet,” Sela said.

“He might die.”

“I know.”

“You’re telling me to let him die quietly.”

“I’m telling you that if I lose my work, we lose the apartment. If we lose the apartment, we lose stable pressure. If I lose my citizenship credits, they can separate us.”

The engines thundered above them.

Sela reached into her pocket and unfolded the expired referral. “I can sell my housing credits. It might buy a treatment allocation.”

“No.”

“It might.”

“It would put us in relocation.”

“I know.”

“The lower maintenance decks don’t have stable pressure.”

“I know.”

“And my apprenticeship would be reviewed.”

“I know.”

“Then what would we have?”

Sela looked at the paper. Across the bottom, beneath the clinic seal, someone had stamped:

**INSUFFICIENT HOUSEHOLD VALUE.**

“Perhaps your brother would breathe,” she said.

The anger in Mara collapsed into something colder. She pressed the paper flat against her palm.

A sound came from the clinic side of the door.

The attendant stepped into the stairwell carrying a sealed cartridge. She looked toward the corridor before speaking.

“He’s in observation. His oxygen is stabilizing slightly.”

“Because of the maintenance dose?” Mara asked.

“No.” The attendant held out the cartridge. “This was logged for another patient. I can’t give it to him. Not officially.”

Sela did not reach for it.

Mara did.

The cartridge was warm from the attendant’s hand. Its silver seal carried a patient code and a green indicator promising six measured doses.

“Who is it for?” Mara asked.

“A Tier One child from the upper gardens. Mild reaction to atmospheric dust.”

Mara stared at the cartridge.

The attendant’s eyes flicked toward the security camera. “His family has three backups registered at home.”

“Then give this to Eli.”

“I’m not giving it to you.” Her voice was nearly soundless. “I’m showing you that it exists.”

Mara looked through the inspection window again. Clouds hid the world below. Lumen’s lights reflected in the glass, making the city appear complete, self-contained, and bright enough to survive anything.

“How long will they keep him?” she asked.

“Until his readings improve.”

“And if they don’t?”

The attendant said nothing.

Footsteps sounded beyond the clinic door.

She snatched back the cartridge and hurried away. Before the door closed, she glanced at Mara—not with pity, but with warning.

Sela took Mara’s hand. “We go home.”

Mara looked at the sealed door behind which Eli waited, at the cartridge meant for someone who could afford to cough safely, and at the corridor lines she had memorized without meaning to.

Every map she had drawn began with an authorized entrance.

For the first time, she wondered who had drawn the doors.

chapters.name: Lines on a Map
chapters.content:
## Lines on a Map

The Office of Cartography smelled of hot dust, metal polish, and recycled water.

Mara had always liked the smell. It belonged to long tables, brass instruments, and ink that dried in precise lines. A route could be measured. A boundary could be checked. A missing corridor could be found if someone had bothered to draw it.

That morning, every line seemed to move.

She sat beneath the western windows, where cloud glare turned the glass white. Beyond it, Lumen’s outer gardens floated in staggered tiers, their lights dimmed to conserve power. The pressure indicators along the office wall blinked amber.

**96.4%.**

Someone had written the number on the central board and circled it twice. Beside it, in Orin Vale’s narrow hand, were the words:

**Routine variance. Maintain calm.**

Mara tried to focus on the map projected across her desk.

Her assignment concerned the lower residential rings: new transit restrictions, maintenance closures, and pressure-control zones around sleeping quarters. The request described the changes as temporary safety measures. The lower rings had experienced “unauthorized crowding” near filtration depots, and the Council wanted to prevent “unregulated movement during atmospheric adjustment.”

Mara placed a point at the eastern access arch and drew the new boundary.

The line cut through a school.

She checked the underlying survey. Ring Nine Learning Hall was still there, with three classrooms, a communal kitchen, and an emergency pressure shelter. The new boundary closed its nearest public transit entrance at the end of the week.

She moved the line around the building.

A warning appeared.

**Boundary conflict. Reconcile with authorized restriction layer.**

She tried again.

**Boundary conflict.**

“Venn.”

Mara looked up. Master Orin Vale stood at the end of her table, a slate held against his chest. His hair was white at the temples, and the skin around his eyes had the gray cast of someone who spent too much time beneath artificial light.

“You’ve been staring at that restriction for six minutes,” he said.

“I’m reconciling the access layers.”

“You’re arguing with them.”

“The school is inside the closure.”

“The system knows.”

“The children still need a transit entrance.”

Orin placed his slate on the desk. “The request is not to improve access. It is to map the restriction.”

“If the map creates an unsafe route, that matters.”

“It matters to the engineers who issued it.”

“And if they haven’t seen the school?”

“They have.”

“How do you know?”

“No one issues a lower-ring restriction without reviewing the population data.”

“Population data doesn’t show where children sleep.”

“Usually, it shows where they are expected to sleep.”

The words settled between them.

Mara thought of Eli in the restricted ward, his breath catching between words. The clinic had known his classification, his age, and his projected value. It had known exactly what he was expected to be.

She drew the boundary as authorized.

The school vanished beneath red.

“Finish the file,” Orin said. “You’re making the restriction reasonable.”

“Isn’t that the purpose of a map?”

“Not always.”

He moved away. Mara saved the file and began the next section.

For two hours, she mapped the lower rings. Transit arches closed. Stairwells designated for emergency use only. Pressure doors that would require occupational clearance after the next inspection cycle. Three medical kiosks marked “temporarily inactive,” though the supply ledger showed they had received filters and power cells that morning.

She opened the logistics overlay.

Cargo routes appeared beneath the public streets, pale lines running through sealed lift shafts and restricted corridors. One began at a filtration depot in Ring Ten, bypassed six residential blocks, crossed beneath the central market, and ended at Garden Crown Three.

Garden Crown Three held fewer than two hundred residents.

The route delivered water membranes, nutrient salts, replacement air filters, and medical compounds every four days.

Mara checked the public map.

Nothing.

The supply route was absent. So were two others leading toward the upper rings. The public map showed only a narrow maintenance road and an inactive freight lift.

She overlaid the layers until the hidden routes glowed through the official streets.

The city became a different shape.

Beneath the broad avenues ran another Lumen, built for cargo and privilege. It had its own entrances, pressure controls, and shortcuts.

Mara thought of the clinic attendant’s hand lifting the restricted cartridge from behind the counter. A dose meant for a child with a mild dust reaction. A child with three backups at home.

The medicine had a route.

Maybe everything did.

“Venn.”

Tavi appeared beside her station carrying two nutrient cups. He set one down.

“You look like you’re planning to murder the map,” he said.

“I’m working.”

“You’ve been working since before I arrived.”

“You arrived late.”

“I was delayed by a Ministry escort.”

“Of course you were.”

Tavi glanced at the layers on her desk. Unlike most apprentices, he wore no technical band. His family’s silver wrist strip allowed him through doors Mara could only see on a map.

“That’s not a public layer,” he said.

“No.”

“Are you supposed to be viewing it?”

“Yes.”

“Are you supposed to be looking at it like that?”

Mara closed the overlay. “Like what?”

“Like you’ve discovered the city is made of bones.”

She studied him. “Where did you hear about trees and rivers?”

His eyes flicked toward Orin’s office.

“I told you. Survey footage.”

“You said it was old.”

“It is old.”

“How old?”

“Twelve years. Maybe more.”

“And you didn’t think to mention that the mainland might not be dead?”

“I did mention it.”

“You said it might have been a training simulation.”

“Because it might have been.”

“Do you have the footage?”

“No.”

“Can you find it?”

Tavi lowered his cup. “You’re asking me to search restricted archives.”

“I’m asking whether the mainland is really uninhabitable.”

“Those aren’t separate requests.”

Mara glanced toward Orin’s office. “Eli is in the hospital.”

“I know.”

“They have the treatment.”

“I know.”

“They’re withholding it because his classification says he isn’t worth the allocation.”

“You don’t know that the exact treatment would help him.”

“The cartridge was in the clinic.”

“That doesn’t mean—”

“Then why was it locked away?”

Tavi had no answer.

A signal chimed from her terminal. The system had found an inconsistency in the restriction file. Mara opened it and discovered an old base layer beneath the current survey.

The image was pale and warped, copied from a damaged physical sheet. It showed the Thames basin before the final flood, though the coastline had been washed in gray. Fragments of labels remained: **Til—**, **Riv—**, **coastal transfer**, **agricultural survey**.

Along the old shoreline were small green squares.

Cultivation sites.

Mara opened the file history. Most of the record was blank. The map had been imported from an obsolete archive, revised, and sealed. One marginal note remained:

**Remove unsupported survivability indicators before public release.**

She read it twice.

“Venn.”

Orin stood behind her.

She closed the historical layer, but not quickly enough.

“What are you viewing?”

“An underlying survey.”

“Why?”

“It appeared in the file history.”

“Then report the fault.”

“I was checking whether the current boundary had been drawn over an old shoreline.”

Orin looked at the screen. “The shoreline is irrelevant.”

“Why was it erased?”

“Mara.”

“The note says survivability indicators were removed.”

“I can read.”

“Were there communities there?”

Orin’s gaze moved to the lower rings glowing red on the wall display. “There are no communities on the mainland.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“It is the answer you need.”

“No. It’s the answer on the public map.”

A silence opened around them. The nearest apprentice lowered her pen.

Orin reached across Mara and shut down the historical layer. “Maps are not arguments.”

“They decide where people can go.”

“They describe decisions already made.”

“What do they describe when the decision is wrong?”

His expression hardened. “You are not a historian. You are an apprentice. Your task is to provide accurate, usable information within authorized parameters.”

“Accurate information,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

“Even if the authorized map leaves out supply routes?”

She had not meant to say it aloud.

Orin looked at her sharply. “What supply routes?”

“The ones running from the lower depots to the upper gardens. They aren’t on public maps.”

“They are restricted logistics corridors.”

“Shouldn’t infrastructure include where resources go?”

“It includes what you are assigned to include.”

“Who decides that?”

“The people responsible for keeping this city alive.”

“Pell said the same thing.”

“Administrator Pell is responsible for medicine.”

“He decides who gets to breathe.”

“So do you, when you draw a route around a pressure shelter.”

Mara flinched. Regret flickered across Orin’s face, but he did not withdraw the words.

“Finish the restriction map,” he said. “Then go home. Your family has had a difficult day.”

Mara looked at him. “What is beneath the western archive levels?”

His hand paused on the edge of her desk.

“Old survey storage.”

“Is it still in use?”

“No.”

“Then why is it sealed?”

“Because old records are not automatically safe records.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means a map can preserve a mistake long after everyone has forgotten who made it.”

He returned to his office.

That evening, the residential arch scanned Sela’s band three times before allowing them through. The apartment was colder than usual. The ceiling vent clicked unevenly, and the pressure gauge had dropped another fraction.

Eli’s sleeping mat remained folded against the wall.

Sela stood at the counter with a citizenship ledger projected above her hands. Numbers moved across it: housing credit, employment credit, dependent allocation, medical reserve.

A red line marked the bottom.

**TRANSFER THRESHOLD: 18 CREDITS.**

Mara set down her work slate. “What are you doing?”

“Counting.”

“You said you weren’t going to sell the housing credits.”

“I said I would consider it.”

“You said relocation would make everything worse.”

“It might.”

“Then don’t.”

Sela’s fingers moved through the ledger. “The clinic has released a treatment allocation to private exchange.”

Mara felt the room narrow. “How much?”

“All of them.”

“For one cartridge?”

“For a treatment course.”

“Will it work?”

“They claim it will.”

“Pell claims a lot of things.”

Sela closed the display and sat. Her face was pale with exhaustion.

“If we wait for official approval,” she said, “Eli may not come home.”

Mara looked toward the folded mat. “He might not come home anyway.”

The words escaped before she could stop them.

Sela closed her eyes.

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t apologize for saying what I’m afraid of.”

The ledger hovered between them before fading.

“If I sell the credits,” Sela said, “we lose our placement in this ring. The system assigns us to lower maintenance housing. Maybe Ring Fourteen. Maybe the underdeck quarters.”

“The filters fail there.”

“I know.”

“Families get split during relocation.”

“I know that too.”

“Your employment band could be reassessed.”

Sela gave a tired smile. “You’ve been listening.”

“I’ve been reading.”

“What happened at the office?”

Mara hesitated, then told her about the hidden supply routes and the old coastal survey. When she mentioned the erased cultivation sites, Sela’s expression changed.

“Your father used to speak like that,” she said.

Mara went quiet.

“He would come home with a maintenance report and say the numbers had been altered. He believed the relay failures followed a pattern. He thought if he found the right map, he could prove it.”

“Maybe he was right.”

“Maybe.” Sela’s voice broke. “And where did it get him?”

Mara thought of the memorial certificate, thin and official, with no body listed beneath Jon Venn’s name.

“Into an accident,” she said.

“Into a place where no one could protect him.”

Sela reached for the ledger and closed it. “I am not selling the credits tonight.”

Relief came first, followed by fear.

“Why not?”

“I need to know whether the treatment is real. And if we move, I may not be able to reach Eli.”

“What if it’s his only chance?”

“Then I’ll sell them.”

“And lose the apartment?”

“And lose the apartment.”

“Your work?”

“Perhaps.”

“My apprenticeship?”

Sela looked at her hands. “Perhaps.”

The city gave a low mechanical shudder. Somewhere below, engines adjusted against the falling pressure. The lights dimmed, recovered, and dimmed again.

Mara took out her personal map slate. She had not meant to bring it to the table. The file was hidden beneath maintenance diagnostics.

She added a new point: the western archive levels beneath the Office of Cartography.

Sela saw the glow. “What are you doing?”

“Making a map.”

“Of what?”

“Places the city says aren’t connected.”

Sela stared at her. Then she reached across the table and placed one hand over Mara’s.

“Every line leads somewhere,” she said.

It was one of Jon’s phrases. Mara remembered his finger tracing routes across a paper map when she was small.

Every line represents someone trying to get somewhere.

She looked at the sealed apartment door, the closed ledger, and the route beneath the hospital that ended at an archive no one wanted her to enter.

“Then I need to find out where this one goes,” she said.

chapters.name: The Sealed Archive
chapters.content:
## The Sealed Archive

Mara waited until the apartment lights dimmed for night cycle before she moved.

The city called it sleep illumination, but in the lower rings it turned every corridor blue and indistinct. Shadows gathered in the corners. The pressure engines trembled beneath the floor, paused, then trembled again, as if Lumen were holding its breath.

In the next room, Eli slept badly.

Every few minutes his breathing caught. A shallow rattle rose in his chest, stopped, and began again. Mara had learned to count the pauses without meaning to. Four breaths. Five. A hitch. Six.

The clinic had given him the diluted inhalant. It had done almost nothing. The real cartridges, sealed in blue and carried through hidden routes, were being sent to upper-ring clinics while his allocation expired.

Mara dressed in maintenance coveralls and lifted Sela’s access band from its hook.

Sela sat at the kitchen table, still wearing her work clothes. Her hair was tied back with a strip of filtration cloth, and gray dust marked the cuffs of her sleeves. She had been repairing membranes for twelve hours, but she had not gone to bed. The household ledger lay open before her, its red figures glowing faintly.

“You said you were going to sleep,” she said.

“I changed my mind.”

“Where are you going?”

“I need to find another treatment.”

“At this hour?”

“The clinic won’t give it to us at any hour.”

Sela glanced toward Eli’s room. “And where will you find it?”

“Records. There may be an older course with the same compound.”

“Pell said it was newly developed.”

“Pell says what he’s authorized to say.”

“Mara.”

The warning was quiet, but it carried the weight of every consequence they had discussed. If Mara were caught using Sela’s band, Sela could lose her employment classification. Without it, their housing credits would fall below the transfer threshold. Mara could be removed from Cartography. Eli could be moved somewhere they could not reach.

“They can remove him from treatment without asking,” Mara said.

“That has already happened.”

The words settled between them.

Sela rubbed her thumb around the rim of her cup. The cup was empty. “You’re going to the western levels.”

Mara did not answer.

“You think I don’t know what you’ve been studying?” Sela asked. “You’ve been looking at old access diagrams every night. You’ve been copying maintenance schedules that haven’t been active in twenty years.”

“I’m looking for a way to help him.”

“You’re looking for a door.”

“Maybe the door leads to medicine.”

“Maybe it leads to a security report with your name on it.”

Mara fastened her tool pouch. “If I stay here, his lungs keep closing.”
