Sela looked toward the bedroom again. Her expression changed when she listened to Eli breathe. The fear remained, but something harder had formed beneath it.

“If you’re caught, they won’t call it a search for medicine,” she said. “They’ll call it unauthorized archive access.”

“I won’t hurt anyone.”

“That is not the standard they use.”

Mara tucked a diagnostic lead into her pouch. “I’ll be back before morning shift.”

Sela’s face tightened. “Your father used to say that.”

Mara stopped.

“He believed the danger was in the thing itself,” Sela continued. “He never understood that the danger was being seen looking.”

“Maybe he understood.”

For a moment, Sela looked frightened rather than angry.

“Do not make me lose both of you in one night.”

Mara could not promise that. She touched her mother’s hand, feeling the roughness left by membrane sealant, then stepped into the corridor.

The lower-ring night cycle had sealed most residential doors. Ventilation grilles rattled overhead, pushing out air that tasted faintly of metal. A wall display announced that pressure remained at ninety-six point four percent and that all fluctuations were routine.

Mara looked at the number until the display dimmed.

Nothing about the city felt routine.

She crossed to the service stair. Sela’s band opened the first door, then the second. At the third, the scanner paused.

AUTHORIZED LABOR PERSONNEL ONLY.

Mara pressed the band against it again.

The lock released.

She climbed.

The transit spine to Cartography had been closed because of the pressure restrictions, so she used maintenance stairs and narrow utility landings. The lights flickered as she passed through each ring. In the middle levels, the walls were cleaner and the air smelled of citrus filters. In the upper transition zone, a transparent panel showed one of the city’s gardens: trees under artificial sunlight, their leaves polished and green.

A sign beneath the window read:

LUMEN SURVIVES THROUGH ORDER.

Mara kept climbing.

The Office of Cartography was dark. Public halls reflected narrow strips of emergency light. Maps hung along the walls: transit diagrams, ring boundaries, pressure zones, authorized districts. Without citizens moving across them, they looked less like instructions than warnings.

She crossed the drafting hall and knelt beside the western wall.

The sealed levels lay behind it. Orin had called them obsolete survey storage, but his hesitation had betrayed him. That afternoon, when he ordered her to report the old coastal file as a fault, he had looked not at the map but at the door behind her.

Mara had spent the hours since comparing old schematics with the office’s current structure. The archive had a service panel connected to the filtration network. It was not on any public plan. It appeared on a maintenance diagram from before the Continuance, when the office had been part of a much larger administrative complex.

She removed three screws and exposed fiber lines and a manual override strip. Her diagnostic lead connected the panel to the office system.

The system recognized her as a maintenance worker, then demanded a work order.

Mara entered the number of a membrane replacement Sela had completed six years earlier.

The system queried the central ledger.

She held her breath.

The panel flashed amber. The wall unlocked with a heavy clunk.

Mara slipped through and pulled the door shut.

The air on the other side was colder and dry enough to sting her throat. Emergency lights came on along the floor, revealing a corridor layered with dust. Raw composite walls replaced the office’s smooth panels. Old conduit bulged overhead. A fan turned once somewhere in the darkness, then stopped.

A thin strip of fresh dust marked the center of the floor, as if carts or people still passed through.

Mara followed it.

The first room held shelves of folded survey film and broken projection plates. Labels appeared in the old pre-Continuance format:

COASTAL ELEVATION.  
ATMOSPHERIC DENSITY.  
AGRICULTURAL RECOVERY.  
POPULATION MOVEMENT.

Mara stopped at the last one.

The official lessons said the Continuance began after the oceans rose over the cities and contamination made the continents unlivable. The remaining population had been gathered into Lumen and the other aerial settlements. No organized communities had survived below.

Why, then, had someone recorded population movement?

She entered the room.

Several cabinets stood open. Their drawers held transparent data wafers and paper bundles sealed in cloudy sleeves. Mara searched for medical classifications first, scanning labels with her lamp.

RESPIRATORY FAILURE.  
PARTICULATE EXPOSURE.  
RECYCLED ATMOSPHERE SYNDROME.  
CHRONIC MEMBRANE INFLAMMATION.

Her pulse quickened.

The files were old, but old did not mean useless. Perhaps an earlier treatment had been replaced because Lumen no longer manufactured it. Perhaps the restricted inhalant was based on a formula preserved here. Perhaps someone had discovered that the city’s illness was not unavoidable.

She opened a drawer marked MEDICAL—ENVIRONMENTAL RESPONSE.

The first report described workers in sealed coastal shelters. Their symptoms were like Eli’s: constricted airways, persistent coughing, unstable oxygen levels, inflammation that worsened after every exposure cycle.

Beside the treatment protocol, someone had drawn a thick black line.

REPLACED BY CENTRALIZED PROTOCOL.

No explanation followed.

Mara photographed the page with her band. She turned to the next report. It listed children. The names had been removed, but ages remained: six, nine, eleven, twelve.

One line had not been fully erased.

Survival improved when patients were removed from—

The rest was a gray smear.

Mara’s hand tightened around the file.

A security chime sounded.

A red line appeared along the doorframe. An old ceiling lens rotated toward her.

“Maintenance inspection,” she whispered.

The lens continued turning.

She pressed the lamp’s power cell against the sensor housing. The light went out. The red line faded to amber.

For several seconds she heard only the distant vibration of Lumen’s engines.

Then the line turned green.

Mara released a breath and moved deeper into the archive.

The next room had partly collapsed. A section of ceiling had crushed several shelves, leaving a gap beneath the wreckage. A warning panel blinked:

STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY: 41 PERCENT.

Dust coated the floor in ridges. Water had leaked through somewhere above and dried into white mineral streaks. Mara crouched beneath the damaged beams, careful not to touch the hanging cables.

On the far side stood a row of transfer bins. Their labels had been scraped away.

ARCHIVE TRANSFER—AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY.

The same words as those on the sealed hospital door.

Mara remembered the corridor behind the clinic, the hidden route she had used to move Eli, and the hospital door with its unfinished warning. Why would medical archives be transferred to Cartography? Why hide treatment records beneath a mapping office?

She approached the nearest bin. Its mechanical clasp was stiff with age. She slid a thin tool into the seam and worked until the lock snapped.

Inside were landscape images.

At first she thought they showed one of Lumen’s agricultural decks. The pictures were grainy and green, full of dark leaves beneath a pale sky. Then she saw the horizon.

There was no deck.

Plants grew in open soil.

Mara lifted the first image. A line of trees stood beyond a field, bent by wind. Behind them rose the broken remains of a tower. Coordinates marked the corner.

THAMES BASIN—SOUTHERN FLOODPLAIN.

The next image showed a settlement along an elevated roadway. Solar cloth stretched between ruined buildings. People in waterproof clothing stood beside long tanks. Another showed a river winding through reeds.

Not a flood current. A river.

Mara sat back on her heels.

The mainland was dead. She had known that as surely as she knew the shape of her own face. It was printed in schoolbooks and announced during every emergency broadcast. Below the clouds lay drowned cities and poisoned mud. Nothing remained that could sustain human life.

The images showed otherwise.

Her first thought was that they were fabrications. The Council had manufactured threats before, creating monsters out of imagined mainland raiders to justify rationing and surveillance. Perhaps these were the opposite: a comforting fiction made by frightened pre-Continuance scientists.

She turned one over.

A handwritten note ran along the back in faded blue ink.

SOIL SALINITY FALLING. SEED BANKS ACTIVE. RETURN NEXT SEASON.

The handwriting looked hurried. Human. That made it worse.

Mara placed the image beneath her lamp and examined the metadata.

Most of it was damaged. Dates flickered in and out: eighteen years after Continuance, twenty-three, thirty-one. One image carried a survey stamp from twelve years earlier.

That was impossible. The last mainland transmission had ended thirty-four years ago.

Unless it had not.

Mara went to a terminal beneath the far wall. Its screen was dark, but her diagnostic lead woke it. The machine shuddered, displayed a field of static, then resolved into text.

ENVIRONMENTAL SURVEY ARCHIVE  
STATUS: RESTRICTED  
PUBLIC RELEASE: MODIFIED  
UNSUPPORTED SURVIVABILITY INDICATORS: REMOVED

She read the last line twice.

The first file opened in layers. A coastline emerged from darkness: the Thames basin, altered by retreating water and silt. Small lights clustered inland and along raised transport routes.

Not stars.

Artificial lights.

She enlarged the image. Fields appeared as geometric patches among drowned streets. Symbols marked water collection, seed reserves, clinics, radio relays.

This was not a prediction. It was an inventory.

Mara gripped the edge of the terminal.

The lights resembled the ones she had seen from Lumen’s underside during maintenance shifts: scattered glimmers beneath the clouds, always dismissed as reflected lightning or sensor error. She had drawn them once, then erased them from her private map because she had not known what they meant.

If people lived below, why had no one told them?

If people lived below, why was Eli dying for medicine?

She searched for respiratory treatment. The archive returned dozens of references, most locked. One opened to a report from a coastal settlement near the former estuary:

Children exposed to concentrated particulate conditions showed improvement after treatment with a compound derived from marsh fungus and stabilized anti-inflammatory carriers. Distribution remains limited due to—

The rest was corrupted.

Mara copied the file, then the satellite image, the settlement map, and the modified-release record. Her band’s storage indicator dropped into the red. She connected a blank wafer from her pouch and began transferring the larger files.

A warning appeared.

UNAUTHORIZED DUPLICATION DETECTED.

Mara tore the wafer free before the transfer completed. The files on it might be incomplete, but the wafer was warm in her palm, holding more truth than she had ever been permitted to see.

The terminal went black.

She returned the papers to the bin, though not exactly as she had found them. One photograph slipped to the floor. A child stood in a field beneath an open sky, one hand holding a bright red cloth lifted by the wind.

Mara tucked the photograph inside her coveralls.

A soft mechanical click came from above.

The archive’s defense system had awakened.

She extinguished her lamp. A blue pulse swept the room. Dust glittered in its path. The inspection drone descended from the ceiling, its lens cluster searching.

“Maintenance,” Mara whispered.

The drone emitted a questioning tone.

“I’m clearing a fault.”

Another tone, sharper this time.

Mara slid beneath the collapsed shelving and pressed herself against the floor. The machine moved closer. Its light passed over the metal wreckage, paused, and returned.

She could hear its tiny rotors correcting against the uneven air. A security drone should not have been active in a sealed archive. That meant the system had reported her to someone, or the archive had never truly been abandoned.

The thought tightened her lungs.

The drone’s lens brightened.

Mara found the magnetic calibration strip in her tool pouch and held it toward the machine. When its lens focused, she twisted the strip.

The drone jerked sideways, struck the ceiling, and released a burst of static. Its light went out.

Mara ran.

The corridor seemed to tilt beneath her as Lumen adjusted pressure. Behind her, the drone clicked back to life. She reached the archive door and pressed Sela’s band to the reader.

ACCESS DENIED—SECURITY HOLD.

She pressed it again.

The drone’s blue light appeared at the far end.

Mara tore open the service panel beside the door, traced the circuit by touch, and bridged the emergency bypass with her screwdriver. Sparks snapped against her knuckles.

The door sprang open.

She plunged through and pulled it shut. Something struck the other side hard enough to shake the wall.

Mara stood in the dark drafting hall, breathing through her mouth.

Then she heard footsteps.

Not the drone. A person had entered the office.

Light spilled across the main hall. Mara crouched behind a stack of folded projection screens and watched a figure cross beneath the framed transit maps.

A dark coat. A narrow shoulder. The pale glint of an access band.

Security would have announced itself. Guards traveled in pairs and broadcast their authorization. This person moved quietly, stopping to examine the western wall.

Mara held the copied wafer against her chest.

The stranger raised one hand and touched the sealed archive door.

Behind Mara, the damaged system gave a faint electronic chirp as it tried to report the breach.

The stranger turned toward the sound.

Mara’s fingers closed around the screwdriver. She could feel the edge of the photograph beneath her coveralls, the red cloth bright against her ribs.

The footsteps came closer.

chapters.name: The Boy from Broadcast
chapters.content:
The screwdriver trembled in Mara’s hand.

The stranger stopped beside the sealed archive door. He was young, perhaps nineteen or twenty, with dark hair that had been cut too neatly to belong to the lower rings. His gray coat was plain but made from fabric that did not shine with recycled fibers. A pale authorization band rested over his sleeve, its surface unmarked by the colored strips used to identify technical and labor citizens.

No Council crest. No security escort.

He crouched beside the damaged panel and touched the warning light. Its red pulse reflected in his eyes.

“Unauthorized duplication,” he murmured.

Mara stayed behind the projection screens. The warm data wafer pressed against her palm. The photograph was tucked inside her shirt, against her ribs, where the image of the child in the open field seemed to burn through the fabric.

The stranger turned his head, listening.

“Whoever you are,” he said, “you have ten seconds to come out before I call security.”

Mara stepped into view.

“Put the device away.”

He looked from her face to the screwdriver. “That’s not much of a weapon.”

“It doesn’t need to be.”

“Right.” He glanced at the archive door. “You breached a restricted level.”

“I was repairing a fault.”

“You copied an environmental survey.”

Her grip tightened.

He saw it. “Give me what you copied, and I can make sure the breach is logged as a systems error.”

“You don’t even know what I found.”

“I know the western archive is restricted under Council continuity law. Anyone who accesses it without authorization is charged with information sabotage.”

“Who are you?”

“Someone who knows what an archive breach looks like.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one you need.”

Mara studied him. His band carried upper-tier authorization, but his coat showed no department markings. His shoes had never seen a lower-ring platform; their soles were clean, their edges unscuffed. He had come through the maintenance shaft, though. That meant either he knew the hidden routes or someone important had told him where to find them.

“You’re Broadcast,” she said.

His expression tightened. “How?”

“The band. The coat. You came through the communications maintenance shaft, not the Cartography lift. Broadcast aides use that route when they don’t want to be seen.”

“You’ve been studying unauthorized routes.”

“I’m a cartographer.”

“An apprentice cartographer.”

“Then you should know I can tell where people have been.”

He looked toward the suspended map of Lumen, its bright routes crossing the dark drafting hall. Transit lines glowed in blue, pressure corridors in white, and restricted districts in red. The city looked orderly from above, every route cleanly connected, every destination assigned.

“Maps don’t tell you why,” he said.

“No. People do.”

“Why were you in the archive?”

“Medical records.”

The word changed his face. Not much. A slight withdrawal around his eyes, an almost invisible tightening at the corners of his mouth.

“Why?”

“My brother is sick.”

“That doesn’t give you permission to access classified environmental files.”

“Your permission system gave him a diluted inhalant while keeping effective cartridges behind a counter.”

“Medical allocation is not my department.”

“No. You just work for the people who decide it.”

“I don’t work for—”

He stopped himself.

Mara took a step toward him. “You knew the records were there.”

“I knew they were classified.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“It is if you work in communications.”

“Why?”

“Because classified facts can be used to make people do things.”

“People are already doing things. They decide who gets medicine, air, and movement. They’re doing it with lies.”

His gaze moved to the photograph hidden beneath her shirt as if he could see through the cloth.

“Are you saying the mainland records are real?”

“I’m saying I saw them.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“You asked the wrong question.”

For a second, something almost like amusement crossed his face. Then it vanished.

A vibration passed through the floor. The projected city flickered. For half a second, the pressure reading changed from 96.4 to 96.2 before correcting itself.

He looked up at the numbers.

“Routine?” Mara asked.

“Usually.”

“Usually isn’t an answer.”

“Neither is panic.”

“I’m not panicking.”

“You’re holding a screwdriver like you’re about to stab me.”

“I’m considering it.”

His device chirped.

The sound was small, but it seemed to split the hall. He looked down at the display, and the color left his face.

“Security?” Mara asked.

“They’re sweeping the office.”

“How long?”

“Less than two minutes.”

“Because of the archive?”

“Because of the alarm. And perhaps because someone saw you enter.”

Mara glanced toward the maintenance corridor. The emergency bypass had sealed behind her. The main lift would open onto the central concourse, where security might already be waiting. She could try the service stairs, but those opened beside the apprentice lockers. Her access band would identify her before she reached the lower rings.

The stranger moved to the projection console.

“What are you doing?”

“Trying to make them search somewhere else.”

“You said you couldn’t order a response.”

“I can still make one look elsewhere if they believe the map.”

He touched the console. The city vanished, replaced by a maintenance schematic.

“Stand there.”

Mara did not move.

“Unless you have another plan.”

“I do.”

“Excellent. Use it.”

The first security boots sounded beyond the lift. Slow, deliberate, more than one person. The sound traveled through the metal floor.

He crossed to a maintenance panel and pulled it open, revealing a narrow cavity behind the projection controls.

“Inside.”

“That’s a cable channel.”

“It’s large enough.”

“For a child.”

“For someone willing to bend.”

“You first.”

“I’m not the one they’re searching for.”

“That makes you either brave or stupid.”

“Probably both. Move.”

He caught her arm and pushed her toward the opening. Mara nearly drove the screwdriver into his wrist, but the lift doors opened before she could decide. Three security officers entered with pulse batons drawn. Behind them came a woman in a dark coat, her pale authorization band lit at the wrist.

“Inside,” he hissed.

Mara slipped sideways into the channel. Metal scraped her shoulder. She pulled the wafer beneath her belt and held the screwdriver between her knees while the young man replaced the panel.

Through a thin gap, she watched the officers spread through the drafting hall.

“Who accessed the archive?” the woman asked.

The young man stood beside the console. “I did.”

“You?”

“I’m conducting a communications integrity review.”

“Your review triggered a duplication alarm.”

“A corrupted archive can produce false alerts.”

“Where is the apprentice?”

Mara’s heart struck hard against her ribs.

The woman continued. “Mara Venn. Tier Four Cartography.”

“I don’t know her.”

The lie came quickly. The woman studied him. He kept his hands visible, but one thumb tapped once against his palm, then stopped.

“You were seen entering the office after night cycle,” the woman said.

“I was sent to investigate the alarm.”

“By whom?”

“Ministerial communications.”

“Which minister?”

His jaw tightened. “My father.”

The officers exchanged glances.

The woman stepped toward the console. “Open the maintenance logs.”

“I can’t. The archive is isolated.”

“Access it physically.”

“I’ve told you. The system is corrupted.”

“This is not a debate.”

“No,” he said. “It’s a jurisdictional dispute. If you seize a Ministry of Broadcast device during an active continuity review, your unit will explain the breach to the Council registry.”

“You’re threatening me with a registry entry?”

“I’m informing you that your authorization may not cover a ministerial investigation.”

“Your father’s name does not make you a minister.”

“No. But it makes me inconvenient to arrest without paperwork.”

The woman glanced at his device. “Transfer it.”

“I’m afraid I can’t.”

“Then you’ll come with us.”

Mara could hear the faint electrical hum beneath the channel. The metal was hot against her back. Her breath came too quickly, and she forced it slower, counting the pulses of light through the gap.

The young man looked at the console.

A tone sounded.

The suspended map returned, but the hall glowed red.

**ATMOSPHERIC CONTAINMENT FAILURE. EVACUATE.**

The officers spun toward the doors.

“What did you do?” the woman demanded.

“Nothing,” he said. “The archive’s damaged.”

A second alarm began, louder and lower, vibrating through the floor. The lights cut out.

The woman shouted for the exits to be sealed.

The young man kicked the base of the console. The panel sprang open.

“Now,” he whispered.

Mara crawled out as the officers shouted. He caught her hand and pulled her behind the screens. They ran bent low while red emergency lights flashed across the hall, turning the projected routes into broken rivers of light.

An officer swung toward them. “Stop!”

The young man slapped a hand against the map console. A wall of false hazard markers erupted across the room. Every route to the eastern lift flashed black.

“Containment breach in the east ring!” he shouted. “Seal the draft hall!”

The officers turned toward the wrong corridor.

“You lied to them,” Mara said as they ran.

“I redirected an assumption.”

“That’s what liars call it.”

“That’s what cartographers call a route.”

At the far wall, he slapped his authorization band against a maintenance hatch. It opened onto a shaft barely wider than Mara’s shoulders.

“You first.”

She shoved through. He followed, slamming the hatch behind them as security pounded on the other side.

They crawled downward through darkness, surrounded by conduit and old ventilation pipes. The shaft smelled of dust, hot insulation, and the metallic tang of recycled air. Mara’s knees struck the ridges of the access ladder. She tried to move quickly, but the young man behind her kept catching on the same narrow bends.

“Where does this go?” she whispered.

“Lower drafting store.”

“That’s not on any current plan.”

“You’re the cartographer.”

“Current plan.”

“Trust the old one.”

The shaft dropped sharply. Mara caught herself against a pipe and felt heat pulse through the metal.

“Stop. Pressure line.”

“It’s insulated.”

“Badly. Your shoulder is against the bracket.”

He shifted immediately. The careful obedience surprised her. Most upper-tier citizens treated warnings from technical workers as interruptions. He moved as if he understood that a map was not an opinion.

They reached a grating above a room filled with rolled maps and disused projection frames. Mara eased it open and lowered herself onto a crate. Dust rose around her. The young man followed, landing hard and catching himself against a cabinet.

“You’re bleeding,” she said.

“Your screwdriver?”

“The security panel.”

He looked at the cut across his palm. “I’ll survive.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I’m choosing optimism.”

“You’re choosing not to look at it.”

“That too.”

He pulled a clean strip from the inside of his coat and wrapped his hand. The cloth was white and soft. Mara thought of Sela washing membrane dust from her fingers with boiled water and ration soap.

She moved toward the service door. He caught her sleeve.

“The wafer.”

She pulled free. “No.”

“I helped you escape.”

“You helped yourself avoid a security report.”

“I need to know what you found.”

“You want to decide whether it’s dangerous enough to hide.”

His face tightened. “You think I’m like my father.”

“I think you’re his son.”

“Those aren’t the same thing.”

“Then prove it.”

“How?”

“Get me the hospital transfer records. The archive labels connected the medical files to the hospital. There’s a sealed door somewhere in the research levels. Find out what was moved through it. Find out who ordered the public release changed.”

He stared at her.

The alarms above had faded, but the room seemed to retain their echo. Somewhere beyond the walls, a pump coughed and restarted.

“You’re asking me to investigate Council records,” he said.

“I’m asking you to use the access you already have.”

“And in exchange?”

“You see what I copied.”

“That’s not enough.”

“It’s more than you had.”

He looked down at the bandage around his palm. When he spoke again, his voice had lost its practiced edge.

“My mother died in a clinic like the one you described.”

Mara said nothing.

“She had a pulmonary infection. Treatable. The doctors said the medication was available, but her allocation had expired because she wasn’t considered essential to continuity work.” He swallowed. “My father appealed. The Council approved a review.”

“Did she receive it?”

“No.”

The word settled between them.

“She died before the review finished,” Tomas continued. “Two days later, they gave my father a commendation for preserving public confidence during medical scarcity.”

Mara felt anger shift inside her, finding a shape she did not understand. She had expected an excuse, perhaps a polished explanation about difficult choices and limited supplies. Instead, he had offered her a wound.

“Did he believe the review would help her?”

“I don’t know.”

“You asked him?”

“Not until after she died.”

“And what did he say?”

“That the city couldn’t survive if every family treated its grief as a reason to break procedure.”

Mara’s fingers closed around the screwdriver. “That sounds like a broadcast.”

“It was.”

“You still work for him.”

“I work for the Ministry.”

“That’s what people say when they want the distinction to matter.”

“It matters to me.”

“Why?”

He looked toward the ceiling, where the security officers were probably reopening doors and checking identities. “Because I don’t know what else to do.”

The honesty left them silent.

Mara remembered Eli’s face in the clinic, his lips pale above the mask, his hand gripping hers while Administrator Pell explained projected productivity. She remembered Sela’s careful voice saying that a family could not survive on righteousness alone.

“You could stop,” she said.

“Stop what?”

“Reading the words they give you.”

His eyes returned to hers.

“You transmit the announcements,” Mara said. “The pressure fluctuations are routine. The mainland is dead. Supplies are stable. Families are safe. You make those words sound true.”

“That is my job.”

“Then choose a different one.”

“You think choice is that simple?”

“No. I think pretending there is no choice is simpler.”

His mouth tightened, but he did not answer.

Another tremor passed through the room. Dust sifted from the ceiling. One of the old map cylinders rolled from a shelf and struck the floor.

“Pressure’s down again,” Mara said.

“Routine fluctuation.”

“You don’t believe that.”

“No.”

The admission was so quiet she almost missed it.

He went to the service door and checked its narrow window. No movement showed in the corridor.

“If I find the records, you show me the survey,” he said.

“If you find them, I’ll show you everything.”

“Everything?”

“Not the photograph.”

“Why not?”

“It belongs to the person in it.”

“It’s a child.”

“Exactly.”

He seemed ready to argue, then stopped. “All right.”

Mara studied him. “And Tomas?”

He looked back. “You know my name.”

“Your family name is enough to make you dangerous.”

“It’s also enough to make me watched.”

“Then you’re watched by the people who need to be watched.”

A reluctant, bitter smile touched his face. “You really do think maps explain everything.”

“No. Maps show where the damage travels.”

The security search moved closer. A door slammed in the drafting store above them.

Mara opened the service door. Beyond it, a maintenance corridor descended toward the lower rings, marked by narrow blue strips of emergency light. The air was colder there, carrying the smell of wet metal and filtration dust.

“Go,” Tomas said.

She stepped through, then turned back.

“Your name,” he said.

“Tomas Rusk.”

The name landed with the force of another alarm.

“Minister Rusk’s son?”

“Junior communications aide,” he said sharply. “You already knew that.”

“I’ve seen his broadcasts.”

“Then you know he is not me.”

“Not yet.”

He reached for the door control. “Tomorrow. First light cycle. Old relay room beneath the east broadcast annex.”

“With the records?”

“With what I can find.”

“And if you bring security?”

“I won’t.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

He held her gaze. “I won’t report you.”

“You can’t promise that.”

“I can promise what I’ll do.”

“Those aren’t the same.”

“No,” he said. “But they’re what people have.”

Mara entered the corridor. Behind her, Tomas shut and locked the door, then turned back toward the noise and authority he claimed to belong to.

She pressed the warm wafer against her ribs. It held fields, rivers, lights, clinics, and a world Lumen had declared impossible. It held proof that someone had edited the truth, though not yet proof of who had ordered it.

Behind the locked door waited a boy whose family had helped write the city’s lies. Ahead waited the lower rings, the sealed hospital, and the long route home.

For the first time since leaving the archive, Mara wondered whether an ally could be as dangerous as an enemy.

Then she heard the distant cough of a pressure pump failing to restart.

She began to run.

chapters.name: The World Below
chapters.content:
At first light cycle, the old relay room smelled of dust, hot copper, and condensed water.

Mara entered through a service hatch with the warm wafer pressed inside her sleeve. The corridor shuddered whenever the pumps engaged. Each vibration traveled through the walls and into her bones, as if Lumen were grinding its teeth.

The relay room had once carried weather reports between the city and the mainland. Now its consoles stood beneath gray dust, their screens dark except for one strip of amber light. Tomas had left the outer door unlatched.

Mara paused before entering.

He could have reported her. He could have copied the wafer while she slept or arranged for security to meet her here. She had spent the night inventing reasons to distrust him and found none that made her safer.

“Tomas?”

“Here.”

He emerged from behind a signal cabinet without his coat, wearing a maintenance shirt too clean to belong to a real worker. A bruise darkened his jaw.

“What happened?” she asked.

“I disagreed with a search supervisor.”

“Did he win?”

“He had the better rank.”

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

Tomas touched his jaw and winced. “Not entirely.”

He carried a narrow data case. His hands were steady, but his face looked gray with exhaustion.

“You were followed?”

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

“No,” he said. “But I didn’t see anyone.”

Mara kept her distance. “What did you find?”

Tomas placed the case on the console. “The hospital transfer logs are split across three systems. One is public and false. One is restricted and mostly false. The third is a continuity archive held by the Ministry because the Council uses medical projections to plan broadcasts.”

“Why would Broadcast have hospital records?”

“So they know what explanation to issue when too many people die in one district.”

The ordinariness of the answer frightened her.

He opened the case and removed a black data shard. “I found references to a transfer from the hospital to Cartography’s western archive. The file was marked ecological exposure research. The patients weren’t all from Lumen.”

“Mainland patients?”

“Some. Children, mostly.”

“Alive?”

“The records don’t say.”

“Then find records that do.”

“I’m trying.”

“You’re not trying hard enough.”

His eyes lifted. “I spent the night breaking into a system that records every action by time, location, and authorization band. I copied what I could before my father’s staff noticed. If I had tried harder, we’d be having this conversation in a security room.”

She had no answer. He connected the shard to the console.

“Show me the wafer.”

Mara did not move.

“You agreed.”

“I agreed to show you the survey. Not the photograph.”

“I remember.”

She removed the wafer and set it between them. Its surface was warm enough to fog the metal. Tomas connected it. The screen flickered, filled with corrupted symbols, and went black.

“Your copy is damaged.”

“It was made while a defense drone was trying to cut me open.”

“That would explain the formatting.”

He bridged contacts with a narrow tool. The screen brightened.

A map appeared: the former British coast surrounded by blue. Tide lines, elevation markers, old flood boundaries, and new channels layered over one another. Around the Thames Basin, water had withdrawn from whole stretches of elevated road and broken rail.

Tomas leaned closer. “This is dated.”

“Twelve years.”

“The shoreline was here before.”

He pointed to a thin white line inland, nearly swallowed by blue. “That was the stable boundary after the Continuance.”

“Officially, the ocean is still rising.”

“Officially, the basin is uninhabitable.”

Mara looked at the map. The change was not miraculous. It was measurable.

“The ocean is receding,” she said.

“Parts of it are.”

“Why?”

Tomas opened another layer. Data columns appeared: salinity, sediment load, atmospheric density, thermal exchange. Red symbols marked the entries.

“Not receding,” he said. “Redistributing. There’s been a circulation shift.”

“Why would the water move?”

“It may be linked to atmospheric discharge from Lumen.”

He enlarged the image. Beneath the coast, arrows spread from the city’s stabilizer zones.

Mara recognized the symbols. Exhaust columns. Pressure vents. Heat sinks. She had mapped some as abstract maintenance points without asking what passed through them.

“What are those?”

“Not weather systems.”

“Tell me.”

He opened a survey report. Its text had been compressed and marked for removal. Tomas restored the original layer.

**ATMOSPHERIC STABILIZATION ARRAY 4: DISCHARGE PLUME OBSERVED BEYOND DESIGN CORRIDOR. PARTICULATE CONCENTRATION EXCEEDS SURFACE TOLERANCE.**

Mara read it again.

“Surface tolerance.”

“The amount of pollution people can breathe before becoming ill.”

“It doesn’t say pollution.”

“It identifies polycyclic compounds, heavy-metal residue, and reactive carbon aerosols.”

She knew enough chemistry to recognize the list. She had seen the gray paste clog lower-ring filters.

“Those are from our exhaust.”

“From the stabilizers.”

“Lumen’s atmosphere has to be balanced.”

“Yes.”

“The systems keep us alive.”

“Yes.”

The two statements sat together, both true.

Mara opened the engineering diagram. The stabilizer network surrounded the city like a crown of invisible chimneys. It drew gases from the pressure chambers, altered them, and discharged them through controlled corridors. Public explanations described harmless conversion: excess carbon removed, oxygen balanced, heat dispersed.

The private notes said:

**DISCHARGE REDIRECTION REQUIRED TO MAINTAIN UPPER-RING PRESSURE. LOWER ATMOSPHERIC LAYERS DESIGNATED ACCEPTABLE RECEIVING VOLUME.**

Her mouth went dry. “They’re sending it down.”

“To the atmosphere around the mainland.”

“Why?”

“Waste has to go somewhere.”

Mara thought of children in the lower rings wearing filter scarves indoors. She thought of Eli coughing until his whole body folded around the sound.

“Is this why pressure is falling?”

“Not directly. The arrays are compensating for structural loss in the outer chambers. More exhaust is required to keep the upper rings stable.”

“And the lower rings?”

“Lower priority.”

She turned on him.

“That’s what the allocation model says,” he added.

“People aren’t allocation models.”

“No. But the system is.”

He opened the survey drone logs.

The first showed a settlement built along the upper decks of a collapsed motorway. Greenhouses stretched between concrete pillars. Solar cloth fluttered above them. People moved between rows of plants.

The next showed a clinic in the shell of a railway station, with a wind turbine on its roof. Another showed a child holding a red cloth in an open field.

Mara’s breath caught.

Tomas glanced at her. “The photograph?”

“No.”

He looked away.

The footage continued: a reed-bed purifier, fog-collecting nets, boats moving through a flooded street, a school beneath an elevated roadway, fields planted in bands, lights scattered across the dark coast.

Not one hidden outpost.

A network.

“There are people there,” Mara whispered.

“Yes.”

“Organized people.”

“Yes.”

“Clinics. Food.”

“Some.”

“Medicine?”

Tomas opened the medical file she had copied. Its header had been removed, but the treatment protocol remained: a compound derived from marsh fungus, stabilized anti-inflammatory carriers, and nebulized delivery.

The patient notes read:

**SYMPTOMS REDUCED WITHIN SEVENTY-TWO HOURS. RECURRENCE ASSOCIATED WITH RETURN TO HIGH-DENSITY ATMOSPHERIC CONTAMINATION.**

Mara read the line until the letters blurred.

“Eli could take this.”

“It’s not a guarantee.”

“It could help him.”

“Yes.”

“Where is it?”

Tomas searched the inventory. “Mainland settlements produced it locally. The hospital requisitioned samples eight months ago.”

“Eight months?”

“They classified it as unverified.”

“Yet they tested it.”

“On patients.”

Mara gripped the console. “They knew children were sick because of the air, and they kept giving us diluted doses while testing treatments on people they had already decided were expendable.”

Tomas did not disagree.

A new file opened beneath the medical records. It bore only a black Council seal and authorization codes.

“I can’t access this,” Tomas said.

“Can you open it?”

“I can try.”

“Try.”

He entered his father’s authorization sequence. The console rejected it. He entered another code. The lights dimmed, and somewhere beyond the walls a lock disengaged.

The file unfolded.

**CONTAINMENT COST ASSESSMENT: SURFACE IMPACTS ARISING FROM LUMEN STABILIZATION OPERATIONS**

A table listed regions: Thames Basin, Northern European Shelf, Western Atlantic Corridor. Each included projected mortality, agricultural loss, atmospheric degradation, and a final classification.

**ACCEPTABLE WITHIN CONTINUITY PARAMETERS.**

Mara could not look away.

The figures were not predictions of accidental harm. They had been calculated, compared, and approved.

A note read:

**Public acknowledgment of viable external populations may compromise compliance, increase unauthorized descent attempts, and destabilize labor allocation. Suppression remains preferable to uncontrolled disclosure.**

“Compliance,” Mara said.

Tomas’s face had gone white.

“They call people compliance.”

“Variables,” he said. “They call them variables.”

“You work for them.”

“I know.”

“You broadcast their explanations.”

“I know.”

“Do you tell yourself you didn’t write the words?”

His expression tightened. “Do you tell yourself your maps don’t trap people in districts without medicine?”

The words struck because they were true.

Then he looked ashamed. “I’m sorry.”

“No. Don’t apologize because it’s true.”

The next file began to decrypt.

A diagram appeared, vast and circular around Lumen.

**CROWN SEAL: PERMANENT ATMOSPHERIC ENCLOSURE AND CONTINUITY PRESERVATION SYSTEM.**

The architecture resolved. A ring of atmospheric collectors would be installed around the city. Pressure chambers would be sealed from outside exchange. Stabilizers would trap and concentrate waste beneath the enclosure. Buoyancy engines would draw energy from the pressure differential.

Lumen would become closed.

Not protected. Contained.

The projected benefits listed stable air, stable altitude, reduced maintenance, and permanent control over population movement. The costs occupied the other side.

**SURFACE ATMOSPHERIC ACCUMULATION: SEVERE.**  
**REGIONAL AGRICULTURAL LOSS: PROBABLE.**  
**COASTAL RECOVERY: REVERSED.**  
**LONG-TERM PLANETARY EFFECT: UNMODELED.**

At the bottom:

**ACTIVATION WINDOW: 143 DAYS.**

Mara felt the floor tilt.

“One hundred forty-three days,” Tomas said.

“Until they seal the city.”

“Until the system is fully operational.”

“And everyone below?”

“Outside the enclosure.”

“Everyone in Lumen?”

“Inside.”

He closed his eyes. “The Crown Seal was designed before my mother died. My father called it a contingency. A way to ensure that what remained of humanity survived if the planet couldn’t.”

“The planet hasn’t failed.”

“No.”

“The mainland is alive.”

“Yes.”

“Then why?”

Tomas looked at the fields and children on the screen. “Because if people knew, they might leave.”

Mara understood. Lumen did not float above a dead world. It floated above a world it had abandoned and damaged, preserving its hierarchy by making departure impossible.

Her faith did not collapse all at once. It shed pieces: the Council’s necessity, then its competence, then its claim to protect humanity. Finally, she lost the belief that its leaders could distinguish survival from ownership.

A warning flashed.

**UNAUTHORIZED ARCHIVE ACCESS. SIGNAL TRACE INITIATED.**

Tomas disconnected the wafer.

“We have to go.”

Mara did not move. The medical file remained in her mind: marsh fungus, anti-inflammatory carrier, seventy-two hours.

“We need the treatment,” she said.

“We need to get this evidence out.”

“We need both.”

“If we release this, they’ll lock the clinics, seize the hospitals, and shut every route to the lower rings. Eli is still there.”

“The city is planning to poison the mainland permanently.”

“I know.”

“And you want to use the information to bargain for one medicine?”

“I want my brother alive.”

The words sounded small beside the projected deaths and the poisoned atmosphere. But Eli was not a variable. He was twelve. He slept with one hand curled around his blanket because coughing frightened him when he woke alone.

Tomas’s expression changed.

“What would you bargain with?” he asked.

“The hospital records. The memorandum. The Crown Seal plans.”

“Those are evidence.”

“They’re medicine.”

“If we go to the clinic—”

“Not Pell. Someone higher.”

“My father.”

Mara looked sharply at him.

“He has access to the central medical authority,” Tomas said. “If he knows we have the Crown Seal file, he may trade.”

“Your father ordered the suppression.”

“He may still want the city protected.”

“By enclosing it?”

“By any means.”

“Then he’ll take the files and kill us.”

“Possibly.”

“You say that too calmly.”

“I’ve spent my life around people who call that a necessary risk.”

The trace warning pulsed red. Beyond the relay room, a door slammed.

Mara retrieved the wafer. “Can you copy the treatment protocol and identify where the samples went?”

“I can isolate it.”

“Do it.”

He reconnected the wafer. The medical file broke into fragments, stripped of archive markers, and reassembled an inventory route.

A destination appeared.

**CENTRAL RESEARCH HOSPITAL — ATMOSPHERIC ADAPTATION WARD.**

Mara’s stomach clenched.

“Eli,” she said.

Tomas stared at the line. “That’s where they send patients from the lower rings when ordinary treatment fails.”

“Why didn’t the clinic tell us?”

“The transfer is classified as voluntary research participation.”

“He never volunteered.”

“Children don’t sign their own forms.”

A heavy vibration rolled through the room. The console flickered. Somewhere in Lumen, an alarm began to sound.

Mara imagined Eli beneath white lights, his breathing measured by people who called suffering data.

“We get the medicine first,” she said.

Tomas looked from the Crown Seal file to her. “And after that?”

She slid the wafer into its sleeve.

“After that, we decide what the truth is worth.”

Outside, the city announcement system came alive.

“Citizens are reminded that atmospheric fluctuations remain within expected parameters. Unauthorized access to restricted infrastructure threatens the safety of all.”

Mara listened to the calm, familiar voice. It spoke as if safety were a place the Council owned and could lock whenever it wished.

She opened the relay-room door.

The corridor beyond filled with pale emergency light. At its far end, boots struck the metal floor in a measured rhythm.

Tomas picked up his case.

For the first time since entering the archive, Mara did not feel that she was stealing a map.

She felt that she was carrying a door.

chapters.name: A Bargain with the Clinic
chapters.content:
## A Bargain with the Clinic

The clinic occupied the lowest level of the medical ring, where the walls sweated condensation and every breath tasted faintly of metal.

Mara stood beside Tomas beneath the flickering intake sign, watching a woman in a yellow work coat argue with the reception clerk over a child’s fever. The clerk kept pointing to a screen. The woman kept pointing to the child.

“Her pressure is falling,” she said. “You can see it.”

“I can see that your household allocation is exhausted.”

“She needs the stabilizer.”

“The stabilizer is restricted.”

The child leaned against her mother’s knees, eyes half closed. The clinic’s air recyclers clicked and coughed overhead. Somewhere beyond the partition, a machine gave a soft, regular hiss—the sound of medicine being administered to someone who had been approved.

Tomas shifted beside Mara. He wore a maintenance jacket borrowed from a broadcast technician, its collar pulled high enough to hide his face from the ceiling cameras. The jacket smelled of dust and hot wiring. He had brought no weapon, only the data case tucked beneath his arm and the authorization band on his wrist, which was no longer pale and unmarked. He had scratched the Ministry seal until it looked damaged.

“Not here,” he murmured.

Mara looked toward the corridor marked AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL.

“The treatment is here.”

“The people who control it are also here.”

“That is usually how medicine works.”

His mouth tightened. “You know what I mean.”

She did. The clinic’s visible dispensary held only diluted inhalants and common anti-inflammatory tablets. The effective cartridges were kept behind a sealed counter, each one recorded, numbered, and assigned. They had seen the inventory before coming. Tomas had pulled it from a continuity archive: thirty-two cartridges in storage, twelve expiring within the month, all designated for upper-ring respiratory events.

Eli had been coughing blood into a cloth that morning.

Mara had left him with Sela asleep beside the heater, though neither of them had really been sleeping. The clinic had sent a message to their household just after dawn: Eli Venn was scheduled for reassessment. No explanation. No appointment time. No mention that the Central Research Hospital had placed a transfer request.

The message had been signed by Administrator Pell.

Mara had read it twice, then handed the screen to Tomas.

“Pell knows,” Tomas had said.

“Then we make him admit it.”

Now Pell sat behind a glass office at the far end of the clinic, surrounded by screens displaying pressure graphs, patient queues, and the green figures of available stock. He was a narrow man with a soft face and an immaculate white coat. Mara remembered his expression when he had denied Eli the cartridge: regret arranged carefully over indifference.

Tomas opened the data case. “We get him to verify the inventory and the public report. I record the exchange. If he refuses, we release the files.”

“To whom?”

“Clinic staff. Patients. Anyone with a receiver.”

“And if they take the case?”

“They can’t erase what’s already copied.”

Mara touched the warm wafer inside the case through its insulating sleeve. The damaged data still held the mainland images, the medical protocol, and the containment assessment. They had made two partial copies in the relay room before security arrived, but the files were incomplete and unstable. If the Council seized the originals, they might lose the only proof tying the clinic’s stock to the withheld treatment.

She thought of the child’s red cloth in the field below the clouds. She had not shown Tomas the photograph. Some things were not evidence simply because they could be used as evidence.

The woman in yellow was escorted away from the desk. Her child’s fever had become an administrative problem, and administrative problems had guards.

Mara walked toward Pell’s office.

The doors recognized Tomas’s damaged band and opened halfway before locking. A red line appeared across the threshold.

“State purpose,” said the door.

“Medical compliance review,” Tomas answered.

“Authorization insufficient.”

Mara raised her voice. “Administrator Pell, you have restricted inhalant cartridges in storage and patients in this clinic who have been denied them. We have the inventory records.”

The office went still.

Pell looked up. His eyes moved from Mara to Tomas, then to the data case. He did not look surprised. That frightened her more than surprise would have.

“Please step away from the security threshold,” he said.

“You know my brother,” Mara said. “Eli Venn. Tier Four technical citizen. Respiratory deterioration. Your clinic supplied him a diluted dose while effective cartridges remained in storage.”

“Treatment decisions are made according to approved allocation standards.”

“You also filed a report saying no restricted stock was available.”

Pell’s gaze flicked toward the nearest camera.

Tomas lifted the case. “We can publish the inventory and the report discrepancy within the hour.”

Pell’s face changed then—not into fear, but calculation.

“You are threatening a medical facility.”

“We are informing you of a choice,” Tomas said. “Release one cartridge for Eli. Release the mainland treatment protocol to the clinic physicians. Correct the public health report. In return, the files remain private.”

Mara stared at him. “That isn’t the bargain.”

“It gets Eli treated.”

“It gets one dose.”

“It gets us inside the system.”

Pell gave a small, humorless laugh. “You think this is a negotiation.”

Tomas leaned closer to the glass. “Your own records show that the treatment works.”

“Your records are classified.”

“Your patients are dying.”

The administrator’s expression hardened. “You have no authority to interpret research data.”

“Then let a physician interpret it,” Mara said. “Open the records. Call the ward staff. We’ll wait.”

For a moment she imagined it happening. Pell unlocking the door. Nurses gathering around the data case. Someone carrying Eli in from the lower ring. A cartridge pressed into his hand. A correction issued. A small crack in the wall.

Pell touched two fingers to the desk.

The clinic lights dimmed.

Mara heard the faint click of locks engaging throughout the building.

“You should leave,” Pell said.

“Or what?”

“Or the clinic will report an attempted infrastructure breach.”

Tomas’s jaw tightened. “You’re going to report us for asking you to treat a child?”

“I am going to report unauthorized possession of restricted medical records, coercive interference with allocation procedures, and suspected transmission of contaminated data.”

“Contaminated?”

Pell looked at Mara. “Mainland protocols are unverified. They may be designed to compromise Lumen’s atmospheric defenses.”

Mara felt something cold move through her chest.

“You know that’s a lie.”

“I know that every unauthorized treatment increases risk to the population.”

Behind him, one of the inventory screens refreshed. For less than a second, the number appeared clearly.

RESTRICTED INHALANT: 32 AVAILABLE.

Then the display turned black.

Pell’s hand remained on the desk. “Security is on its way.”

Mara pulled the data case from Tomas before he could stop her and held it against her ribs.

“Publish it,” she said.

Tomas looked at her.

“Now.”

He opened the case. His fingers moved over the transmitter panel. The clinic’s local network appeared, a list of patient terminals and staff channels. He selected all available receivers.

A warning flashed.

UNAUTHORIZED DISTRIBUTION WILL INITIATE COUNCIL REVIEW.

“Do it,” Mara said.

Tomas pressed transmit.

Nothing happened.

The screen displayed a single line: CONNECTION OVERRIDDEN.

Tomas swore under his breath.

Pell sat down.

Not hurriedly. Not with relief. As if the outcome had been decided before they entered.

Mara heard boots in the corridor.

“They were waiting,” she said.

Tomas closed the case. “Move.”

The door behind them opened. Two security officers entered, helmets sealed, shock batons hanging at their sides. A third officer remained in the corridor, speaking into a throat mic.

Mara backed away from the office.

“By order of the Civic Continuity Council,” the first officer said, “surrender all restricted materials and submit for questioning.”

“Where is my brother?” Mara demanded.

The officer’s visor reflected her face back at her, stretched and dark.

“Eli Venn has been transferred for urgent respiratory observation.”

“When?”

“During this interaction.”

The words struck harder than the officer’s baton could have.

Mara turned toward Pell. “You transferred him while we were here?”

“His condition required specialist care.”

“You put him in the Atmospheric Adaptation Ward.”

Pell did not answer.

Tomas grabbed Mara’s arm. “We have to go.”

She twisted free. “You said he was still at home.”

“I said the request was pending.”

“You knew.”

“I suspected.”

The officers advanced.

Mara threw the data case at the nearest ceiling camera. It struck the lens, burst into sparks, and dropped. For three seconds the clinic’s alarms screamed. Tomas pulled her through a side door marked STERILE MATERIALS, and they ran.

They did not make it past the service stairs.

A security barrier rose from the floor, sealing the lower corridor. On the other side, another team waited. Tomas stopped so abruptly that Mara collided with him.

“Down,” he said.

They dropped as a pulse discharged overhead. The air flashed blue. Mara felt the charge crawl across her teeth.

When she looked up, Pell was standing at the end of the corridor with the security officers.

“Take the girl for questioning,” he said. “The Ministry aide is to be held under continuity review.”

Tomas’s face went blank.

“Mara,” he whispered, “when I say run—”

A hand seized her from behind.

She kicked, struck armor, heard someone shout. Tomas lunged toward her, but two officers pinned him against the wall. His damaged authorization band snapped under a gloved hand.

Mara screamed Eli’s name.

The sound vanished beneath the alarm.

Then the clinic doors closed between them.

They released Mara three hours later.

No one questioned her. No one asked for the files, the names of the mainland settlements, or the reason she had entered the clinic. She was placed in a white room with a drain in the floor and watched through dark glass. Every twenty minutes a speaker announced that cooperation would be recorded as evidence of civic responsibility.

When the door opened, a clerk handed her belongings back in a sealed pouch.

The data case was gone.

Tomas was gone.

The clerk did not meet her eyes. “Your residence has been placed under administrative restriction.”

Mara ran.

The medical ring connected to the lower residential rings by a transit shaft, but the public gates rejected her band. She took maintenance stairs, climbed two levels, crossed a ventilation gallery, and emerged behind the school where Eli had once drawn pressure balloons in the dust.

The city felt wrong.

Announcements played at the intersections, calm and bright.

“Atmospheric fluctuations remain within expected parameters. Residents are reminded that unauthorized access to medical, infrastructure, or archival systems places all citizens at risk.”

Every screen displayed the same blue circle.

Lumen’s pressure was 96.1%.

Mara reached the Venn apartment and found a seal across the door.

PROPERTY UNDER CONTINUITY REVIEW.

Her household terminal showed no credit balance. Housing authorization: suspended. Employment access: pending investigation. Dependent status: under reassessment.

For a long moment she simply stood there, unable to understand the shape of the words.

Then she pressed her palm to the door.

“Sela?”

No answer.

She tried the emergency override. The panel flashed red.

“Eli?”

Still nothing.

A neighbor opened her door two units away. Mrs. Anik, who repaired school uniforms, looked at Mara and then at the seal.

“They came before noon,” she whispered. “Your mother was here.”

“Where did they take her?”

“I don’t know.”

“You saw them.”

“I saw officers.”

“Where?”

Mrs. Anik glanced at the corridor cameras. “Mara, go.”

“Where?”

Her neighbor shut the door.

Mara stood beneath the announcement speaker until her knees weakened. She slid down the wall and pressed both hands over her mouth.

Eli had been transferred. Sela had been taken. The apartment was no longer theirs. Their credits, their food allotment, their right to remain in the city—all of it could be erased with a few commands.

The system had not broken.

It had noticed her.

A maintenance hatch opened at the end of the corridor.

Tomas stepped out.

His cheek was bruised, and one sleeve of his borrowed jacket had been torn away. He closed the hatch behind him and leaned against the wall, breathing hard.

Mara stood.

“You knew where they took her?”

“I found out after they separated us.”

“You let them take me.”

“I was locked in a compliance room.”

“You’re the minister’s son.”

His expression flinched. “That stopped mattering when they broke my authorization band.”

“Where is Sela?”

“Transport holding, lower civic intake. She was arrested trying to get into the clinic.”

Mara stared at him.

“She went back?” she asked.

“She had a cartridge.”

The corridor seemed to tilt.

Tomas continued quickly. “One of the lower-ring technicians had an unregistered dose. Sela tried to bring it to Eli. They caught her at the ward entrance.”

“Is she hurt?”

“I don’t know. The holding record says unauthorized medical interference. It also says she resisted transfer.”

“She wouldn’t.”

“Records don’t require truth.”

Mara looked at the sealed apartment. “And Eli?”

“Central Research Hospital. Atmospheric Adaptation Ward. Transfer completed under emergency authority.”

“Can we get him out?”

Tomas took a breath. “Not through any route my family controls.”

“Then what good are you?”

“Less than I thought.”

He reached inside his jacket and removed a thin gray authorization plate. It bore the seal of the Lumen Maintenance Directorate, along with a string of numbers and a time stamp.

Mara did not take it.

“What is that?”

“A work order.”

“It looks real.”

“It isn’t.”

“Who did you steal it from?”

“No one. I made it.”

She gave him a flat look.

Tomas held the plate out. “The Ministry has access to old maintenance templates. The Directorate still accepts emergency orders if the pressure data attached to them looks severe enough. I wrote one for a stabilizer inspection beneath the hospital. It grants temporary access to restricted service levels.”

“Temporary how?”

“Forty-six minutes before the system flags the mismatch.”

“Why would it let us into the hospital?”

“Because the hospital’s lower pressure chambers are connected to the atmospheric network. The Directorate prefers technicians over doctors when the alarms are technical.”

Mara took the plate. It was warm from his hand.

“And Sela?”

“The holding area is below civic intake. The same service levels connect to it.”

“You made this to rescue both of them?”

“I made it because my father’s office can no longer protect me,” Tomas said. “I might as well use what it taught me.”

Mara studied his bruised face. “Your father knows?”

“He will soon.”

“Will he help?”

Tomas looked toward the announcement speaker.

“His office sent the order to seal your home.”

Something inside Mara tightened, though she had expected it.

“Then we go now.”

“We need equipment. The hospital levels have automated locks, biometric checks, and security patrols.”

“Where do we get equipment?”

“Maintenance depot three corridors east. I can spoof the inventory request, but we’ll need a pressure mask, cutting tool, and transport harness.”

“For Eli?”

“For anyone we move through the restricted ward.”

Mara’s eyes lifted. “Anyone?”

Tomas hesitated.

“The transfer list had more than Eli’s name,” he said. “Children, mostly. Some are marked as voluntary participants. Some have no consent record at all.”

The corridor filled with the distant hum of a pump cycling.

Mara thought of Pell’s thirty-two cartridges. Of the child with the fever. Of the invisible fields beneath the clouds. Of her mother walking into a clinic with medicine clenched in her hand because the official world had left her no other choice.

“Then we don’t only take Eli,” she said.

Tomas’s expression sharpened. “Mara—”

“We get Sela. We get the patients we can carry. We take the treatment and the records.”

“That is not an escape. That is an uprising inside a hospital.”

“It became that when they took my family.”

He looked at the false work order, then at the sealed apartment.

“Once we enter, we may not be able to come back.”

Mara slid the authorization plate into her sleeve.

“We can’t come back here anyway.”

Above them, Lumen shuddered. The lights dimmed, recovered, and dimmed again. From somewhere deep in the city came the slow groan of metal under pressure.

Tomas opened the maintenance hatch.

Mara followed him into the dark.

chapters.name: The Descent Capsule
chapters.content:
## The Descent Capsule

The counterfeit work order lasted forty-six minutes.

At minute thirty-one, the hospital noticed they did not belong there.

Mara heard it in the ventilation. The lower service levels had breathed with a steady mechanical pull, air dragged through filters and pressure gates in measured cycles. Then the rhythm faltered. A valve opened somewhere behind the walls and slammed shut.

Tomas stopped beneath a strip of yellow light.

“Did you hear that?”

“Yes.”

He glanced at the stolen pressure mask hanging from his shoulder. “The system has queried the order.”

“How long?”

“Not enough.”

Ahead, a sealed hatch bore the faded designation CIVIC INTAKE—LOWER TRANSFER. Tomas pressed the work order to the reader. For a second, nothing happened.

Then the hatch unlocked.

Mara shoved it open.

The holding area beyond was divided by waist-high rails. Empty transport chairs stood in rows, restraint straps hanging loose. A sanitation drone pushed a smear of blood toward a drain.

Sela sat on the far side of the room.

Her hands were bound in front of her. Her hair had come loose, and one side of her face was bruised beneath the eye. When she saw Mara, she rose so quickly that her chair toppled.

“Mara?”

Mara crossed the room. “Are you hurt?”

“Only where they expected me to be.” Sela’s gaze went to Tomas. “You brought him.”

“He got us in.”

“He got us arrested.”

“That was Pell,” Tomas said.

“And who are you?”

“Later,” Mara said. She knelt at the restraint. “Hold still.”

The cutting tool whined against the band. Sparks jumped. Mara’s hands shook so badly she nearly cut Sela’s sleeve.

“You shouldn’t have come,” Sela said.

“We’re getting you out.”

“Eli?”

Mara looked toward Tomas.

He had moved to the intake terminal. Lines of text crawled across the narrow screen beneath his fingers.

“Where is he?” Mara asked.

Tomas did not answer.

“Tomas.”

“He was transferred.”

Sela’s face tightened. “Transferred where?”

“The log says Central Research, pressure annex seven.”

“That is where he was,” Mara said. “Where is he now?”

Tomas leaned closer. “The transfer was executed eleven minutes ago.”

“Executed?”

“Completed.”

“Find the destination.”

“I’m trying.”

Mara cut through the final strand. Sela’s hands dropped into her lap, red marks circling both wrists.

“Eli was in the Atmospheric Adaptation Ward,” Mara said. “You said the lower levels connected to it.”

“They do,” Tomas replied. “But not if they moved him through the research shaft.”

“Can we reach it?”

“No.”

The answer came too quickly.

Mara stood. “You said we had forty-six minutes.”

“We have twelve now.”

“Then we go to him.”

“The research shaft is under central security. If we force it, every guard in the hospital comes here.”

“Let them.”

“Mara.” Sela took her arm. “Listen to him.”

The chamber speakers clicked.

“Unauthorized maintenance activity detected in civic transfer sector. All personnel remain in assigned positions. Security response is in progress.”

Sela gripped Mara’s sleeve. “You have the evidence?”

Mara felt the warm wafer against the inside seam of her coveralls. Tomas had hidden it there after they stole the harness, wrapping it in insulation. It was no bigger than her thumb, but heat pulsed through the fabric.

“Some of it,” Mara said.

“The records?”

“Partial copies. The treatment protocol. The Crown Seal plans.”

“Then you leave.”

Mara stared at her. “Not without Eli.”

“You leave with what you have.”

“I can’t.”

“You can.” Sela’s voice took on the firm tone she used when a membrane split and an entire ring depended on her hands. “You think saving him means standing in the same room as him. It means making sure what they did to him cannot disappear.”

“We can still reach him.”

“No.” Sela stepped closer. “I heard them talking. They moved the children because security was coming. They were afraid someone would find the consent files.”

“Then we go to the shaft.”

“And get taken before you can tell anyone what you saw?”

Mara’s throat closed.

Sela pressed both hands against her face. Her palms smelled of filter resin and antiseptic.

“Your father went back,” she whispered. “He found something wrong in the arrays. He thought that if he proved it, they would have to stop. They killed him before he could show anyone.”

Mara had spent eight years refusing to imagine Jon’s last day. Now she saw fragments: his coat beside the kitchen vent, unfinished tea, the official notice folded into Sela’s hands. Accident during atmospheric-relay pressure maintenance. No body recovered.

“Don’t use him to make me run,” Mara said.

“I’m using him to make you understand.” Sela’s thumb brushed the bruise beneath Mara’s eye. “The truth is not safer because you keep it close. It is safer when it belongs to everyone.”

A burst of static tore through the speakers. Tomas looked toward the entrance.

“Security is inside the intake corridor.”

Mara turned to him. “What can we do?”

“Get her to the external service deck.”

“And Eli?”

“Not now.”

The words struck harder than a blow.

For one moment Mara imagined abandoning him: Eli strapped to a bed beneath the hospital, breathing air measured by people who called his pain useful. She imagined him waking and asking where she was.

Sela caught her hand.

“If you surrender, they will take the evidence,” she said. “They will say Eli was sick. They will say you were unstable. They will say I attacked a clinic. They will turn us into a story that protects them.”

Mara looked at the terminal. The last transfer log still glowed.

PATIENT ELI VENN—ATMOSPHERIC ADAPTATION OBSERVATION  
DESTINATION: SEALED  
STATUS: CONTINUITY PRIORITY

She reached for the service port.

“What are you doing?” Tomas asked.

“Copying the transfer record.”

“It will alert the system.”

“It already knows we’re here.”

Mara jammed the wafer into the terminal. The screen flashed white. Data poured through it—patient names, movement codes, chemical protocols, redacted consent forms. The terminal shrieked.

“Take it out!”

She pulled the wafer free. Its casing burned her fingers.

The hatch at the far end buckled inward.

Sela grabbed a discarded transport coat and threw it around her shoulders. Tomas pulled on the pressure mask and helmet.

“Which way?” Mara asked.

“Left, then down two levels.”

“Down?”

“The external decks are below the hospital.”

They ran.

The first corridor gate rejected Tomas’s damaged authorization band. He tried again.

“Use the work order,” Mara said.

“It’s tied to my identity.”

“Then lie better.”

He held the counterfeit order to the reader. The gate opened.

They slipped through as security boots thundered behind them.

The maintenance stairs descended through a narrow shaft filled with hot metal air. Sela went first, one hand on the rail, breathing hard but steadily. Mara followed, listening to Tomas count doors.

At the third landing, the city trembled.

Dust sifted from the ceiling.

Sela stopped. “What was that?”

“Pressure adjustment,” Tomas said.

“You’re lying.”

“Yes.”

Another tremor rolled upward through the shaft. Machinery groaned below them.

Mara pressed her palm to the wall. It pulsed beneath her skin.

Ninety-six point one percent.

The city was losing the invisible force that held it up.

“We move,” she said.

They reached the service-deck access. Tomas removed a small metal key and slid it into the manual lock.

“Where did you get that?” Mara asked.

“Ministry emergency cabinet.”

“You stole it?”

“Borrowed it.”

“Planning to return it?”

“Only if we survive.”

The lock turned.

The outer door opened onto darkness.

Wind struck Mara and stole her breath. Beyond the narrow deck, clouds streamed beneath Lumen in vast white rivers. The city’s underside stretched away in girders, tanks, cables, and glowing maintenance lights. Far below, breaks in the cloud revealed black water and scattered pinpoints of light.

“The capsules,” Tomas said. “Bay four.”

They hurried along the deck. A row of cargo capsules waited beneath a retractable canopy, each shaped like a blunt metal seed, their undersides scorched from earlier launches.

Tomas reached the nearest control panel.

A red light blinked.

“Cargo authorization required.”

“Give it authorization.”

“I’m working on it.”

Behind them, the external door burst open.

Security officers spilled onto the deck in pressure armor.

“Stop!” one shouted. “By order of the Council, remain where you are!”

Tomas slapped his band against the panel. “Ministry emergency evacuation.”

“Your authorization is revoked.”

“Then you’ll have to revoke the Council’s pressure data too.”

The guard raised his weapon.

Mara shoved Sela toward the capsule. “Inside!”

The first shot struck the canopy. Metal rang. Sparks scattered across the deck.

Sela fell into a harness seat. Mara crawled beside her and locked the straps across both their chests.

Tomas remained outside.

“Tomas!”

He ducked behind a supply crate, pulled a cable from his belt, and jammed it into the launch panel. Three officers advanced.

Then Tomas punched the panel.

The capsule dropped.

Mara was crushed into her harness. For one impossible instant it hung in open air, and Lumen spread above them like a second sky—towers, bridges, and luminous gardens turning behind cloud.

Then the descent engines fired.

The capsule plunged through the clouds.

White swallowed everything. The walls groaned. Loose tools spun through the cabin. Sela’s fingers found Mara’s and locked around them.

“Where is Tomas?” she gasped.

Mara looked toward the forward compartment.

He had thrown himself into the pilot’s seat, though the capsule had no true pilot controls. He worked through flashing error screens.

“Descent guidance is damaged,” he said.

“Can you fix it?”

“I can make it less broken.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“It’s what we have.”

The capsule burst beneath the clouds.

For the first time Mara saw the world below.

Water covered much of the old basin, but not all. Dark channels wound between drowned roads. Towers rose from the flood like snapped bones. Farther inland, an elevated structure crossed the marshlands, its upper levels dotted with green lights.

Green lights.

“There,” Mara whispered.

Sela followed her gaze. “What?”

“Nothing.”

The capsule lurched sideways.

Warning symbols flared. A pressure alarm began to pulse.

Tomas pulled a lever. One descent engine roared; another coughed into silence.

“We’re losing attitude control,” he said.

“What does that mean?” Sela asked.

“It means we may land hard.”

“How hard?”

Tomas looked at Mara.

“Very,” she said.

The capsule rolled. Through the forward window, the landscape spun: cloud, water, sky, Lumen’s underside, then a streak of green climbing over concrete.

Tomas fought the controls. “The stabilizer isn’t responding.”

“Restart it.”

“Not from here.”

“Where, then?”

“The external housing.”

Mara unfastened her harness.

“No,” Sela said.

“The housing is already gone,” Tomas told her.

Through the side port Mara saw only twisted struts where the fin had been.

A calm voice announced, “Impact projection: ninety seconds.”

Sela began to laugh, a brittle sound at the edge of fear.

“Ninety seconds,” she said. “They always make everything sound manageable.”

Tomas found a manual ballast release.

“Will it help?” Mara asked.

“It might slow the roll.”

“Why might?”

“The system was designed for an intact capsule.”

He released the ballast. Crates and emergency canisters tore free and vanished below. The capsule jerked upward, then dropped more steeply.

The elevated structure grew larger.

Not a structure. A station.

Its roof had collapsed in places, but vines covered the surviving platforms. A wind turbine turned in the sunlight. Along old tracks, bright rectangles moved slowly through the reeds.

Vehicles.

People lived here.

The alarms merged into one continuous shriek.

“Brace!” Tomas shouted.

Mara pulled Sela’s head against her shoulder and wrapped both arms around her. Tomas folded over the console.

The first impact struck the capsule’s underside.

Metal screamed. The world snapped sideways. Something exploded behind them, filling the cabin with heat and the bitter smell of burned insulation.

They hit again.

The window shattered.

Cloud, sky, and ground became one white-gold blur. The capsule tore through branches or cables, something whipping across Mara’s face, then slammed into a hard surface that gave way beneath them.

They rolled down a slope.

Mara heard Sela shouting her name. She heard Tomas say something about the hatch. Then the ground rose.

The impact drove all the air from her lungs.

Darkness closed over her.

When she opened her eyes, the capsule lay on its side among reeds and broken concrete. Smoke drifted through the torn hull. Sunlight poured through the missing roof, warmer and more yellow than Lumen’s artificial dawn.

For several seconds Mara could not remember how to breathe.

Then Sela moved beside her.

“Mara?”

“I’m here.”

“Your head?”

“Attached.”

Tomas groaned from the forward compartment. “A low standard for success.”

Mara tried to unfasten her harness. The buckle had jammed. She reached for the cutting tool.

Outside, something moved through the reeds.

A voice called from the distance.

Not an announcement. Not a security command.

A human voice.

“Is anyone alive in there?”

Mara froze.

Through the fractured window, beyond the smoke and ruined station, figures approached with tools in their hands and cloth wrapped over their mouths. Behind them stood elevated garden beds, leaves bright against the drowned city.

The mainland was breathing.

So was she.

chapters.name: The Living Shore
chapters.content:
## The Living Shore

The first thing Mara heard was water.

Not the measured rush inside Lumen’s pipes, not the thin hiss of recycled air through a wall vent, but water moving without permission. It slapped against something hollow, withdrew over stones, and returned with a patient force that seemed to come from everywhere.

She opened her eyes.

Grey daylight leaked through the torn side of the capsule. Reeds bent in the wind beyond the gap, their narrow leaves silvered with moisture. A hand appeared above her, then another, both wrapped in dark gloves. Someone was saying something, but the words reached her through layers of ringing metal and blood.

“—alive. I can see three. Get the brace.”

Mara tried to move and discovered that the world had fastened itself to her ribs. Pain flared beneath her left shoulder. She made a sound.

“Don’t,” Sela said somewhere near her feet. “Mara, don’t move.”

Her mother’s voice was hoarse, but real.

Mara turned her head. Sela lay half beneath the collapsed equipment rack, one cheek streaked with blood and black grease. Her hands were free. That was enough to make Mara breathe again.

“Tomas?”

A shape shifted in the cockpit. Tomas was wedged against the forward bulkhead, eyes closed, one arm hanging at an angle that made Mara’s stomach clench.

The gloved hands reached through the rupture. A face appeared behind them: brown skin, close-cropped hair, and a strip of green cloth tied over the mouth and nose. The stranger’s eyes moved quickly over the capsule’s interior.

“Which one is breathing badly?”

“Sela,” Mara said.

“Wrong,” Sela muttered. “The boy is worse.”

“I’m not—” Tomas coughed. His eyes opened. “I’m not a boy.”

The stranger looked at him. “You’re bleeding into your sleeve.”

“I’m aware.”

“Then be aware quietly.”

A second figure climbed onto the broken hull. She was younger, perhaps Mara’s age, with a braid tucked beneath a yellow cap and a set of tools hanging from a belt around her hips. She looked down at Tomas, then at the capsule’s ruptured engine housing.

“Pressure cell’s leaking,” she called. “If it catches, we lose the whole frame.”

“Can you stop it?”

“Can you make the water stop being wet?”

The first stranger ignored them. “We’re cutting the side panel. Move when I tell you.”

The panel screamed as a cutting tool bit through it. Mara closed her eyes. The sound shuddered through her bones, and for one impossible moment she was back on the descent, clouds spinning outside the capsule, security fire blooming against the hull. Sela’s hand had been locked around hers. Tomas had been shouting that the ballast was gone.

Then the mainland had appeared beneath them.

Not a wasteland. Not a drowned silence.

Lights in the green.
