“That is the point,” Mara said. “No one should be forced.”

“Even if refusal kills people elsewhere?”

Mara looked at the lines crossing the map. “Then we explain the cost. We give them the data. We let them answer.”

Imani’s mouth tightened. “You are asking for a decision process the Council spent a century destroying.”

“Yes.”

“Under pressure?”

“Yes.”

“While the Seal activates?”

Mara folded the map along its old creases. “There is no safe time to learn how to be responsible.”

Imani studied her. “Do not confuse restraint with virtue, Mara. If we hesitate until everyone is safe, the Seal will be complete.”

“And if we act as though everyone is expendable, we will build another Lumen.”

For a moment, the only sound was rain on the roof.

Then Imani nodded. “We go in. We broadcast the truth. We attempt the conversion.”

Nia came to the table and pointed at the submerged route. “If you enter through the Thames, you will need a mechanic.”

Imani’s head snapped toward her. “No.”

“The outer conduits are older than the city’s public systems. Their seals will be improvised.”

“That is exactly why you are staying here.”

“Who else knows improvised seals?”

Imani opened her mouth, then stopped.

Nia looked at Mara. “You said people inside need a chance to act. Someone has to find them the broken things.”

Mara thought of Nia beneath the railway walkway, listening to water move through a pipe as though it spoke. “She comes.”

“I do not need permission to be a fighter,” Nia said.

“You need to be alive when the work begins.”

Nia considered that, then nodded.

Across the hall, a woman holding a sleeping child rose. “If you broadcast, what will you tell them?”

Mara looked at the blank side of the map. She had tried to write a statement on the boat, but every sentence sounded like Ministry language: The truth must be heard. We act for the future. Lumen citizens deserve to know.

“I will tell them what happened,” she said. “What we know and what we do not. I will show them the people living below. I will show them the children harmed by the emissions. I will tell them that the systems keeping Lumen alive are connected to the systems harming us. Then I will tell them how to open the doors.”

“And if they choose not to?”

“Then we keep answering the people who do.”

Imani stopped Mara as the delegates began organizing channels and supplies.

“You understand what you are asking,” she said.

“Not entirely.”

“You may not get Eli out.”

“I know.”

“You may enter Lumen and find that its people will not help you.”

“I know.”

“You may broadcast the truth and make the conversion impossible.”

Mara’s fingers closed around the map. “If we do nothing, the outcome is already decided.”

“That does not mean your plan will work.”

“No.”

Imani’s expression softened. “Good. People who believe they alone can save everyone become dangerous very quickly. Do not become indispensable.”

Mara glanced toward Tomas, who was unwrapping the transfer module. “I will try.”

“Trying is not a structure.”

“Then we build one.”

They returned to the table.

The first copy of the transfer logs failed. The second opened with numbers and no names. The third revealed a route designation, then froze.

Tomas tapped the casing. “It wants an authorization handshake.”

“Can you give it one?”

“Not without a source.”

Mara removed the warm data wafer from inside her jacket. Its surface glowed faintly through the protective sleeve.

Imani caught her wrist. “That may erase the hospital evidence.”

“Or unlock the transfer record.”

“That is a risk.”

Mara thought of the names trapped inside the wafer: children, workers, patients reduced to categories by the same machines that had reduced her father to an accident.

“We cannot rescue what we cannot locate.”

Imani released her.

Mara connected the wafer.

For several seconds, nothing happened. Then the module’s dead screen flickered. A line appeared, blurred and incomplete.

**WARD 6-B TRANSFER—**

The next characters dissolved into static.

Tomas leaned closer. “Again.”

The system tried to read the damaged data. Beyond the walls, the radio network answered with bursts of voices: a storm warning from the islands, a pump failure near the southern channel, a request for antibiotics from an elevated school.

The habit of answering.

Mara placed one hand on the map while the module struggled to open.

“We go at first light,” she said.

Imani nodded. “We go to Lumen.”

Nia marked the submerged route in blue.

Tomas adjusted the radio frequency.

Around them, the mainland began preparing not for a battle, but for a conversation dangerous enough to change the direction of an entire city.

chapters.name: The Route Beneath the Thames
chapters.content:
### The Route Beneath the Thames

Mara found the tunnel because the river had lied.

Not deliberately. Rivers had no intentions, only gradients and memory. But the old Thames had been forced into new channels around collapsed embankments, flooded stations, and buried foundations. Its surface told one story while the structures beneath it told another.

She spread the oldest map across the geology hall floor and weighted its corners with relay batteries. The paper was the color of weak tea, its edges marked by tide stains. Across it, someone had drawn the Thames in careful black lines: docks, ferries, pump stations, rail crossings, flood barriers.

Lumen appeared nowhere.

Mara had to remind herself that this was natural. The city had not yet been built when the map was made. Yet Lumen’s infrastructure had older roots. Its first platforms had been anchored to submerged service towers and pressure conduits driven into the basin floor.

She traced the river with one finger.

“Here,” she said.

Nia, lying beside the map with a dismantled valve assembly, lifted her head. “That’s the river.”

“Not the river. The old maintenance line.”

“It’s a dotted line.”

“Exactly.”

Nia squinted. “You’re excited about a dotted line?”

“The surveyor couldn’t verify the entire route.”

“Or got bored.”

Mara fetched three more maps. The first showed the line as a faint red scar. The second showed nothing beneath the river. The third, printed twenty-two years later, bore a handwritten note:

**LOWER ACCESS RETAINED FOR AERIAL SUPPORT NETWORK. ENTRY FLOODED.**

Mara’s pulse quickened.

“Imani,” she called.

Imani was at the radio table, arranging a pump repair with a settlement in the eastern marshes. She raised one finger without turning. Mara waited, though waiting had become almost impossible. The case containing Eli’s transfer module sat beside her knee. Its screen remained dark. Her warm data wafer, wrapped in cloth and sealed against moisture, rested in an insulated sleeve.

The words **WARD 6-B TRANSFER—** had appeared for less than a second before dissolving into static.

A fragment was barely a promise.

Imani finished the radio exchange and crossed the hall. Mara pointed to the maps.

“This is beneath the Thames. It connects to a lower pressure-control conduit.”

Imani bent over them. Her face changed with recognition.

“I worked from the northern side once,” she said. “Before the lower city was closed.”

“You knew it was here?”

“I knew there had been a service route. I thought it collapsed.”

“The newer maps show it as collapsed.”

“Newer maps show many useful things as collapsed.”

Nia sat up. “Can we get through?”

“Possibly.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only honest one.”

Mara marked distances from old landmarks: a church tower visible only at low tide, the broken roof of a rail terminus, a submerged ventilation stack. “If the tunnel still reaches the northern shafts, it could take us beneath Lumen’s lower infrastructure.”

“And if it doesn’t?” Tomas asked.

He stood near the doors in a mainland rain coat over the remains of his Ministry uniform. The silver broadcast insignia was gone, though the cloth still held its shape.

“Then we come back,” Nia said.

Tomas looked at her. “Through a flooded tunnel beneath a poisoned river?”

“Preferably by another route.”

Imani rolled the maps and tied them with cord. “We need a survey drone, dry suits, three air cylinders, pressure lamps, line reels, seal compound, and a manual override kit.”

“We have two air cylinders,” Tomas said.

“Two functional cylinders.”

“That is not better.”

“It is more accurate.”

The hall filled with motion. Once the equipment list was spoken, everyone found something to contribute. A woman from the island battery federation brought insulated cable. The marsh clinic provided inhalant ampoules and a medical pack. Two rail workers arrived with a hand-cranked winch repaired with a spoon. Kesi contributed red line and warned Mara to record its meaning.

“Red means no passage,” she said. “If you use it for danger and someone sees it tied to the wrong thing, people die.”

Mara wrote the rule into the route ledger.

Nia objected to the survey drone.

“It’ll announce us,” she said. “Anything with a powered propeller will.”

“It may keep us from walking into a pressure sink,” Imani replied.

“Then send a float.”

“A float cannot read structural stress.”

“A float can tell us if it sinks.”

Imani gave her a flat look.

Nia grinned. “The drone should be last resort.”

Imani did not smile. “Noted.”

When the expedition list was finalized, Mara saw that Nia’s name was absent.

Nia noticed too.

“No,” she said.

Imani continued checking the air cylinders.

“You didn’t put me down.”

“I did not.”

“You’re going. Mara’s going. Tomas is going.”

Tomas raised both hands. “I have argued against this repeatedly.”

“You’re still going.”

“Against my better judgment.”

Nia stepped between Imani and the equipment. “The outer platforms will need repairs.”

“That is not our first objective.”

“It will become our first objective when something breaks.”

“Something will break whether you are there or not.”

“Then you’ll want someone who knows how to fix it.”

Imani’s expression hardened. “You are a child.”

Nia’s grin disappeared. “I’m a mechanic.”

“You are both.”

“I can be both and still do the work. If the outer platforms fail, you’ll need someone who can make a repair from junk. Someone who doesn’t wait for the correct part from a warehouse that no longer exists.”

Imani studied her.

“And if I say no?”

“Then I’ll go anyway.”

“That is not persuasive.”

“It’s accurate.”

For a moment, only the radios hissed. Then Imani opened the expedition ledger.

“Nia Vale. Field mechanic. Outer-platform systems, improvised seals, pump assemblies. You remain under local command.”

“Whose?”

“Whoever is nearest and competent.”

“That could be Mara.”

“That could be dangerous,” Imani said.

Mara looked up from the map. “I’m standing here.”

“Exactly.”

The statement took longer than the equipment.

Tomas found them a recording room lined with salvaged acoustic panels. A cracked camera waited on a tripod. Behind Mara hung a blank cloth concealing flaking mineral charts.

“Say who you are,” Tomas instructed.

“My name is Mara Venn. Apprentice cartographer of Lumen.”

He stopped her. “Not apprentice.”

“That is what I am.”

“Not to them. They’ll hear a technical citizen repeating a Ministry title. Tell them what you know.”

Mara faced the camera again.

“My name is Mara Venn. I was born in Lumen, in the lower residential rings. I work in the Office of Cartography. I have seen records proving that the Council concealed living mainland communities and redirected atmospheric damage toward them.”

“That sounds like an accusation.”

“It is one.”

“People need more.”

“They need the truth.”

“Truth is not a shape that fits every mouth.”

She turned. “What does that mean?”

“The Ministry always began with certainty. The lower atmosphere is stable. The mainland is uninhabited. The transfer is voluntary. The treatment is unavailable. They never said, ‘Our records are incomplete.’ They never said, ‘We may be wrong.’”

“Because they knew they weren’t.”

“Because they knew uncertainty makes people ask questions.”

“Then why include it?”

“Because we are not them.”

The camera waited.

Mara began again.

“My name is Mara Venn. I was born in Lumen, and I believed what I was taught about the world below us. I believed the mainland was dead. I believed our restrictions were necessary. I was wrong.”

She paused, then continued.

“Some of what I am going to tell you is confirmed. Some is still being checked. The Council has used mainland relays without permission. Its atmospheric systems are discharging harmful material into living communities. It has classified lower-ring residents and mainland workers as acceptable losses. We have records of people transferred into dangerous labor and medical programs without consent.”

Her hands tightened.

“My brother is one of those people.

“Eli Venn is twelve. He has a respiratory illness. The city denied him treatment, then moved him into an atmospheric-adaptation ward. I do not know exactly where he is now. I do not know whether he is safe. I am going back to find him.”

She looked directly into the cracked lens.

“We are not asking you to trust one person. Check the data. Compare it with your own air readings, your own water, your own missing people. Open your records to one another. If we are wrong, tell us.

“But if we are right, do not let the Council close the city in your name. Do not let it tell you survival requires someone else’s death. There are routes, systems, and people prepared to help. They are not all ready. They are not all safe. We will tell you what we know and what we do not know.

“We are going to try to change Lumen from a closed fortress into part of a living network again. We may fail. If we do, no single group should control the emergency. Open what you can. Share what you have. Ask who is missing from the plan.”

Tomas lowered his gaze to the recorder.

“That’s good.”

“It sounds like an instruction manual.”

“It sounds like a person.”

“Which person?”

“The one you’re becoming.”

Before she could answer, a radio crackled in the next room.

Udo’s voice came through from the eastern relay camp. “Geology hall, we have a hospital confirmation. Authentication through the medical exchange.”

Tomas adjusted the receiver. “Send.”

Coded tones filled the room. Then Udo read the message.

“Patient Venn, Eli. Ward six-B. Status active. Respiratory response unstable. Atmospheric exposure trial in progress. Medical team requests mainland anti-inflammatory protocol if transfer window opens.”

Mara felt the floor tilt.

“Is he alive?” she asked.

“Record says active,” Udo replied. “Confirmed at the time of transmission. Timestamp twenty-three minutes ago.”

Twenty-three minutes.

“What is an atmospheric exposure trial?” Mara asked.

Imani answered. “They’re changing the air around him.”

“Why?”

“To measure what his lungs tolerate.”

“Can they stop it?”

“We don’t know.”

“Can the treatment help him?”

“If the hospital has functioning equipment. If they haven’t altered the protocol. If—”

Mara seized the radio. “Send them that he is not authorized for further exposure. His family refuses consent.”

“They may not recognize either.”

“Send it anyway.”

“We will.”

She kept hold of the receiver after the channel closed.

Tomas placed one hand on the table, not touching her. “We’ll get there.”

“You don’t know that.”

“No.”

“You just said—”

“I said we’ll get there. I didn’t promise what happens next.”

Imani opened the case containing the transfer module. “We leave in forty minutes.”

Outside, the rain had stopped.

The expedition moved through the settlement by lantern light. People watched from the paths, offering tools, food, and questions no one had time to answer. Clinic workers loaded stretchers into a cart. Pip slept beside the stove with a cloth over his mouth. Kesi tied yellow markers toward the riverbank.

At the edge of the settlement, boats waited among the reeds. Their hulls had been sealed with resin and woven plastic. The larger carried equipment; the smaller held the expedition and a folded raft for the tunnel.

Mara climbed in beside Nia. Imani took the stern. Tomas secured the radio case beneath his coat.

They traveled by memory and submerged markers. Nia navigated around a broken pump tower. Imani steered past black water shining beneath the moon. Mara kept the old map inside her coat, its edges pressing against her ribs.

At the ruined rail terminus, they found the entrance.

The river had swallowed the station roof. Only an iron arch remained above the tide. Beneath it, a maintenance stair descended into green-black water. A warning sign hung from one chain, its letters mostly gone except for **PRESSURE**.

Nia secured the first line around a support beam.

“Once we enter,” Imani said, “we stay clipped together. If the current takes one of us, the others pull against it. No one disconnects without saying so.”

Tomas checked his mask. “And if the line breaks?”

“Remember which way is up.”

“That was not reassuring.”

“It was not intended to be.”

Mara looked through the stairwell. Water covered the lower steps, disturbed by a slow inward pull. Somewhere beneath it, the old tunnel led toward the city where she had been born, the hospital where Eli was being measured and exposed, and the machinery that had made a prison of the air.

She took the guide rope.

“Ready.”

A patrol light swept across the river.

Then another answered from the south.

“They’ve started searching,” Tomas said.

“How close?” Nia asked.

“Too close.”

Imani clipped Mara’s line to the main rope. “Go.”

They entered the water.

Cold closed over Mara’s head. The world became pressure, bubbles, and the dim cone of Nia’s lamp. The drowned stair fell beneath them, each step furred with pale growth. Mara followed Imani downward, one hand on the rope, the other pressed against the case holding the unreadable transfer record.

Above, a patrol beam slid across the surface.

Then the river sealed them in darkness, and the line drew them beneath the Thames.

chapters.name: Return to Lumen
chapters.content:
The conduit narrowed after the third pressure gate.

Mara felt the walls close around her shoulders before she saw them. Her lamp revealed flaking ceramic, old cable brackets, and black water trembling along the floor. The guide line ran through her gloves, taut between Nia ahead and Tomas behind. Every few breaths, the current tugged at their ankles and carried a whisper of silt through the beam.

The air in her cylinder was nearly half gone.

She tried not to think about the distance behind them, or the distance ahead. The Thames pressed on every side of the conduit, patient and immense. Somewhere above, the river moved through the drowned city. Somewhere beyond the walls, patrols were searching the shore.

Imani lifted one hand.

Stop.

They froze.

At first Mara heard only their breathing: four separate rhythms, metallic and frightened. Then a vibration grew beneath the floor. It passed through her boots and into her knees.

A pump, perhaps. Or a patrol vehicle moving through the infrastructure above them.

Imani pointed upward.

The ceiling hatch shuddered. Blue light appeared around its edge.

“Pressure route three is still reading active,” a voice said above them.

“Then mark it and move on. The lower shafts are being sealed before the morning shift.”

The hatch opened. Water poured through in a thin sheet.

Imani pointed ahead.

Move.

Nia pulled the line. Mara followed, bending beneath a sagging cable tray. The current struck her sideways, and for one breath her shoulder hit the wall. Nia reached back without looking and caught the strap of Mara’s cylinder. Together they pulled her forward.

Tomas came behind, his radio case scraping the ceramic.

The patrol voices faded. They descended into a chamber where the water reached Mara’s waist. Her lamp found three rusted ladders. Two were broken. The third ended at a circular door set into the wall.

“Lumen access,” Imani said through the radio.

Mara stared at the door. She had drawn the northern shafts hundreds of times, though never this one. On the official maps, the route ended in a blank field labeled collapsed infrastructure. She had believed the label because believing it had been easier than asking who benefited from the blankness.

Imani fitted the manual override kit to the lock. Nia steadied the hand-cranked winch while Tomas watched the submerged passage behind them.

The lock resisted.

Imani braced both feet against the wall. “Again.”

Nia turned the crank. Metal groaned. Something inside the door clicked, then slipped.

A crack split the silence.

The door opened inward.

Air rushed through with such force that Mara’s lamp swung from her wrist. Bubbles streamed toward the opening. Imani shoved herself through first, then held the door while Nia climbed after her. Mara followed, dragging the equipment case against her chest. Tomas came last and pulled the door shut.

For several seconds none of them moved.

The shaft beyond was dry, its walls lined with old pipes and lamps that flickered overhead. Water dripped from their suits onto the metal floor.

“Remove the gear,” Imani said.

Mara’s fingers shook as she unfastened the cylinder. She had not realized how hard she was gripping the case. Inside lay the transfer module wrapped in waxed cloth and the warm data wafer containing Eli’s broken hospital record.

WARD 6-B TRANSFER—

The rest had dissolved into static.

Eli was alive when they left the mainland. The medical exchange had confirmed it only twenty-three minutes before their departure. Active subject. Respiratory response unstable. Atmospheric exposure trial in progress.

The next movement was sealed.

She forced herself to breathe.

At the top of the shaft, Imani found another hatch stamped with a maintenance seal dated eleven years earlier.

“Can it open?” Tomas asked.

“It was built to.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

Imani looked at him. “The city was built to remain open, too.”

She climbed. The hatch opened into a room full of broken carts and collapsed shelving. A faded sign read:

MUNICIPAL AIRWORKS—AUTHORIZED ACCESS ONLY.

Mara recognized it from an old map. On the public version, the depot had been colored gray and labeled structural loss. She had drawn this place out of existence.

They stripped off the dry suits and changed into gray coveralls and orange utility vests from the equipment case. Tomas removed the mainland stitching from their sleeves. Imani smeared grease over their identity plates. Nia tied her hair beneath a work hood and tucked the loose ends away.

“Repair crew seven,” Tomas said. “Northern transit ventilation. Temporary authorization.”

“From whom?” Nia asked.

“A department that exists in the records but hasn’t had a functioning supervisor for three years.”

“So, an ordinary department,” Nia said.

Imani almost smiled.

A sound came from the corridor.

A boy appeared carrying a crate of filter cartridges. He wore a lower-ring work jacket too large for him, the sleeves rolled several times. His cheeks were gray beneath the depot lights. He stopped when he saw them.

“Depot’s closed,” he said.

“Emergency ventilation order,” Tomas replied.

The boy looked toward the corridor. “North checkpoint is stopping crews. They’re checking plates.”

“Why?” Mara asked.

“Because they said to.”

He started away, then glanced back. “If you’re going that way, don’t use the main stair. They’re holding people there.”

“Thank you,” Imani said.

The boy hesitated. “Is it true?”

Mara knew what he meant. “Which part?”

“That the mainland is sending people into the city.”

The question entered the room like cold water.

“I don’t know,” Mara said.

The boy examined her face. “They said surface people were dead.”

“So did we.”

He nodded, as if she had confirmed something, and vanished down the corridor.

Mara watched the place where he had stood.

“His filter cartridge is empty,” Nia said.

“What?”

“The crate. They’re reusing casings. There’s no filter media inside.”

Imani looked toward the corridor. “Keep moving.”

They left through a service passage. Its walls carried layers of paint: old blue directional arrows beneath newer white ones, then emergency orange markings over both. Mara read them as she walked. Airworks. Cooling exchange. Transit control. She knew the notation, the angle of the arrows, the shorthand for access hatches. It was like seeing a childhood language scratched beneath a stranger’s handwriting.

At the passage’s end, Tomas opened a door.

Lumen’s transit music drifted through the wall: three bright notes followed by a soft chime, the arrival signal for the upper-ring loop.

Then the door swung wide.

Light flooded the passage.

The city had not changed in the way Mara had imagined. It was still glittering. Trains slid through transparent tubes above the concourse. Artificial sunlight caught on suspended gardens. Vines spilled from balconies, their leaves waxy and perfect beneath the lamps. Markets filled the lower levels with people carrying baskets, ration tins, school satchels, and work coats.

A vendor shouted the price of algae flour. Someone laughed. A delivery drone bumped a hanging lamp and apologized in a cheerful synthetic voice.

Mara stood motionless.

She had expected to return to a prison. She had not expected to return to a Tuesday.

A train passed overhead. Its windows showed a sleeping man, a teenager reading, an old couple holding hands beneath the blue transit map. No one looked like a monster. No one looked like someone who had chosen the Crown Seal.

“They’re going to work,” Nia murmured.

“They always are,” Tomas said.

Mara watched a woman balance three meal packets while fastening a child’s coat. The child complained about school. The woman kissed his forehead and told him not to forget his inhaler.

Mara’s sympathy rose so quickly it hurt.

These people were not innocent of everything. They had repeated lessons, accepted ration tables, ignored the smell of soot on the lower winds. But most of them were frightened and dependent. Their whole world had been designed so that survival required permission.

A school group crossed the concourse. Their teacher stopped beside a display showing a gray mainland beneath red warning symbols.

“Unregulated surface zones remain unsafe for civilian contact,” she told them.

One child raised a hand. “My grandmother says there are gardens.”

The teacher’s face tightened—not with anger, Mara realized, but fear.

“Your grandmother is remembering stories from before the Continuance.”

“Can we see them?”

“No.”

“Why?”

The teacher glanced at the ceiling cameras. “Because questions do not make them safe.”

The group moved on.

A security announcement sounded overhead.

“Due to ongoing sabotage attempts, all maintenance personnel must report for identity verification. Unregistered movement will be treated as an atmospheric threat. Please remain calm and continue normal transit.”

The crowd slowed. A woman pulled her daughter closer. People looked up at the speakers, then away.

Mara understood that obedience was not one wall. It was a thousand small calculations: If I speak, will my housing be revoked? If I help, will my child lose medicine? If I refuse, will they blame me for the next failure?

Tomas touched her elbow. “We need to move.”

They crossed the concourse with the other maintenance crews. Familiarity struck her at every turn—the bakery that sold cinnamon protein cakes, the cracked fountain, the stair where she had once fallen and torn her uniform. She remembered sitting there with blood on her knee while her father carried her home. She remembered the transit music continuing overhead, bright and indifferent.

At the northern checkpoint, two officers inspected crews one group at a time. Their weapons were not drawn, but their hands rested near them.

Tomas led the group toward a side corridor marked FILTER ACCESS.

A woman stepped from a kiosk.

“Mara?”

Mara stopped.

Lessa Quill wore a Broadcast Ministry badge and held a stack of notices. She had supervised captions during Mara’s short Ministry assignment, teaching her how to make a warning sound calm. Lessa had once changed “unverified reports of respiratory distress” to “temporary discomfort during atmospheric adjustment.”

Her gaze moved from Mara to Tomas. For one terrible second, Mara thought she would call security.

Instead, Lessa dropped the notices.

“They’re searching hospital access routes,” she whispered. “Ward movement orders went out twenty minutes ago.”

“Eli?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know his name. The list is sealed. Six patients from six-B are being transferred before the next pressure cycle.”

“Where?”

“Central tower research levels. Or lower loading platforms. The order uses two destinations.”

Tomas stepped closer. “Can you access the full notice?”

“My clearance was revoked.”

“Why?”

Lessa looked at her Ministry badge. “Because I refused to change the timing on the black-rain report.”

Mara’s throat tightened. “You knew?”

“I knew the report was being altered. I didn’t know how much.”

“Can you search the transfer system?”

“I can’t search anything now.”

“Then who can?”

Lessa glanced toward the checkpoint. “People who still think they are only doing clerical work.”

She bent to gather the notices. Beneath them lay a narrow access card. Tomas picked it up without seeming to.

“Take the east service bridge,” Lessa said. “There’s a lift that still recognizes old maintenance bands. It will get you below the checkpoint.”

“Are there others?” Mara asked.

“Some report everything. Some report only what they think they can survive reporting. Some leave doors open and call it an accident.”

She straightened.

“If they ask,” she continued, “you were repairing a pressure sensor in the lower ring.”

“What if they ask where?”

Lessa’s eyes met Mara’s. “Say you were sent by someone important. They prefer lies with hierarchy in them.”

Then she returned to her kiosk.

At the lift, Tomas pressed the card to the reader. The doors opened.

“We need Sela first,” he said as they entered. “She may know where Eli was taken.”

Mara nodded, though uncertainty twisted beneath her ribs. Sela had been released from civic intake, according to one message, but no one had confirmed where she was now. The last information placed her in unpaid filtration labor. It might have been a threat, a mistake, or a trap.

“Lower civic intake,” Imani said.

“Then filtration labor blocks,” Tomas replied. “If she was moved, we follow the work assignments.”

Nia unfolded a maintenance diagram. “Three routes down. Central shaft watched. West route flooded with condensate. East bridge is open.”

“According to Lessa,” Tomas said.

“According to a frightened woman who just risked her daughter’s home,” Mara said. “That is not nothing.”

The lift descended.

With every level, the gardens dimmed. Polished wall panels became patched metal. Artificial sunlight shifted to a colorless white. The air smelled of warm dust and disinfectant.

At Ring Eight, the lift stopped.

“Temporary hold,” the voice announced. “Please remain calm.”

The doors did not open.

People were packed into the carriage: workers with tools, a mother holding a sleeping infant, two men in filtration masks, and an elderly man whose fingers shook around an empty ration card. Someone muttered that the upper markets were still receiving fresh fruit. Someone else told him to stop before a camera heard.

The infant began coughing.

Mara noticed an emergency cabinet beside the doors. Behind its transparent seal were two portable filters. She broke the panel with the heel of her tool and handed one to the mother. The other went to a coughing worker.

“Maintenance violation,” the lift announced.

“Then fine me,” Mara said.

The worker stared at her. “They’ll charge it to your household.”

“My household is already being charged for everything.”

The lift jolted. The lights flickered. Several people cried out.

For a moment, Mara saw the city as the Council described it: a machine requiring obedience to remain in the air. Then she saw the empty filter cartridge in the boy’s crate, the coughing infant, the sealed hospital ward.

The machine was not failing because people disobeyed.

People were disobeying because it had been made to fail them.

The doors opened.

The mother caught Mara’s hand for half a second. “Thank you.”

Then the crowd carried her away.

They moved through the lower ring. Gardens were filmed with gray residue. Water dispensers displayed red ration warnings. A queue stretched outside a clinic, silent except for coughing.

Above it, a screen showed the Council seal and the words:

CONTINUITY REQUIRES TEMPORARY SACRIFICE.

Mara took out a grease pencil.

“What are you doing?” Tomas asked.

She marked the clinic entrance, water dispenser, emergency cabinet, and the service corridor leading toward the east bridge. She added symbols for danger and safe passage.

Nia crouched beside her. “Mark the filter cabinet. And the clinic queue.”

Mara did.

Imani pointed toward a side passage. “There’s a storage room with membrane sealant.”

Mara marked that too.

At the bottom she wrote:

CHECK BEFORE ENTERING. UPDATE IF WRONG. LEAVE WHAT YOU CAN.

Tomas studied the wall. “You’re making a public map.”

“For whoever needs it.”

“Without verifying every route.”

“I’m marking what we have seen.”

“And if someone follows it into danger?”

“Then the next person marks the danger.”

“That isn’t a guarantee.”

“No,” Mara said. “It’s an invitation to correct the map.”

He looked at her for a long moment. “That’s what maps become when people are allowed to answer back.”

A siren sounded.

The clinic queue broke apart. Doors slammed. On the overhead screen, the Council seal vanished, replaced by a red notice:

UNAUTHORIZED MAINTENANCE CREW IDENTIFIED. REPORT SUSPICIOUS PERSONNEL.

Tomas’s radio crackled.

“Mina,” he said after pressing the receiver to his ear.

Mina Pell had worked beside him in the Broadcast Ministry, preparing schedules and deleting words from statements before they reached the announcers.

“Your father knows the breach originated in the lower archive,” Mina said. “Security is locking the central tower. I can give you three minutes on the internal maintenance channel.”

“What do we use it for?”

“I thought you would know.”

“We need hospital transfer records. Ward 6-B. Patient movement. And a location for Sela Venn.”

“I can search.”

“Don’t search. Ask someone who already knows.”

Silence.

“There are people listening,” Mina said.

“Good. Tell them the lower rings are not empty.”

“Tomas—”

The line went dead.

A maintenance panel beside the clinic blinked green. Mara opened it. Someone had taped a strip of paper inside.

EAST BRIDGE. TWO CAMERAS DEAD. DO NOT USE LIFT.

Below the words was a symbol she did not recognize: a circle crossed by three lines.

“Someone else is mapping,” Nia said.

Mara folded the paper and placed it beside her own map.

“East bridge,” Imani said.

They entered the passage.

Behind them, the clinic screen resumed its warning. But beneath it, on the wall, Mara’s symbols remained: water, medicine, shelter, a route through the dark.

She added one more mark before following the others.

A small circle for a question.

At the center of the map, where no official boundary had ever been drawn, Mara marked a place for anyone who was still looking.

chapters.name: The Lower Rings
chapters.content:
The east service bridge was narrower than Mara remembered, and she had never seen it on an official map.

It ran along the outside of Ring Nine, behind the residential towers, where polished public surfaces gave way to exposed braces and maintenance housings. On one side, the wall curved upward in a sealed gray sweep. On the other, a waist-high rail looked down through grating at the lower rings. Pipes shuddered beneath the bridge. Soot-dark runoff clung to the rail in frozen beads, and every few seconds a drop fell into the darkness below.

Nia stopped beside the entrance and lifted two fingers.

Mara froze.

Behind them, a security announcement echoed through the service corridors.

“By order of the Continuity Council, all maintenance personnel are to report for identity verification. Unauthorized movement between civic rings will be treated as infrastructure sabotage. Failure to comply will result in immediate suspension of housing and medical privileges.”

The announcement repeated in three languages. The first voice was calm. The second sounded almost compassionate. The third was a child's voice, bright and practiced.

Nia leaned toward the nearest camera. Its lens was dark.

“Dead,” she whispered.

“Lessa said two.”

“Which means the third is watching.”

She pointed upward. A narrow black slit had been cut into the ceiling panel above the bridge. No lens showed, but Mara felt the attention behind it. The city had learned to hide its eyes.

Nia handed Mara the tool case. “Walk like you’re angry at the bridge.”

“I am angry at the bridge.”

“Good. Make it professional.”

They crossed.

The lower rings fell away beneath them. Their residences had been built in stacked circles around the city’s central support, each level meant to be efficient, clean, and easily controlled. From above, the districts would have looked like bands of light. From here, Mara saw the fractures between them.

Whole gardens had been closed behind mesh. Gray residue coated the leaves. Water dispensers flashed amber warnings. A crowd gathered around a ration station while two drones recorded from above. Far overhead, the upper districts blazed with light. Gold panels moved across the central tower, forming the words:

CONTINUITY IS SECURITY.

THE FUTURE BEGINS WITHIN.

Music drifted down, bright and weightless, a string arrangement she remembered from school ceremonies.

Nia looked up. “They’re celebrating.”

“They haven’t told them what it is.”

“They told them it would protect the city.”

Mara thought of the archive classifications.

Upper rings: preserve.  
Technical rings: selective transfer.  
Lower rings: dispersal as required.

She looked toward the crowd below. “Protection for whom?”

Nia did not answer. She had found a service hatch hidden behind dead ventilation units. The metal was stained with oil and marked by a faint symbol: a circle crossed by three lines.

Mara touched it. “The same mark.”

“Someone wants people to find this.”

“Or wants us to think they do.”

“Both can be true.”

The old maintenance band opened the lock after three attempts. Beyond was a vertical shaft. Warm damp air rose from it, carrying the bitter smell of overheated wiring.

They descended.

Mara went first, one hand on the ladder and the other gripping the tool case. The shaft vibrated with the passage of a train somewhere above them. Dust shook loose from the walls. Halfway down, a light snapped on below. Nia caught Mara’s boot before it struck the lower rung.

They waited in darkness.

A worker passed beneath them, pushing a cart of empty filter casings. He wore no mask. His lips were gray around the edges.

“Keep going,” he muttered without looking up. “If you’re going to keep going.”

At the bottom, they emerged behind compressor housings. The air smelled of wet metal, mold, and exhausted filter media. Mara checked her wrist display, then added the route in pencil along the inside of her sleeve: east bridge, dead cameras, hatch, shaft, compressor block.

Nia glanced at it. “You’re going to run out of arm.”

“I’ll use yours.”

“Ask first.”

Mara looked at her.

“That was a joke.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t. You make the same face when people joke as when a pressure seal ruptures.”

“I’ve seen people joke during pressure ruptures.”

“Exactly.”

They followed a corridor marked FILTERING—AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The sign had been painted over, but the old letters showed through. A door stood open at the end. Inside, workers in stained coveralls replaced membrane cartridges by hand.

A supervisor came toward them. “Repair crew seven?”

Nia lifted the tool case. “Emergency intake fault.”

“Which line?”

“Line three.”

“Line three isn’t in your assignment.”

“It is now.”

“Who authorized it?”

“Your system did.”

The supervisor’s eyes narrowed. “Systems don’t authorize work.”

“They do when they’re about to fail.”

Before Nia could add anything, a worker dropped a cartridge. Its casing rolled across the floor, empty. It struck the supervisor’s boot and spun in place.

The supervisor looked at the cartridge, then at Mara and Nia. “Come with me.”

Her office contained three monitors displaying green air-quality readings. Mara recognized the numbers immediately. The particulate counts had been copied from an old baseline, before the western arrays began discharging into the lower atmosphere.

“They’re false,” Mara said.

The supervisor shut the door. “You’re not repair crew seven.”

“We’re looking for Sela Venn,” Mara said. “Filtration labor assignment. She was arrested from lower civic intake.”

The woman studied her face. “You’re Mara.”

Mara’s hand moved toward the maintenance knife at her belt.

The woman raised both palms. “If I meant to report you, I would have opened the door.”

“How do you know me?”

“Your mother talks when she works. Mostly about membranes. Sometimes about you.”

Mara did not know whether that comforted or frightened her.

The supervisor opened a cabinet and removed a stack of handwritten lists: names, blocks, filter allotments, symptoms, children needing inhalants. Several entries had been crossed out and replaced with dates. Others were circled in red.

“She was here,” the woman said. “Block Four filtration crews. They moved half the intake workers yesterday.”

“Where?”

“Some to the western membranes. Some to pressure decks. Some to medical quarantine.” She found another page. “Sela Venn was assigned to emergency seal repair in the lower civic blocks. Unpaid labor. Housing continuation conditional on compliance.”

Mara’s throat tightened. “Is she still there?”

“She was transferred at dawn. Block Twelve. Old nursery tower.”

“Why would filtration labor be moved to a nursery tower?”

“Because it has a usable membrane bay and no functioning cameras.”

Nia looked at the lists. “You’re tracking everyone?”

“Someone has to know who disappears.”

The supervisor glanced toward the wall. “If they find you here, they’ll lock this block and cut our air.”

“We won’t use your name,” Mara said.

“That won’t matter if they find you.”

She removed a maintenance badge and handed it to Nia. “Old corridor. It should open the nursery tower.”

Mara looked at the lists. “How many people are keeping records like these?”

“Enough to keep the city alive,” the woman said. “Not enough to stop it from dying.”

A buzzer sounded in the outer workroom. Everyone went still.

“Inspection,” the supervisor said.

Mara reached for the door.

“Not that way.” The woman lifted a floor panel beneath her desk. “Crawlspace. It comes out behind the refuse chutes.”

Nia dropped into the opening. Mara followed, then looked back.

The supervisor was already gathering the lists.

“What will you tell them?” Mara asked.

“That our readings are accurate.”

“They aren’t.”

The woman met her eyes. “They will be when we finish fixing the line.”

The panel closed above Mara.

The route passed through three residential rings. There were no signs, only chalk marks and colored threads tied around pipes. A triangle meant water. Two parallel lines meant an operating clinic. A black dot meant an unsafe filter room. The circle crossed by three lines appeared twice beside stairwells.

Mara stopped at the second mark.

“This is larger than us.”

Nia kept walking. “Everything is larger than us.”

“But someone has been mapping these routes.”

“Someone has been surviving.”

They came out behind a refuse chute in Ring Ten. The corridor smelled of grit and overheated plastic. People crowded a water dispenser while an attendant argued with a man whose daughter had a fever.

“The ration is reduced again,” he said.

“The pressure feed is failing.”

“You have three full tanks behind you.”

“For the clinic.”

“My daughter has fever.”

“So does half the ring.”

The man slammed his cup against the dispenser. A security drone turned toward him.

Before it could descend, a woman at the edge of the crowd passed metal cups to those who had waited longest. Two maintenance workers removed a wall panel and examined the water line. Another person stood between the father and the drone, pretending to read the ration notice.

The argument did not end, but it became a task more people could touch.

Nia leaned close. “That’s how it starts.”

“With fighting?”

“With people refusing to let one person decide who waits.”

Mara watched the woman recording each cup on the back of a school notice. “They could be arrested.”

“They could be arrested for coughing.”

The old nursery tower stood beyond the dispenser. Faded animals still covered its walls: foxes, whales, birds with wings too large for their bodies. Artificial sunlight had failed, leaving the corridor blue-gray. A broken speaker repeated part of a lullaby whenever the ventilation system surged.

A door stood open.

Mara heard a tool scrape against metal.

“Sela?”

The tool clattered.

Her mother stepped into the doorway wearing oversized filtration coveralls. A temporary brace bound her left wrist. A cut crossed her lower lip, but her eyes were clear.

Mara crossed the corridor and fell against her.

Sela caught her with one arm. For a moment Mara could not speak. The fabric of her mother’s uniform was damp with chemical condensation. Beneath it, she was frighteningly thin.

“You came back,” Sela said.

“I thought—”

“I know.”

“I left you.”

“You got me out.”

“I left before I knew where you were.”

“You left because you had to.”

“I chose it.”

“Yes,” Sela said. “That is what choosing means.”

Mara pulled back. “You’re hurt.”

“Door jammed during intake.”

“Did someone help you?”

“A clerk opened the wrong gate.”

“The wrong gate?”

“He decided he had made a mistake.”

Mara almost laughed. The sound broke in her throat.

Sela touched her cheek. “Don’t apologize when what you mean is fear.”

Mara looked toward the work bay. Filter membranes hung from lines like translucent skin. Workers patched tears with heated tools. One man had wrapped a strip of membrane around his forearm where his sleeve had dissolved.

“Are you afraid?” Sela asked.

“Yes.”

“Good. Fear tells you where the edge is. It doesn’t tell you to stop.”

Mara took out the transfer module. “Eli?”

Sela’s hand tightened around the edge of the workbench. “Tell me.”

“Ward Six-B. Active subject. They’re moving six patients before the next pressure cycle.”

“Where?”

“We don’t know. Central research levels or lower loading platforms.”

“Is he alive?”

“As of the last medical exchange.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one we have.”

Sela stood too quickly and caught the workbench. “Then we go to the hospital.”

“We may not reach him before the transfer. The central tower is locked, and security has our descriptions.”

“Then we reach him after.”

“It could be a trap.”

“Of course it could.”

“They used you to lure us before.”

“They used me because they were afraid you’d come.”

Mara stared at her. “They may be expecting us.”

Sela’s eyes hardened. “They have expected me to obey for twelve years. They expected me to accept ration cuts, failing filters, and medicine withheld from my son because a number on a file said he was less valuable than an administrator’s daughter. Let them expect one more thing.”

“We don’t know what’s happening in the upper rings,” Mara said. “If the broadcast goes out, if the Crown Seal starts and the systems fail—”

“People could die.”

“They are already dying.”

“That does not make chaos harmless.”

The words struck harder than Mara expected. Sela lowered herself onto a crate.

“You think I don’t know what they’ve done?” she said. “I repair the membranes that carry it. Every shift, I see which rings receive clean air and which receive what remains. But if you tear everything open without a way to keep the city breathing, the people who die first will still be down here.”

Mara looked at the patched membranes, the stained gloves, the workers who had not stopped listening.

“Then we need a way.”

“Yes,” Sela said. “Not merely a revelation. A way.”

Nia looked into the corridor. “We don’t have much time.”

Sela turned to her. “You’re Nia.”

“Yes.”

“Your mother said you broke a pump in Tilbury.”

“I improved it.”

Sela nodded. “Good. Then you can improve a hospital.”

Mara looked at the workers. A silver-haired woman with a respirator beneath her chin stepped forward.

“If you’re going to the central tower, take the old waste-return corridor,” she said. “The medical crews use it when they don’t want to be seen carrying bodies.”

“Where does it open?” Mara asked.

“Below the research hospital. Service lock behind the oxygen reclamation tanks.”

“Can you get us there?”

The woman glanced at a worker carrying empty cartridges.

“Not now,” he said. “The lower exchange is failing. If we don’t patch it, Ring Eleven loses air before shift change.”

Mara looked at the schematic spread across a workbench. It showed the exchange lines and three routes feeding the residential blocks. One line had been altered on the official diagram, concealing how much air was diverted toward the upper rings.

“This bypass is still active,” Mara said.

The silver-haired woman handed her a roll of sealant tape. “Can you read airflow?”

“Enough.”

“If you close the secondary vent, pressure will rise in the lower exchange.”

“And the upper ring drops by point-three.”

“That’s where the celebration is.”

“That’s where the reserve compressors are,” another worker said. “They’ll compensate.”

“If they notice,” Nia said.

“They’ll notice,” Mara answered. “But not before this ring gets air.”

The workers exchanged looks.

“Can you do it?” the woman asked.

“Not safely from here. The control junction is behind the ration station.”

“The one with the crowd?”

“Yes.”

Nia took the tape. “Then we go through the crowd.”

Sela followed despite Mara’s protest.

By the time they reached the ration station, the argument had become a distribution effort. The man with the feverish daughter carried one of the water tanks. The attendant had opened the clinic reserve and was recording every cup. The woman with the school notice checked each line twice. The crowd made space for Sela.

“Is the lower exchange going?” someone asked.

“Not yet,” she said. “But it will.”

The answer traveled through the ring—not as certainty, but as a promise requiring everyone’s hands.

Mara and Nia opened the panel beneath the dispenser. Hot air rushed from the junction, carrying scorched insulation. Nia checked the pipes.

“This one?”

“That feeds the clinic. The next.”

Nia turned the valve halfway. The gauge climbed. Lights flickered in the upper corridor. A warning tone began, then stopped.

“More,” Mara said.

“If the seal slips—”

“More.”

Nia turned it another quarter. The pipe bucked. Mara pressed the sealant tape into the split while Nia braced the valve with both hands. The heat burned through Mara’s glove.

“Hold it,” Nia said.

“I am.”

“You’re shaking.”

“So are you.”

“That’s because I’m doing the useful part.”

Mara laughed once, breathlessly, and pushed harder.

The air changed almost imperceptibly. It was still dirty and thin, but the strain eased. On the stairwell, the sick boy took a deeper breath. His father began to cry without making a sound.

Mara felt the city answer through its pipes.

Not the Council. Not the maps. People touching the machinery that kept one another alive.

Sela came beside her. “Now.”

Mara looked toward the tower. Gold light spilled through its upper glass, bright enough to turn the cloud ceiling into a second sky.

“Now we find Eli.”

Sela took her hand. “Together.”

Behind them, workers passed around the filter lists. The ration attendant copied the hospital route onto the school notice. Someone marked a safe stairwell with yellow tape. Someone else carried cups toward Ring Eleven.

Ahead, the old waste-return corridor waited beneath the hospital, and somewhere in the central tower six children were being prepared for transfer under a system that had already decided what their lives were worth.

Mara tightened her grip on the map drawn along her sleeve.

For the first time since returning to Lumen, she did not draw the route alone. Along the corridor walls, new marks appeared as they walked: a water cup, a patch of yellow tape, a circle crossed by three lines.

Answers, left for whoever came next.

chapters.name: The Father’s Secret
chapters.content:
Tomas entered the Broadcast Ministry through the door reserved for people who had already been forgiven.

The guard at the east checkpoint glanced at his cracked authorization band, then at his maintenance coat.

“Minister’s office?”

“Emergency transmission review.”

“Those are suspended.”

“Tell Minister Rusk his son is waiting downstairs with a message from the lower rings.”

The guard touched her comm bead. After a pause, she waved him through.

The Ministry’s voices folded around him as he crossed the lobby. Weather reassurance, school announcements, ration notices, all speaking in the same measured tone.

“Pressure remains within managed variance.”

“Unauthorized mainland reports have been identified as destabilizing misinformation.”

“Temporary medical delays are necessary to preserve treatment continuity.”

A display showed a smooth green line labeled ATMOSPHERIC STABILITY: 98.7%.

The real reading was 96.1%.

Tomas had once helped approve the captions that concealed it. He had not invented the number. He had only changed “critical” to “under review,” delayed warnings, and removed words that might alarm families.

He had called it preserving confidence.

At the end of the lobby, Mina Pell looked up from her terminal. Her hand moved once beneath the desk: a warning.

Not the lift.

Tomas turned into the old editing corridor and slipped through a service hatch behind a rack of obsolete projectors. Three levels higher, he emerged above the broadcast floor. Below him, operators monitored dozens of channels while Minister Rusk appeared on the central wall.

“Lumen cannot be governed by unverified claims,” his father was saying. “We will not permit isolated incidents, however tragic, to be weaponized against the continuity of the city.”

Tomas crossed the gallery and entered the studio through the rear access door.

The guard outside caught his arm. “You can’t go in.”

“Tell him I have the hospital transfer schedule.”

“You were detained.”

“Then your report will need to explain why I’m here.”

The studio door opened. Minister Rusk stood there, older than he looked on the broadcast.

“Tomas.”

“Take me somewhere without cameras.”

His father studied the cracked band around Tomas’s neck. “Clear the west archive.”

They entered a narrow conference room. The Ministry seal glowed on the wall: blue for truth, white for continuity, gold for service.

“Where is Mara Venn?” Rusk asked.

“You know who’s involved.”

“I know you accessed restricted archives. I know mainland transmissions have reached the lower rings. I know hospital routes are being searched.”

“Eli Venn is in Ward 6-B.”

Something tightened in his father’s face.

“He’s an active subject,” Tomas continued. “Atmospheric exposure trial. Unstable respiratory response. Six patients are being moved before the next pressure cycle. I need the destination and the emergency channel codes.”

“No.”

“You can access both.”

“I can access information. That doesn’t mean I can give it to you.”

“You gave the Council information about every lower-ring family.”

“I gave them population data so aid could be distributed.”

“You gave them names so people could disappear.”

Rusk stood. “You have no idea what you’re talking about.”

“I know there are transfer lists marked selective transfer and dispersal as required. I know lower-ring families are being sent to mainland relay camps. I know medical consent forms are altered. I know the Council has decided that some people are worth saving only if they can still work.”

His father’s voice dropped. “And what do you think happens if the city learns all of this at once?”

“They deserve to know.”

“They deserve to survive.”

“Not if survival means killing everyone below us.”

“Lumen was built to preserve human life.”

“It was built to preserve some human lives.”

Rusk looked away. “You think truth is a lever. Pull it, and the machinery changes direction. You don’t understand panic. People don’t become generous when afraid. They become precise about who should be sacrificed.”

“Then give them something besides fear.”

His father’s expression altered.

“You sound like your mother.”

Tomas went still. Rusk rarely spoke of her. He spoke of her illness as an allocation failure, her death as a private tragedy, her work as something she had been too proud to abandon.

“I know you signed her allocation denial,” Tomas said.

Rusk sat. “The treatment was not stable.”

“It worked.”

“For some patients.”

“She could have been one of them.”

“I was told that extending her dose would take treatment from three children in the technical rings.”

“So you chose her.”

“I chose the numbers I was given.”

“You chose not to look.”

Rusk pressed his hands against his knees. “Do you think I don’t know what that makes me?”

“You became the voice that made her death acceptable.”

His father closed his eyes. For a moment he looked less like a minister than a man trapped inside the first lie he had told himself.

“I need Eli’s location,” Tomas said. “And the codes.”

Rusk rose and went to the wall. Beneath the Ministry seal, a panel unlocked, revealing a shallow compartment containing a black data wafer and a folder tied with red thread.

“There are no emergency codes anymore,” he said. “The Council moved them to a closed authorization lattice. I can access one channel. Perhaps two.”

“Then use them.”

“Your sister is in Ward 6-B, lower research level, chamber six. The transfer order is active. I can see the originating authorization, not the receiving site. That separation was deliberate.”

“Who authorized it?”

“Ministerial Continuity Committee.”

“Names.”

“No.”

“Tomas.”

“If you broadcast names before you know what they did, frightened people will decide punishment is more urgent than oxygen.”

“You don’t get to lecture me about restraint while my brother is being poisoned.”

“I am not lecturing you.”

He took the wafer from the compartment, but did not yet hand it over.

“There is something else you need to know,” he said.

Tomas waited.

“About Mara’s father.”

The room seemed to shrink.

“Jon Venn did not die in an accident.”

Tomas stared at him.

“Eight years ago, Jon was assigned to the western atmospheric array. He found that the emissions redirection protocols had been altered. Waste was being sent toward the mainland relay fields. The official explanation called it a temporary balancing measure.”

“It wasn’t.”

“It was the first version of the Crown Seal.”

Tomas thought of Mara’s maps, the erased routes, the smooth official curves hiding the jagged ones.

“Jon tried to stop it,” Rusk said. “He sabotaged a control junction and copied the emissions records. He intended to send them through an open maintenance channel.”

“What happened?”

“He was taken by Council security. The command logs were falsified. They reported a pressure accident.”

“Who killed him?”

Rusk looked at the sealed door.

“The Council’s security division.”

Tomas felt the floor tilt, though the stabilizers reported no tremor.

“And you knew?”

“I knew afterward. I was twenty-eight. A junior broadcast aide. Your mother had just died. The Council showed me a command log bearing Jon’s authorization and said he had endangered thirty-one workers, including Imani Okafor’s brother.”

“Falsified.”

“Yes.”

“And you believed it.”

“I believed what I could bear to believe.”

“They recruited you.”

“They said the mainland communities would attack the arrays if the truth became known. They said secrecy was containment.”

“You joined them.”

Rusk met his eyes. “Yes.”

The answer was worse than an excuse.

“I learned the full truth years later,” he continued. “By then I had access. I delayed activation notices. Buried relocation language. Redirected some medical reports.”

“You made the lies gentler.”

“I kept them from becoming worse.”

“Every person who carries out an order says the next person would have done worse.”

Rusk placed the red-threaded folder beside the wafer. “It contains the original western-array command log, Jon’s maintenance report, the security authorization that removed him, and the Council transcript classifying his death as an accident.”

“Why keep it?”

“Because I could not destroy the last proof that I had betrayed him.”

“You kept it hidden.”

“I was afraid.”

“You’re still afraid.”

“Yes.”

That admission made Tomas angrier than denial would have.

Rusk pushed the wafer toward him. “Use the channel. Get the boy out. Then decide what to do with the record.”

Tomas took both.

A red light appeared above the door.

“Security lockdown,” announced the Ministry system. “Remain in assigned—”

Rusk seized the desk terminal and entered a manual override. The lights went dark. Alarms began on the broadcast floor, then cut off.

“What did you do?”

“Bought you ninety seconds.”

“You’re coming with me.”

“No.”

“They’ll arrest you.”

“They were going to do that anyway.”

“Why help me now?”

His father’s face had become very tired.

“I spent eight years telling myself that protecting people from the truth was a form of love. I would like, once, to do something that is not a lie.”

The door unlocked.

Tomas stepped into the corridor, then turned. “Did Jon suffer?”

Rusk’s expression broke.

“No,” he said. “They vented the chamber before they took him. He was unconscious.”

It was not comfort. It was all he could offer.

Tomas ran.

Mina Pell stood beside her terminal in the service gallery. When she saw the folder beneath his coat, she did not ask.

“East service bridge,” she whispered. “Two cameras dead. Don’t use the lift.”

He nodded and kept moving.

At a dark alcove near the lower-ring access hatch, he connected the wafer to his portable receiver. A map unfolded in pale lines.

CENTRAL RESEARCH HOSPITAL.

WARD 6-B.

CHAMBER SIX.

A route descended through the lower service levels, then split toward two destinations marked only by time windows.

TRANSFER WINDOW: 00:41:12.

RECEIVING SITE: SEALED.

He copied the route to a relay card. The map flickered. For half a second, another line appeared beneath it—an old emergency broadcast channel.

Then the wafer went cold.

He climbed down.

He found the others in the waste-return corridor almost an hour later. The passage smelled of rust, disinfectant, and stagnant water. Mara stood beside the service lock. Nia crouched at a valve assembly, and Sela sat against the wall with her injured wrist braced against her chest.

Mara turned at the sound of Tomas’s steps.

“Where were you?”

“Broadcast Ministry.”

Nia rose. “You went back alone?”

“I had to.”

“You don’t have to do anything alone,” Mara said.

He looked at her. Gray residue marked one cheek. Her hair had come loose. She looked both younger and older than she had when they entered Lumen.

“I saw my father,” he said.

Her relief vanished into suspicion.

“He gave me a route to Ward 6-B. Eli is still in chamber six. The transfer window begins in less than an hour.”

“The destination?”

“Sealed. Two possible sites. The channel couldn’t identify which.”

“Then we find out inside.”

Tomas handed her the wafer. “This opens an emergency route. Temporary access. Three minutes.”

“How did you get it?”

“He gave it to me.”

“And what did he want?”

“Nothing.”

Mara waited.

“There’s more,” Tomas said. “About your father.”

Her fingers tightened around the wafer.

“Jon Venn did not die in an accident,” he said.

Mara did not move.

“He was assigned to the western atmospheric array. He found that emissions were being redirected toward the mainland relay fields. The Council called it balancing. It was an early Crown Seal design. Jon tried to stop it, copied the records, and sabotaged a control junction.”

Sela pushed herself upright.

“Security took him,” Tomas continued. “They falsified the command logs and reported a pressure accident.”

For a moment Mara seemed not to understand.

“He was killed,” Tomas said. “The Council concealed it.”

She struck the wall once. The corridor rang.

“Why?”

“My father said they feared the mainland would attack if Lumen learned the truth. They recruited him afterward.”

“Your father.”

“Yes.”

“He helped bury him.”

“Yes.”

Mara laughed, but the sound broke. “My father was called careless. They said he ignored warnings.”

“The warning was issued after the breach. The original log is in the folder.”

She snatched it from beneath Tomas’s coat.

“He knew my mother was waiting for a body,” she said.

“He should have told you.”

“He knew I thought my father died because he failed.”

“He should have told you.”

Her eyes filled. She pressed the folder against her chest.

Sela reached for her. “Mara.”

Mara stepped away. “And now he gives you the truth because he wants forgiveness?”

“I don’t think he expects it.”

“Good.”

The hospital lock chimed.

Nia glanced at the indicator. “We have access.”

Mara wiped her face, leaving a gray streak across her skin. She tucked the folder beneath her coat.

“We don’t let this decide what happens to Eli,” she said.

Tomas moved beside her at the lock. Beyond it, the hospital’s lower infrastructure rose in tiers of steel and glass, lit by pale emergency lamps.

Somewhere above them, six patients waited to be moved. Somewhere inside, Eli was breathing air chosen by people who had already decided what his life was worth.

Mara looked at Tomas.

“Your father told you where the truth was buried,” she said. “Now we find my brother.”

Then she stepped through the door, and the others followed her into the hospital.

chapters.name: The Hospital of Useful Lives
chapters.content:
The oxygen-reclamation service lock opened with a sigh.

Mara held her breath until the inner seal closed behind them. Beyond it, a narrow corridor ran beneath the hospital, ribbed with pipes and lit by emergency-blue strips. Condensation trembled on the walls. Somewhere above, machinery cycled, making the floor rise and settle beneath their boots.

Nia pressed her palm to the door.

“Nothing,” she whispered.

“Nothing you can hear,” Sela said.

Mara’s mother leaned against the wall, her injured wrist bound beneath a filtration glove. She had refused to remain behind in the nursery tower, and again in the waste-return corridor. Now she looked as if the hospital itself had challenged her to keep moving.

Mara checked the route wafer. Its surface was black except for a thin green line pulsing toward the lower research levels.

“Ward Six-B is two tiers below,” she said. “Chamber Six.”

“And the transfer begins in thirty-four minutes,” Nia said.

“Thirty-three,” Imani corrected.

The former atmospheric engineer studied the pipes overhead. “They’ve changed the supply routing. Research wards used to have independent air. This is pulling from the same exchange that feeds the lower rings.”

“Why?” Sela asked.

Imani looked at Mara. “Because the patients are part of the experiment.”

They moved.

The hospital differed sharply from the clinics in the lower rings. Its floors shone. Its glass partitions were spotless. The air smelled of antiseptic, hot metal, and a sweet chemical that caught in Mara’s throat.

At the first junction, a display flickered awake.

**CENTRAL RESEARCH HOSPITAL**  
**PATIENT MOVEMENT RESTRICTED**  
**UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS WILL BE RECORDED**

A camera lens emerged from the ceiling.

Imani pulled Mara back. Sela kicked open a maintenance panel, and Nia tore out a bundle of insulated cable. Sparks snapped across the corridor. The camera turned toward them.

Nia crossed two wires with her wrench.

The lens went dark.

“Temporary,” she said.

“Everything is,” Sela muttered.

The official map showed no route to Six-B, only a gray block marked **AUTHORIZED CLINICAL STAFF ONLY**. Mara compared it with the paper route copied from Tomas’s wafer.

“The hospital is lying about its own floors.”

“Partitioning,” Imani said. “A lie wants to be believed. This wants to be obeyed.”

“Then we disobey accurately.”

They crossed a sterilization room and descended a service stair. Pumps beat inside the walls like enormous hearts. At the lower landing, a window opened onto the research ward.

Six sealed chambers stood in a circular depression beneath them, each surrounded by monitors and silver tubes. Figures lay inside.

Six chambers.

Six beds.

Mara found Chamber Six.

Eli lay beneath a thermal sheet, his narrow face turned toward the wall. A mask covered his mouth and nose. Tubes ran to an amber regulator, and a sensor band circled his chest. He looked younger than twelve.

Sela made a sound that was almost a word.

Mara gripped the railing.

“He’s alive,” Nia whispered.

The relief vanished as Eli’s monitor flashed:

**EXPOSURE CYCLE: 4 OF 6**  
**RESPIRATORY RESPONSE: UNSTABLE**  
**CONTINUE**

A second display showed the protocol.

**ADAPTIVE RESPONSE TRIAL 8—ATMOSPHERIC VARIANCE**  
**SUBJECT POPULATION: LOWER-TIER RESPIRATORY CASES**  
**CONTROL MEDICATION: WITHHELD**

“Control medication,” Mara said.

Imani was already opening the stair door. “We need the clinical station.”

A technician looked up as they entered. “Authorized personnel only.”

Sela presented her filtration badge. “Membrane failure in the lower exchange. We were ordered to check your ward intake.”

“This is a research level.”

“Then explain to the Council why your air intake is collapsing.”

The technician hesitated. Imani pressed a tool to the nearest access panel. The lock clicked.

Nia smiled without amusement. “Very authorized.”

They entered the ward.

The air was colder there. Each chamber held a faint distortion around the patient’s face. Mara passed the first and saw a girl no older than nine with a swollen throat. In the next, an old man trembled beneath a foil blanket. A woman clawed weakly at her mask.

Their names appeared on the monitors.

**JUNO ARAM, TIER FIVE**  
**KELL DORR, TIER FOUR**  
**MIRA SETH, TIER FIVE**

A console stood between the chambers, demanding a clinical authorization code.

Nia knelt beneath it. “Manual bypass.”

Sela snatched the technician’s tablet. “The code.”

“I can’t give you that.”

Sela smashed the tablet against the rail. “You can give me the code, or explain to six families why you watched them die.”

The technician stared at her.

Imani pointed to a lower panel. “Open that.”

Nia began undoing the screws.

Mara pressed her hand to Chamber Six. “Eli.”

His eyelids moved.

She touched the intercom. “I’m here.”

“I knew you’d come.”

“Of course I came.”

“Is Mum—”

“She’s here.”

Sela leaned toward the speaker. “I’m here, love.”

Eli’s eyes opened. “You sound angry.”

“I am angry.”

“At me?”

“Never at you.”

A warning tone sounded. Pale vapor entered his chamber.

Imani turned. “Stop the cycle!”

Nia exposed a row of mechanical switches. “Which?”

“Blue, then white. Not red.”

“Why?”

“Red vents the ward.”

Nia flipped blue. Nothing happened. Imani struck white with her palm. The vapor stopped, and warning lights strobed.

“You interrupted the sequence,” the technician said.

“Yes,” Mara answered.

Imani opened a supply cabinet and removed a sealed case marked with the mainland cooperative’s three-wave symbol.

Mara recognized it. “The anti-inflammatory treatment?”

“Mainland-developed,” Imani said. “Stabilized marsh-fungus carrier. It suppresses the response to black-rain exposure without blocking oxygen exchange.”

“Can it help Eli?”

“If we administer it.”

Inside the case were six ampoules and a compact injector. Its indicator was dark.

Nia examined it. “No power.”

“The hospital equipment is incompatible,” Imani said. “It needs a low-voltage pulse.”

Mara looked at the chamber regulators. “Use those.”

“Not without risking pressure shock.”

“Can we risk doing nothing?”

Imani met her eyes. “No.”

They worked quickly. Nia stripped a wire from the console and connected it to the injector. Sela moved between the chambers, checking hands and breathing. Imani reduced the exposure concentration. Mara searched Eli’s record.

The first files listed symptoms and lung capacity. Then she found the classification layer.

**SUBJECT GROUP 6-B**  
**EVALUATION BASIS: OCCUPATIONAL AND CIVIC UTILITY**  
**PRESERVE / SELECTIVE TRANSFER / DISPERSAL**

Her fingers went cold.

The categories were not medical. They matched the continuity module.

She opened the directive.

**Patients assigned to Ward Six-B have been selected from populations with limited political continuity value. Treatment protocols may be withheld where observational benefit exceeds individual survival probability. Families need not be informed of experimental status if disclosure risks noncompliance.**

A table listed the six patients. Beside each was a column titled **EXPECTED SOCIAL LOSS**.

Eli’s row read:

**LOW—DEPENDENT MINOR / TIER FOUR / NO REGISTERED SPECIALIZATION**

Mara’s breath caught.

The mainland treatment was marked **restricted pending Council authorization**. A note explained that broad distribution might reduce labor compliance by improving lower-ring survival expectations.

They had withheld medicine from sick children because healthy children might expect to live.

Mara copied the file to the warm wafer, then to the hospital’s local cache. Static shivered across the wafer, but the records held.

“Are you getting it?” Nia asked.

“Enough.”

She opened the transfer schedule. “The six patients are moving together. Their destination is sealed.”

Imani came beside her. “What does the route say?”

“Two possible access points: central tower research levels or lower loading platforms. Neither is the receiving site.”

Imani studied the transfer justification.

**CONTINUITY PRIORITY / ADAPTIVE MATERIAL**

“That phrase was used in the original atmospheric trials,” she said. “They’re measuring how much the body can tolerate before changing the network’s pressure composition.”

“For the Crown Seal?” Mara asked.

Imani looked at Eli. “For the Crown Seal.”

Nia’s wire sparked. “Injector’s ready.”

Imani loaded the ampoule. “We need to open the chamber without exposing him to ward air.”

Mara searched the controls. “There’s no reserve setting.”

“They disabled it.”

Sela lifted the broken tablet. “Put it back.”

“The regulators are connected to the lower exchange,” Mara said. “If we reopen the secondary vent, we can draw pressure from the corridor.”

“The lower ring will lose what we restored,” Imani said.

“For a minute.”

Sela looked toward the chamber. “Make it count.”

Nia climbed onto the housing and opened a panel. “The intake has a restrictor.”

“Remove it.”

“It’s welded.”

“Break the weld.”

Nia braced her wrench against the coupling. Metal shrieked. Eli stirred.

“Mara,” he said through the speaker.

“I’m here.”

“Is Mum—”

“She’s here.”

“Good.”

Nia broke the coupling. Air hissed through the regulator.

“Now,” Imani said.

Mara keyed the bypass. The chamber door unlocked with a heavy clunk.

Imani opened it a handspan. Nia passed in the injector. Eli lifted his arm, but his fingers missed. Mara reached inside, caught his wrist, and guided the injector into his arm.

The device clicked.

Eli gasped.

“Close it,” Imani said.

Mara dragged him toward the opening. His feet tangled in the sheet. Nia grabbed his shoulders, Sela his legs, and together they pulled him into the ward. Imani sealed the chamber.

For three seconds Eli did not breathe.

Then he coughed.

Air followed.

“Mum,” he whispered.

Sela dropped beside him and wrapped him in both arms.

The other chambers began to sound. Juno’s monitor flashed red. The old man had slid from his bed. The woman struck the glass.

“We can’t leave them,” Mara said.

Imani looked toward the ward door. “We have minutes.”

“Then use them.”

“Six ampoules,” Imani said. “Six patients.”

“Then no one gets left.”

Imani nodded. “Nia, open them in sequence. Sela, get them breathing. Mara, keep Eli conscious and take the records.”

The first chamber opened. Juno fell forward, and Sela caught her. Imani injected her while Nia moved to the next control.

The second patient came out vomiting. The third could not stand. Mara pulled a wheeled oxygen frame between them, one hand on Eli’s shoulder.

“Stay with me,” she said.

“I am.”

“What did you eat today?”

“Half a protein square.”

“That isn’t food.”

“It was blue.”

“That makes it worse.”

He laughed weakly, then doubled over coughing.

The ward door locks began to cycle.

Security had reached the outer corridor.

Sela emerged from the fifth chamber carrying the old man’s arm over her shoulder. “This one needs a stretcher.”

“We don’t have one,” Nia said.

“Then become one.”

Nia and Mara lifted him between them. Imani brought out the final patient, a woman with blood beneath her nose. Her eyes fixed on the screens.

“Are we being transferred?” she asked.

“Not where they planned,” Mara said.

The woman looked at the console. “I was a teacher. They wrote that I was a failed technician.”

She caught Mara’s sleeve.

“You said the records should be open.”

“Yes.”

“Then take mine.”

Mara looked at the six names and six classifications.

“I’ll take everything.”

The ward door burst inward.

Two security officers entered wearing respirators and carrying shock batons. Behind them stood a hospital administrator in a sealed coat.

“Put the patients down,” the administrator ordered. “You are interfering with a continuity trial.”

Sela stepped in front of Eli. “He’s twelve.”

“He is a registered subject.”

“He is my son.”

The administrator glanced at the monitor. “His response has improved. That is clinically valuable.”

Mara felt something inside her settle into a hard, clear shape.

“His name is Eli Venn,” she said. “Not adaptive material. Not low social loss. Eli.”

The administrator raised a hand.

Imani slammed the emergency vent control.

Every light in the ward went white. Air roared from the ceiling. The officers staggered. Nia threw a metal tray into the nearest baton, and electricity cracked across the room. Sela shoved Juno behind a supply cart.

Mara seized the console and pulled out the warm wafer. Records streamed across its surface in broken bands.

“Move!” Imani shouted.

They ran.

The waste-return corridor filled with alarms. Red indicators blinked above every junction. Doors slammed shut in the upper levels.

Tomas’s voice burst through Mara’s radio.

“Mara, answer.”

“We have Eli. Six patients. Security knows.”

“I’m still in the Ministry. The central tower is locking down. Reach the old broadcast lift.”

“We can’t use the lift.”

“Not the lift. The shaft beside it. Lessa marked the route. There’s a maintenance bridge to the tower.”

Imani took the radio. “Are they moving the Crown Seal schedule?”

A pause.

“I don’t know,” Tomas said. “The Ministry is preparing a continuity announcement.”

Mara looked back. Security officers were forcing their way into the ward.

“They’re coming,” Nia said.

The old man sagged against her shoulder. “I can’t.”

“You can,” Nia told him. “Complain later.”

Eli clutched Mara’s sleeve. His breathing had steadied, though every inhale still whistled.

“Do you have the medicine?” Sela asked.

Imani held up the case. “Enough for all of them. If we reach proper equipment.”

“Then we reach it.”
